The object of the Lancashire Platevray Company is to cheapen and improve the Conveyance of Goods and Minerals in that portion of Lancashire lying mainly between the Ribble and the Mersey. It is net denied that railways and canals are numer- ous in the district, but the traffic already occasionally taxes seriously their powers, and is yearly increasing; moreover, the charges they have combined to make are so heavy, as to have been the subject of long-standing:and general dissatisfaction and hitherto unavailing remonstrance. These reasons, added to the necessity that our national indus- tries be not hindicapped in their competition with foreigners, seem to oor.stitute at once a cause and a justification for a new and cheaper system of inland conveyance. Besides the advantage of eheaper carriage, the Pateway Com- pany will be abra to convey goods in better cdndition, more conVeniently, and probably, throughout Lancashire, in a:shorter period of time. If, therefore, lower charges, better condition, greater eon- venience. and sefficient speed be realised, a fair basis for an ire. portaut public convenience is established, and also a probability of a good profit to the shareholders. it is desirable that the attitude of the present carriers towards the various industries of Lancashire should be plainly stated, to serve as a needful justification for offering them competition. It will hardly be found one that the trading public can be ex- pected to submit to, if escape be possible. The English system of allowing carriers to charge "what the trade will Lear," as the phrase is, taken in conjunction with their undisputed power of combination, has resulted in the abandonment of what would prima facie appear an equitable te.sis of charge, viz.: cost, plus a profit. , The carriers have recognised that trade is strong In Lanca- shire, and that. as hen combined, they have only to ask in order to have; aud that however traders grumble they pay, and that distant and often unremunerative portions of their systems can be conTeniently supported by disproportionate charges over this vigorers district. The result is that it is difficult to find in the world, except in small and exceptional cases sir:Lt as the Panama Railroad, equally high rates of carriage; and as a result of the whole, it is believed that along the main line of Lancashis • traffic, namely, that between Liverpool and Man- chester, fifty years ef, railways have increased the cost of car- riage and not materially lessened the time of transit. Yet Lancashire is presernineatly suitable for cheap transpor- tation. The country presents no engineering difficulty, fuel and material are cheap, labour of every description good and abundant, and the stream of trade flows both ways. It should be well understood that the complaint is not of a minute or small fractional overeharge. If the railways its Lancashire stood alone, and were not mixed up with other lines, they would probably only need ts exact, for working and pr-.fit, a sum considerably less than their present charges, , and the p'ateway system contemplates even further aid I material reduction.

It is admitted that the fear of opposition en routes cut of Lancashire by companies having no interest, or only a slight one, in Lancashire, has kept up excessive charges in that county. This arrangement has diverted goods from their teatural channels, and acquiescence by Lancashire traders in such an arrangement is hardly to be expected. The conveyance on the same line of both passengers and goods has increased the cost of the latter in a manner few would suspect. It has also diminished the cargo-carrying power of the line, by demanding a considerable interval be- tween the trains, and has caused needless and costly speed to the heavy traffic in order to clear the lines. These °causes combined have both narrowed the capacity and increased the cost of carrying goods by rail. The proposed plateway will be constructed on land, acquired under Parliamentary powers, in such a way as to admit of wagons being at any point draws on or off. Such wagons can be taken by horses to the point where drawn onlo the plate- way, or from the point where drawn off along the ordinary roads to their final destination. Under this system cotton loaded at the ship side, or immure loaded at the stable, will be I carried along road and plateway and delivered at its ulti- mate destination' (whether mill or farm) without change of vehicle. A great difficulty of the present system, and one that in Lan- espial a seems inseparable from it, is the necessity of removing the goods to and from horse-drawn carts at the stations. This is a somewhat eostly process, by reason of the time lost by carters and their teams, and of the great station space and ap- pliances required for handling the goods. It has always been held to justify. under the name "terminals" a considerable portion ef the heavy charges. This on the plateway system it is hoped in great measure to avoid. Thus the present handling at stations would not take place, and many of the costly appliances incidental to the railway system will be rendered unnecessary. In thus differing from railways by avoiding handling, the plateway will have the advantage of not damaging the goods, and may therefore expect a preference for nearly every article of eemme ce. It needs no argument to show that a distinct money value attaches to the conveyance of bale goods direct from warehouse to ship, or of cotton from ship or-warehouse to mill. This advantage of diminished handling will be noticed to apply to an extensive list of articles of varying values, such as coals, slates, bricks, fruit, liquors, glass, earthenware, Ice., in fact, wilt in some degree affect all, except nninjarable articles, like timber and metals. To the grain trade it will offer the advantage of the aboli- tion of seeks. 'the heavy charge these involve will evidently be saved, when the article can be carries in bulk from the; wharf or warehouse to the miller. The trade in coals for use in the towns will have the advan- tage that the actual cart or wagon delivering at the house or , factory will have been loaded at the pit, thus cheapening car- riage and avoiding breakage at d loss of weight. Branches of the system may be expected to spread over the agricultural distriot, and produce in time come to be loaded at the farm, drawn by horses to the nearest point on the pate- war, and the/ ee conveyed at a low rate and without breaking bulk to the best market. The system promises a much-needed advantage to agriculture, which railwaysl have only conferred to a very limited extent. The remoteness ef the stations,at one end from the farm arid at the other from the consumer, have weighed the p educe with the cost and damage of hand- ling which, added to the high citarge for temple carriage, have debarred the fat mer from his fair participation in the general benefit. tn the plateway system these disabilities may be ex- pected to disappear. from the moderate speed at which it is proposed to work the piateway, the cost atteadant on an expensive system of signal- ling will be avoided. In fact, the plate% ay aims to be simply an improved high road adapted to steam traction. Termini near the centres of the towns, as have been obtained by the railways, would only be sought as they were felt to be required. The facilities afforded by the wagons leaving the piateways at any point, and being thence taken along roads and streets greatly reduces the, importance of having such stations. The saving in capital would be very eensideratile.

PRELIMINARY FI7ID. An undertaking of the magnitude described can only be set on foot by carefully and patiently going through all necessary preliminaries. For this a preliminary fund is required, and it is estimated that £75,000 will suffice. The present object is to obtain subscribers to that fund. It is wanted for the following purposes :- 1. Complete survey, design, and parliamentary estimate of capital. 2. The preparation of such drawings and models as will serve to illustrate the mode of working. L S. The applioation to Parliament for the necessary powers, followed. if those powers are obtained, by 1 applications to the public for the capital. The mode proposed for obtaining this preliminary fund is as follows Each subscriber will, if an Act be obtained, become entitled to have allotted to him at par an amount of stock equal to ten times his subscriptions, and the bum he has contributed will be taken as part payment for the same. There is no doubt that the bill will encounter opposition. A new system of carriage is not likely to receive legislative sanc- tion without searching and adverse criticism. This can only be overcome by submittiog careful designs, accurate estimates, and clear demonstration of a public advantage. The surveys and estimates a, e so far advanced that they wil be completed in time to apply :for a bill in the session 1382-8, when, if the Act be obtained, a public Company, with a reli- able amount capital, will be announced, and the usual machinery for permanent management put into operation. The amount promised to the preliminary fund has warranted the making the surveys and other preparations for depositing a bill (all these are in an advanced state), but further aasistance Is required for meeting the expenses of carrying the bill through Parliament. A " preliminary committee "of five is proposed. The f glow- ing three gentlemen, with power to add two others hereafter, have agreed to constitute the nucleus of this committee, viz.. Mr. Thos. D. Hornby, Mr. John Greenwood, and Mr. Alfred Holt. Messrs. Hawksley and Woods are proposed as engineers, and Mr. J. C. Bees as parliamentary agent; Messrs. Thornely and Dismore solicitors and secretaries in Liverpool, and Messrs. Bircham & Co. solicitors in London. The gentlemen named be'ow (tosether with others) are willing to pro.vide about £35,000 to the fund for preliminary expenses. It is sought by this advertisement to obtain the remainder. -"WHO WILL LOCK THE DOOR?"

A. BALLAD. " C h, who will heir the door, love?" a widow sadly cried, " For you are not at home, love, but in the cold, outside! Am Ito fi'l your place, love? It makes my heart so sore For you to be from home, love, and me to lock the door ! " "Bit must I lock the door. love I cannot, cannot, dear, With yoryso far away, love, and me left weeping here. You may not come again, love, not ever, evermore, Yet oh! itwou'd break my heart, love, if I should lock the door! "how can I lock the door, love, when I am here alose ? My heart has not grown cold, love, I am not turned to stoae ! To-day y.. 0 left your home, love, and you will nevermore B?iturn to give it joy, love; so I may -lock the door! " Yet, if I lock the door, love, how can I, can I, sleep! With you not by my side, love, sad vigils I shall keep! .My memory will ily, love, to happy days of yore. !I Whilst now it is too true, be, that I must lock the door! "So I will look the door, love, for though your cold, cold form • Llea seeping in the tomb, love, where all forget life's storm, I know that it will rice, love, and on some fairer shore Rejoice with me in peace, love; yes! I will lock the door! "But though I lock the door, love, within my silent room The window I s` all seek, love, and p?er into the gloom! For !my soul will faint, love, till Death has borne me o'er, And brought inc to your arms, love, no more to lock the door."

SEQUEL. . • slde the window open, within her ''silent room," The widow sat in-sorrow, enshrined in deepest gloom. She sat with eyes exploring the long dim vale of night. Whose darkness hid all sine of his presence from her sieht. No zephyrs murmured o'er her, but gusts blew rude and bleak, No mem t/tam stooped to hallow the tears that kissed her cheek. She Fat immersed in sadness, o'ercome by bitter grief, For costs who soon lead left her, whose stay bat been too brief ! She sat, and gazed, and stirred not through hours that came and went, As waiting for some message her darling might have sent. , Who, stiff and cold though lying, of life'e dream dispossest, She thought might be returuing to take has' to her rest! Yet, eth. she knew his footfall could reach her ear no more, And fell asleep, repeating "How can I luck the door ?" File slept against the window, her head ucem the sill, And as she slept a glory the chamber seemed to fill. The night wore on all calmly. the stars looked sweetly en. And watched the sleeping mourner, whose grief at last had. gone; For ere the early morning its rosy Washes spread, Her sorrow, ;ike her spilt, had past, and she lay—dead.' Her lovely face teas lifted to give one wistful look 33 re death in solemn pity her grievhg spirit took. WATER FLEAS.—Common as water fleas are, it may Safely be affirmed that there i's no more beautiful or sur- prising sight than that which they reveal to the astonished vision of those who see them for the first time under the reicroecope, nor will the interest thus excited be found to flag under a more extended acquaintance. The exceeding fineness and delicacy of their limbs are specially remark- able, but perhaps the most pleasing and instructive feature they prsemt is the transoarency of their tissues, which allows all the tanations of life to be carried on under the eye. The waole of the digestive proms, from the first in- eepti)n of the food into the month, its trituration by the =redibles its passage through the gullet into the stomach, its eubjeltion to the vermicular action of the intestine, its drg stioi, and final expulsion from the body, are all vhible ; the beating of the heart, the course of the circulation, the movement of the respiratory organs, the contraction of the muscles, the formation of the eggs in the ovary, and their subse.--ittent development, are all clearly presented for our Instruction and wondering admiration.— &ience for AU. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c. The Gadiys estate, comprising 153 a. 129,e, situate about midway between Menai Bridge and Beau marls, was on Thurs- day offered for sale by Messrs. Dew and Son, at the Ball Hotel, Llangetni. The High Sheriff of Lancashire (Colonel M'Coremodale) was the purchaser at £14,256, inclusive of the value of the timber. A woman went into an apothecary's shop the other day with two prescriptions—oue for her husband and the other for her cow. On inquiring the price, she found that she had not money enough for both; then reflecting a moment, she said, "Give me, at all events, the one for the cow. I can send for my hutband's to-morrow." A Cleveland man named Jones has a cow addicted to the uncomfortable habit of switching her tail in his face while milking her. The:other day Jones took the tail and tied it firmly to his leg. The cow, irritated by tlee flies she could rot drive away, started off, and feeling the curious attach- ment to her tail, became frightened and ran. Jones is now walkieg about on crutches and remarking, "About the tenth time I had been hauled around that lot I began to see where I missed it. I oughter tied her tail to her leg and not to rnine." THE FARE, NOT ram HOESE.—The scene was Waterloo I Station on a t-et evening; the hour was late, and a passen- ger just arrived from the Weat of England is discovered ;conversing with the driver of the only hansom left, in which there is an exceptionally knackerish and dilapidated steed. • "Well," Paid the would-be passenger at lengh, "how much I will you take me to Hammersmith for ?" "Twelve-and. ix," responded cabby, without the slightest heaitation. ; "No; no !" returned the traveller, "what are you talking ; about? I did not ask you the price of year horse." One of the most noteworthy features of the recent horti- cultural show at Paris was the superb collection of to ge!,able, produced en the drainage farm of Gennevilliers. Since 1863, ;when the Dr Anage Commission chaee this peninsula as the theatre of the'a• experiments, the letting value of the land has increasel from an average of 425. per acre to an average of 128. per acre. Fruit trees of various kinds thrive in the sandy soil, and the health of the tenants is generally excel- lent. Notwithstanding all this, the inhabitants of the dis- trict of Saint Germain have raised a tremendous outcry agalnet an extension of the system, which it has been pro- ; posed to carry out behind the forest, the lands at Gennevil- ! liers being found by no means sufficiently extensive as being able to purify only a traction of the daily supply. The I municipal authorities have lust expended £4,800 in the pur- lchase of land for a pumping station. THE SYSTEMATIC SLAT/6111TE. OF UNFINISHED STOCK, as a result of straightened circumstances on the part of the I breeder, has been made the subject of a letter to the Irish 11‘...rmers' Ga:ette (Dablin), by Mr. W. Stawell Garnmett, cattle ,aleernan, of Liverpool and Manchester, in the course of which he remarks as follows:—"! allude to the very great national loss annually sustained by the slaughtering of immature cattle and sheep for the prirpoes of so-called food. Any perzon visiting the large fat cattle markets and abat- toirs on this side of the Channel, must be struck with the immense number of young stock—ie ,so-called veal calves,' the majority of which are really either only very recently born, or are animals of the store class, and only in store con- , dition. Then .comes another elate made up of yearlings and lanimals under two years old, neither matured in bane or meat, comparatively speaking, most valuable to the farmer, but almost valueless as food, and merely forced out either to tfLet an immediate sale for some needy owner, or sent by those who, when beef is dear, imagine that anything bovine ehould be at once converted into porter-house steak, utterly ignoring the fact that one or two years' more careful tending would be necessary with the farmer's asaiatar ce ere that de- sideratum could be attained." A similar state of affairs exist with regard to sheep. THE Hay TRIatS AT REaDING.—" After seeing the report of the judges of the Royal Agricultural Sociaty on the trials of hay-driers in the Fobney Meadows, I plid a vleit to the meadows, in company with an extensive hay-dealer, to ex- amine the hay made by the different processes, and judge for ourselves. We came to the conclusion that the hay made by the Gibbs' hay-drier was as good as we could expect it to be, considering all the circumstances, and is at least fifty per cent. better than the hay made by the exhaust fan pro cess. Prime hay cannot be made when it is cut four or five weeks later than it ought to be, especially when the crop is large, as was the case here, at least two tons per acre. The Foeney Meadows was ready to cut in the last week of May, but not being cut till the last week of June or the beginning lof July, by that time the grass was lodged,' the seeds of the coarse grasses ripe, the bottom part of it rotting, and the worms raising the soil into the crop before it was out. When it was dried, the seed, the half-rotten stalks and the soil, were converted into dust and intermixed with the other par- tion. The hay Wes quite as good a quality as anyone had a right to expect, and did not require any spicing to make it palatable, for my horses ate it with avidity; but to ex- pect a prime rick of hay made even with the natural process c f the finest haymaking weather, with the grass cut in the Fobney Meadow in July, 1882, is an outrage on practical farming.—J. DAVIES, Englefield, Reading." —[Mr. [Mr. Jenkins Davies was awarded a special prize by the R.A.S.E. in the farm competition, and his opinion on this subject may there- fore be considered to be that of a thoroughly practical and competent man.]) Dge.s.—THEBULL TERRIER.—This breed of dog Is an offshoot of the bull dog, crossed with the terrier, ard is more popular than the former as it is much better locking. For pluck and determination bull terriers are unequalled, and in the Midlands and South of England they are to be seen almost as frequently as the fox terrier. In general ap- pearance they resemble the terrier, being generally three Iparts terrier and one part bull, but have more power, mus- colar development, and width across the top of the head, which should be long with a sharp muzzle and perfectly level ; jaws not in the least degree underhung, the lower ore to be very powerful; the chest rather wide; neck long; back and loins very strong; shoulders sloping and power- ful ; the hindquarters and thighs in perfect proportion and v.ry muscular; the tail should be fine and whip-like, not carried in a hcop, and it should not be devoid of hair; the coat soft, fine, short.- and lie down close to the skin ; the colour white with black nose and eyes, though good speci- mens of the breed are semetimes known of other colours; the temper cheerful, courageow, and obedient; the expree- sten of e)unteuance thoroughly pleasing and good tern- nered ; and the c Jeri tge jaunty and striking, combined with evident symmetry and great power. The weights of these dogs vary very much, so much so that at all good shows peoarate clesses are provided for both large and small ones. Of the larger variety, dogs are found varying from 25 to 45 lbs., while small ones have been known as low as 91bs. in weight. The most useful terrier for real work is one from 15 to 20 lbs., about 181bs. beitg reckoned a very good size. Bull terriers are very hardy and faithful, with good tempers and St iendly dispositions, without which they are worthless brutes, and should not be tolerated. They are very useful for vermin of the larger sort, will take to water readily, are acted, obedient, and docile which qualities, combined with god looks, make them rival the fox terrier in the estima- tioa of young men, who regard a dog as a neceseary part of , their °refit. They need to be exercised regularly and be groomed with a hand glove daily, as their chief beauty is when in good hard condition. If kept indoors they will make a handsome pet, bat must not be overfed or in any way neglected. Woeets —An animal troubled with worms or internal parasi'es of any kind cannot positively thrive, and as nearly all young dogs are so troubled more or less, it is important ; that they should be got rid of. Some experienced dog ' breeders have advanced the theory that if worms were al- ways got rid of in puppies very few would die of distemper, and ;here Is very great reason to suppose that this is largely true. It is at any rate a fact which cannot be gainsaid, that dogs are better able to fight against that troublesome die. ease when free from parasites. When a dog is seen to be thin and out of condition, though he may eat very well, then worms may he suspected, and the fences should be ex- amined, though this is not by any means a sure guide. There are various worm medicines sold, such as Spratt's, Haldaire'r, Rackham's, &c , all of which are very good, but the great thing is to prepare the dog for the medicine. This is best done by starving it for 18 to 24 hours before the reedicine is given, which should always be first thing in the morning. The evening before let a tablespoonful of linseed oil be administered, and two hours after the worm medicine a good dose of castor oil as .a purgative. This treatment should be repeated two or three times at intervals of three or four days. Feed liberally daring all the time, and give moderate exercise.
HOUSEHOLD PETS.

PrGross —FEEDERS AND Fouerraiss.—The next acces- sories for the pigeon-keeper are feeders and fountain;, and It is better, if possible, to get these of the proper shape, though they may be rather more costly than dishes, but the saving in food will soon compensate for this. The throwing of grain down on the floor of a loft, where it gets mixed with sand or the droppings of the birds, deserves our strongest reprobation. For the food there is nothing better thin the zinc or tin hoppers, which can be bought for a few shillings in the shops. These are of different shapes and sizes, but all are alike in some respects. namely, that the birds cannot perch comfortably on them, that several can feed at one time without inconveniencing each other, and that the droppings from flying birds cannot fall lot° the food. The most common shape is round, with half-a-dozen feeding holes in the Bidet, and a small quantity of food is pat in every day, but the most useful is one with a tray at the bottom, divided by wires into a number of small apart- ments, and with a large V shaped hopper, a foot or more in length, into which a large supply of corn is put. As the birds eat the corn in the tray more falls into it, and thus there is a constant supply, refilling of the hopper itself being necessary only once a week. A domed cover is put on this hopper, which, protruding over the traf, keeps the droppings from falling into it. We have seen wooden ones made to answer the same purpose, and knowing what is re- quired, any one handy with tools can soon make such as which will answer the purpose. Fountains can be used of the ordinary shape, but if so, then they must be placed under a shelf or a cover for purposes of cleanliness. There are fountains made with holes in the side through which the birds can drink, but whatever be the kind used let it be one into which the hand can be got for purposes of cleanliness. Thoze which are filled through a small hole are a great cause of disease, as there is a slime gathers inside which cannot be removed without a great deal of trouble, and even then there Is a risk about it. Ware or tin are equally good so long as the* conditions are observed. In addition to the hoppers and fountains, a bath must be provided, for birds are very fond of having a good wash, and withont it they cannot be kept in proper health and cond:tion. The best kird is a eieare or oblong one, ay thirty inchss by twenty arid three icches d3ep, with sloping sides. Abrat an inch from these

The ob- ject of this is that when they are bathing the splashes may be caught, and thus prevented falling upon the floor. Baths can be placed in the outside aviary in fine, mild weather, but in severe weather this is, of course, impracticable. KEEPING PARROTS.—When there are the means as well as the inclination, a large, well-built aviary is a great source of pleasure, as all kinds of foreign birds can be kept in it; and though the sweet singing of our English birds may not be obtained, yet the brilliant plumage will make up for it. Most people have, however, to be content with something more modest than this, and the great bulk of parrots kept in this country are in the ordinary bell•shaped cages, than which for single birds, nothing can be better. They are constructed so as to allow the inmate to climb about in any direction or in any attitude he may prefer. The light ad- mitted is equal all round, and the wires are strong enough to withstand the attacks of his powerful mandibles. A cage like this is an ornament to any room, and with a good parrot need not be. hid in a corner. The former are sold by nearly all good ironmongers, and the latter can be obtained at reasonable prices from such men as Mr. William Cross. of Liverpool, who imports thousands every year. He is called the Liverpudlian Noah, and well deserves the title, and is also a most trustworthy dealer. At one time it was customary to keep the larger breeds of foreign birds chained to a perch, but fortunately this custom is dying oat, for the chain was a constant source of discomfort to the bird, and also very apt to cause diseases of the legs. The ordinary idea was that a bird on a perch had more liberty than one in a cage, but this le not so, and in a good cige there is more real freedom. Besides, meet parrots when they have got accustomed to their cages can be trusted outside it, but their destructive habits require that they be vrat.thed. Feeding parrots we have already dealt with, and we need now only warn our readers against overfeeding. ItSI3EITS—MOULTING.—Mcat rabbits will now Fe found deep in moult, that is. of course, the older ones. Tnis sometimes affects the animals in various ways, and if any- one is noticed to be hangy and languid, it may safely be concluded that there is something wrong with it, and that it requires attention. In order to secure a good solid silky coat, a little boiled linseed should be given, mixed with a mash. This is the best prepared as foilows :—Take three handfuls of whole linseed and put it into a pan with a quart , of water. Let ibis simmer on the edge of the fire riftil the same is reduced to a pint, when add another half pint of water and let it again simmer for a Acne time. This should then be rill/red with brim until the whole is of a loose, friable nature, when it is ready to be given to the rabbits. It should not, however, be given more than twice or thrice a week, and the effect will be found in the loosening of the old coat and stimulating of the new one. In addition, a good rubbing down with the hand every two or three days will have the effect of bringing away the fur. Rabbits moulting should be kept warns and comfortable, not exposed to draughts, and fed well, as the strain upon the system is much greater than at ordinary times. ing a magnificent surplus. Between 1878 and the present time its exchequer receipts have risen nearly one-half, while; its expenditure has not increased one-fifth. In 1881 there ' was a surplus of revenue over expenditure of a million and a half, of which £700,000 were expended on public works, leaving £BOO,OOO to be. carried forward. The surplus for the present year is expected to exceed a million, bringing up the total surplus to nearly 1,850,000, and next year's surplus is estimated at £580,000. The Government contem- plate expending a large portion of this surplus upon perma- nent public works, and also to about double the amount applied to the encouragement of immigration. Railways are also to be largely extended by the construction of inex- pensive branch lines, and the steam tramway system, which has been so successful in the capital, is to be extended to the suburbs and to other towns. The remarkable prosperity of the colony is all the more striking when contrasted with the stagnation that exists in the neighbouring colony of Victoria, where a strict Protectionist policy is adhered to. New South Wales is the most Free Trade of the Australian colonies, and it is by far the most prosperous. GREAT FIRE AT SYDNEY.—A telegram received through Reuter's agency, dated Sydney, September 23, states that a fire broke out at six a.m, the previous day in the, Garden Palace in this city. Smoke was seen issuing from the dome, and flames burst forth simultaneously from several parts of the building. In less than an hour the whole edifice was a heap of ruins. The dome itself, being filled with hot air, burst with a loud report, scattering fragments to a great dis- tance. All the efforts made to subdue the flames proved un- availing, and nothing was saved. The extent of the Ices is incalculable, as the building contained the offices of many Government departments, including those of the Lands, Railway Construction, Survey, Harbours, and Mines, besides the Technological Museum, the Library of the Linnean Society, and the art collection. The loss of the railway department is particularly serious, as the majority of the surveys will have to be made again, whereby much delay ! will be caused in the construction of the new lines. The ! census statistics were destroyed, and the bulk of the docu- ments burnt cannot be replaced. The origin of the fire' is unknown, but is suspected to have been the work of in- cendiaries, two men having been seen in the vicinity of the building shortly before the fire was noticed.

At a meeting of the delegates of the London Trades Council, on S4turday, it was resolved to instruct the execu- tive to prepare a plan to be submitted to the trades of the metropulis for the purpose of forming an organisation and a fund for supporting workingmen candidates at parlia- mentary and municipal elections. On Monday the delegates representing the North Wales colliers agreed to accept the offer of the masters to grant an advance of 71 per cent. in response to the demand for 15 per cent., and to allow the 71 percent. not granted to remain in abeyance until the general conference to be held next month.

TER LANCASHIRE IRON TBADEL—Buyers appear to be still holding back against the advanced prices,and prices are being fairly well maintained. There were very little doing on 'Change on Tuesday, although the attendance was good. Lancashire makers of pig iron report orders coming in very slowly, but being well sold they are firm at 495. to 50s. per per ton, less 21- per cent., for delivery equal to Manchester, and district brands remain without practical alteration from last week, averaging from 495. up to 51s. and 525. per ton, less 21. Finished iron is only in moderate demand, but the principal makers, who are well sold, are very firm in their prices. Bar iron can, however, be bought at considerably under the top rates at present quoted, and merchants in some cases are underselling to the extent of 2s. 6d. per ton. The average prices for barsdelivered into this district remain at 20 10s. to £6 15s. per ton,

. - THE 'WEATHER AND Tlll3 CORN TRADI3.—The Mark Lane Ea-press says :—.‘• Another week of rough and stormy weather, with a recurrenee cf floods in some district, has further retarded wheat sowing. Very little threshing has been done, and improvements in the condition of grain has been impossible under the circumstances. There has been but little quotable change in the value of home grown bread- stuffs during the week, but it has become difficult to place damp samples even at lower rates. The consumptive (1( mand for flour has decreased, owing to milder weather, but prices for the best makes remain unaltered. There is a fairly good trade for malting barleys, and for a few exceptionally fine samples over 50s has been paid in London. New malt is also in fair request. Old oats are scarce and dear. Beans and peas do not appear to be plentiful, and full rates are easily maintained. Trade kr foreign vher in London remained throughout the week in a dull and lifeless condi- tion. On Friday lower rates had to be accepted to effect sales. In Liverpool, on Tuesday, there was a decline of a penny per cental on most descriptions of foreign wheat, and on Friday prices were barely so good. Flour in London has been difficult of sale throughout the week." THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—The pressure of new business in the coal trade of this district is less, but a gener- ally good demand is still kept up. The men, as a rule, are still working only irregularly, and in the West Lancashire district operations have been seriously interfered with dur- ing the past week by disputes with the underground day- men, who have demanded an increase of wages in proportion to that obtained by the collie's. House-fire coals are still moving off well; for steam and forge coal there is a good inquiry, although the shipping demand is less active than it has been. Burgy, of which the production has been only limited, meets with a ready sale, but slack, if anything, is rather plentiful. Prices at the pit mouth average about as under :"Best coal us, seconds 8s to 9s, and common coals 6s 6d to 7s 6d, according to quality; burgy 5s to 5s 3d, and good ordinary slack 3s 91 to 4s 31 per ton, with special qua!ities at 3d to 6d per ton more. For coke there is a good demand at an advance upon late rates..

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE. THE STATE OF EGYPT.
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE. THE STATE OF EGYPT.

The incendiaries who were arrested in Crete are to be given up to the Khedive by the Sultan's orders. Lord Dufferin reached Cairo on Tuesday evening. His visit is much discussed by both natives and Europeans and there is much speculation as to the special objects to which he will devote himself. There is, however, no reliable statement on the subject put forward. A Cairo correspondent gives an abstract of various pro- posals submitted some weeks ago to Lord Granville by the chief diplomatic and financial representatives of England in Egypt, recommending a reduction in the staffs of the Rail- way, Daira, and Domain Boards. The health of the army of occupation is unsatisfactory and it is too probable that we shall lose by disease a far, larger number of men than were struck down on the fields of battle. Her Majesty has inquired as to the health of the men. It has been stated by a professional journal that a peculiarly virulent form of enteric fever is prevalent among the garrison of Cairo. The 19th Hussars are to be removed from the city to the neighbourhood of some sulphur baths in the desert. THE REVOLT IN THE SOUDAN. The attention of the Egyptian Government is now largely given to the revolt in the Soudan. A number of amnestied officers, who formed part of the force under Arabi have volunteered for service against the mysterious "false prophet." Black soldiers are coming forward in considerable numbers for the Khedive's new army. The Egyptian com- mander telegraphs from Khartoum that he has defeated the rebels at three different points; and that, after he had circu- lated the report that the English troops were coming, the rebels became somewhat demoralised, and Khartoum for the ' moment is relieved ; but he demands immediate succour in men and ammunition. It is announced from Cairo that Sir A. Alison is about to send throe British officers to Upper Egypt, for the purpose of obtaining accurate information in regal d to the Soudan and the possibility of putting Khartoum in a state of defence against the Mandi. A correspondent at Cairo telegraphs that aociordiug to the latest reports the Soudan is not wholly C4l the aide of the "false prophet," but is rather divided among rival chiefs. This would render tho work of pacification easier, and the War Minister is ready to despatch 3,000 men this weeh. THE CONTROL. It is understood that the Government of France refuse to acknowledge that the Joint Control is a thing of the past. The Duclerc Cabinet are at present decidedly opposed to the proposal of Her Majesty's Government that the control of the Egyptian Debt should be undertaken by a single Com- missioner, to be nominated by the Khedive. The French Government .have not at any time, we are told, swerved from their position that the Joint Control still exists, and can be broken up only by the mutual consent of the two Powers which established it. The Council of Ministers have replied to the request of the French Controller General for information as to the grounds on which he was excluded from their meeting. Sir A. Colvin having reiterated his declaration that he will abstain until further orders from attending the Council, Cherif consequently replied to M. Bredif by saying that in view of this declaration, and as the Control could not be carried on by the French Controller alone, he thought it advisable to abstain from inviting him to the Council. THE PROSECUTION OF ARABI.—THE SULTAN'S DUPLICITY. The Prosecution Committee at Cairo have already handed in "true bills " against fifty of the accused rebels, and sent them before the Court-martial. The counsel for and against Arabi are still engaged in preliminaries. The translation of the Arabic documents which were given up by the friends of the prisoner is now complete, and Mr. Broadley, it is said, considers that they prove three poinis. Firstly, that Arabi received direct encouragement from the Sultan, who, ex- pressing entire disregard for the Klifdive, appealed directly to Arabi to defend the interests of Egypt and the rights of the Caliph against foreign aggression. Secondly, that Arabi had the unanimous support of the Egyptian people, as is proved by numerous petitions, bearing the signatures of 25,000 of the mast influential representatives of every class and section of the population—officials, military officers, civilians, merchants, landowners, and Bedouin chiefs. Thirdly, that he had the sanction of the representatives of the religion of the country, as shown by the Fetwa signed by the heads of all the four Mahometan rites, pro- nouncing the deposition of the Khedive, and enjoining the continuance of the war. Among the papers is the text of the Sultan's firman conferring the Order of the Medjidie upon Arabi, in recognition of his zeal, honesty, and in- telligence. This document is dated Yildiz Kiosk the 23rd of June, twelve days after the massacre in Alexandria. Among the letters received by Arabi from Constantinople is one from Mohamed Zafer, a Sheikh who resides at Yildiz Kiosk, and whose influence with the Sultan is a matter of public notoriety. Mohamed Zafer, after announcing that two letters from Arabi premising to guard the Sultan's interest had been presented to His Majesty, says that be has been commissioned by the Sultan to write as follows "As the maintenance of the integrity of the Caliphate is a duty which touches the honour of every one of us, it is in- cumbent on every Egyptian to strive earnestly after the consolidation of my power to prevent Egypt from passing Out of my hands into the rapacious grasp of foreigners, as the vilayet of Tunis has passed; and I repose all my con- fidence in you, my son, to exert all your influence and to put forty every effort to prevent such a thing happening." Nothing new has been made public with regard to the trial of Aralli. The allegation that his present judges were his former accomplices is renewed, with the additional em- bellishment that two of them actually assisted in construct- ing the earthworke at. Kafrdowar. A Cairo correspondent states that the Egyptian Govern- ment has refused Mr. Broadley free access to the prisoners whom Arabi has requested him to call as witnesses in his defence, amongst others, Ali Idagliib, the naval officer who was arrested some time since, and found, by documents upon him, to be an intermediary between the Porte and the National Party. His evidence, the correspondent adds, will be highly important, but had it not been for the inter- ference of Colonel Wilson this essential witness would four days ago have been sent away to Dongola by order of the Commission of Inquiry. A CANINE HEROINE AT. TEL-EL-KEBIR. Land and Water says:—At Tel-el-Kehir, Juno, an old Irish setter, belonging to the Ist Battalion Gordon High- landers, bravely " rushed " into the entrenchments at the head of the Highlanders, and displayed a coolness inside and a courage which elicited universal applause, no more minding the rain of bullets than if she was out snipe shoot- ing. Whether she tackled the enemy we do not know; the rest we can vouch for. But even if her teeth did not meet in any Egyntian leg, her appearance must have spread con- sternation in the rebel ranks. Here, they thought, no doubt, was one of the "2,000 bloodhounds" which Sir Garnet Wolseley was credited with keeping in reserve, and the dauntless pluck exhibited by Juno must have duly im- pressed upon their timid minds the awful consequences which would befall them if they waited for the arrival of her 1,999 canine comrades. They did not wait, but bolted . for their lives, with Private Juno merrily snapping at their ; heels. Juno has long been a pet of the reziment. When . the order came to proceed to Egypt, everyone said that Juno must go too, and go she did, very much to the delight s of the men."

It is stated that the ex-Empress Eugenie has made a will bequeathing her property to Prince Victor Napoleon, son of the present pretender,to the Imperial throne. The Paris express ran into a goods train near Boulogne, the other day. The carriages were damaged, and the per- manent way oloughed up for some distance. Countess Somers, one of the passengers in the mail, was seriously kart. A Constantinople correspondent learns that the Porte has prepared a Note to the Powers, stating that it has executed its pal tof the clauses of the Berlin Treaty, and declaring that the clauses in its favour have not been carried into execution

The North China Herald has published a letter from the King of Corea to the Emperor of China, in which His Majesty announces that he has agreed to a treaty of com- merce with Great Britain, of a similar tenor to that which he had previously concluded with the United States. A severe earthquake has occurred near Aleppo, in the north of Syria. Several villages were destroyed, and a la,ge number of lives were lost; but so many of the home- less people have fled to neighbouring villages that it is lin- possib'e to form even an approximate idea of the extent of the disaster. The earthquake extended over a wide area. No cmfirmation of the report current at Alex indria that cholera was increasing at Mecca has been received at Cairo. On the contrary, the British Consul at Jedda tele- graphed on Tuesday that according to unofficial advices received from Mecca cholera had disappeared from that city. The statement telegraphed from Madrid with regard to the intentions of the Cabinet to detain the Cuban refugees is now declared, by the same authority, to have been inaccu- rate. The Cabinet, it is now said, has come to no decision on the matter, and is" understood to be actuated by a con- ciliatory disposition." A court of inquiry has been held at Gibraltar.

FIGHTING IN THE TRANSVAAL : 300 BOERS SLAIN.—A Times Durban telegram says :—Natives from the Transvaal report two engagements between the Boers and Mapoch, re- sulting in the defeat of the Boers with great loss. The natives state that Mapoch sent a decoy party, who retreated after skirmishißg, drawing on the Boers in pursuit through a neck, where the Caffres fell upon them and defeated them with a loss of three hundred men. The subsequent en- gagement occurred in the open, when the Boers were again defeated with loss, having to retire to the laagar. The Transvaal Caffres are jubilant, saying that they will pay no taxes to anyone but Shepstone. A Moscow TEELTIZEI SET ON FIRE: DASTARDLY CON- DUCT or AN AfiTOß.—During a rehearsal at the Grand Theatre, Moscow, a day or two ago, aloud explosion WAS heard, and immediately afterwards fire and smoke were seen issuing from the wings. Assistance was speedily at hand, and the flames were soon extinguished. At first it was be- lieved that the affair was due to Nihilists, but it now appears to have been the work of an actor recently discharged from the theatre, who formed the design of setting fire to the building by means of a bomb placed underneath the wooden stairs leading to the stage. Fortunately the explosion occurred at a time when most of the officials eonnected with the theatre were at their posts. _ -

div.head: BURGLAR'S ENCOUNTER WITII A BRAVE WOMAN AT LYTHAM
div.p: A BURGLAR'S ENCOUNTER WITII A BRAVE WOMAN AT LYTHAM

At the Manchester Assizes, on Niontla y, before Mr. justice Day, John Kelley, aged 37, a private in the 3rd Lancashire FLsiliers Militia, was indicted for having, at Lytham, on the night of the 15th September, broken into the house of Edward Handley, with intent to steal. Mr. Shea prosecu- ted ; the prisoner was not defended by counsel. The case possessed some rather amusing features. On the night in question he broke into the prosecutor's house, searched various rooms, took away an umbrella, collected several things in the scullery, and was coming down the attic stairs when Mrs. Handley, who had been awakened by the priso- ner's proceeding-s, confronted him. He then made some pretence of being in liquor. No doubt he had had drink, but it was held that he was not so drunk as he seemed. If intoxicated, he went about his work, as Mr. Shea put it; in a very sober-like way. Seeing prisoner was a militiaman, Mr. Handley went out to acquaint the officers at the camp, leaving his wife to keep guard over him with the poker. When asked if she had this weapon, Mrs. Handloy naively replied, "I just had it if I required it." The prisoner asked her to let him go, saying he knew he was in the wrong house, but she told him she could not let him go. Mrs. Handley further stated that she heard the prisoner try the bedroom door ten minutes before she got up. She was awakened by the noise and aroused her husband, but he said " she was such a nervous creature?' The sergeant who arrested the pris,mer was of opinion that lie was not drunk. The prisoner's defence was that he was in liquor at the time, and had no felonious intent. He had been teetotal for some time, had saved money to send to his wife and " four weakly children," but happening to meet some friends he had drink with them, and got drunk with "liquor and beer mixed," and eventually'found himself in custody for an offence which he had no knowlege of having committed. The jury acquitted the prisoner of any intention to steal, which was equivalent to "not guilty." He was thereupon discharged, the judoremarking that it was a fortunate escape for him.

div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. John Murphy, one of the Irish Sub-commissioners, dial at Skibbereen ou Tuesdiiy morning, aged 66. Mr. Parnell, replying to an invitation to be present at the opening of a new bridge at Cork, named after him, has tele- graphed that his doctor will not allow him to travel, and that he must postpone addressing his constituents until the session is over.

_ The peasants in several districts of Clare are already suffering severe privations. The potato crop has failed, and there has been a very fatal epidemic amongst pigs. A cor- respondent of the Irisit Times, ho has been eXploring the county, states that it presents a most melancholy appearance. Fields and meadows are deluged with water, and men, women, children, pigs, calves, cows, dogs, and chickens all herded together in miserable dwellings. The Rev. P. White, parish priest at Miltownmilbay, writes to the Freeman's journal stating that in two months 100 families in his parish will be utterly destitute. A CURIOUS OMISSION—In its report of the examination before theCiray Committee of Mr. Johnson, a shorthand writer employed by the Crown in the prosecution of Patrick Walsh, the Freeman's Journal says :—" It was elicited from Mr. Johnson, on cross-examination by Mr. Sexton, that in sentencing Patrick Walsh Judge Lawson had omitted the usual words that you be hanged by the neck until you are dead,' And, therefore, as was remarked by some members of the Committee, Patrick Walsh had been hanged without having been sentenced to be hanged. This state- ment created somewhat of a sensation among the Committee, more especially as it was pointed out that all the reporters present in the court agreed as to this omission from the sen- tence, and that the learned Judge himself never questioned the fact."

div.head: DISASTROUS COLLIERY EXPLOSIONS,
div.p: DISASTROUS COLLIERY EXPLOSIONS,
LOSS OF FORTY-FIVE LIVES.

On Tuesday morning a very serious colliery explosion occurred at the Parkhouse Pit, owned by the Clay Cross Company, about five miles from Chesterfield. The pit em- ploys a large number of men, but fortunately all the hands were not down at the time, or the loss of life would have been far greater. Although it was an "off day," about 100 men descended to work, intending to labour on stock in the bends, but at ten o'clock about 40 of them came up the shaft, and immediately afterwards a terrific explosion, which was heard for miles, too place. The heading of the shaft was blown high above the pit • bank, and the mouth of the pit was wrecked. Exploring parties were soon at work, but the extent of the workings, and the fact that all the passages were filled.with debris and afterdamp, made the attempts to reach the men extremely difficult, and it was not till after some hours had elapsed that a portion of those underground were reached, all being alive, but suffering much from tin effects of the foul air.

A telegram despatched from Sheffield, on Wednesday night, says :—The explosion turns out to have been more disastrous in its character than was at first anticipated. There are at least forty-five miners missing, and it is feared that their lives have been sacrificed without exception. The exploring party that descended the pit late on Tuesday night, under the direction of Mr. Laverack and Mr. Mills, mining engineers', made a most important discovery—that the explosion had not really sprung from the workings lying between the Parkhouse shaft and the Clay Cross shaft, but in the more remote stalls on the north side of the pit. The explorers, who have shown the utmost fearlessness, turned to the left after descending the Clay Cross shaft, and got within 1,700 yards of the Parkhouse shaft without seeing any very great evidence of the explosion, except heaps of dust and displaced timber, but at this point they had to force open some doors, and then found the air so impure that it was scarcely pos- sible to proceed. They persevered, however, and now began to find numerous evidences of the explosion. About three hundred yards on the Clay Cross side of the shaft, where the two sons of Mr. Dunn, the underground manager were found, the roadway was completely wrecked, and in places the bind and earth had to be dug out before the party could continue along the path. In this locality, not far from the bottom of the Parkhouse shaft, several masons and brick- layers had been engaged in putting down new engines to increase the hauling power in the pit, and here the damage was very extensive. Within a short distance of this place eleven bodies were counted, none of them were greatly dis- figured, and there is no doubt that the men discovered in this spot had been overcome by the afterdatnp. Several other bodies were found near the Parkhouse shaft, and these were more seriously burnt North of this shaft the works extend more than a thousand yards, and it was in this remote part of the pit that the explosion originated and worked the most devastation. The coal in the left portion of the north workings has ,been got out, and ininers have not laboured there for some time; indeed boards had been fixed warning the colliers that that portion of the pit was dangerous, and it was scarcely ever visited except by the fire trier going his rounds. On the right hand of the roadway the coal has been got lately, and the miners worked in a part known as the cross cuts. When the exploring party reached here Dr. Chawner divided the men into small working gangs, and cautioned the men to use the greatest care, but on en leavouring to enter the :benks they were driven back by the impure air and nitrous gases. The seam bf coal dips considerably at this point, and the cross cuts are worked in flats or floorings of different heights, each containing several stalls. None of the men working here had up to noon been recovered, for owing to the foul air it was impossible to get beyond the Parkhonse Shaft. A later exploring party was organised, and they endeavoured to reach the cross cuts, bat with what success has not yet transpired. The cause of the explosion has net been ascer- tained. Early on Tuesday morning a large number of miners expressed their willingness to aid the work of exploration. The services were readily accepted, for there was a long distance of roadway to clear before the bodies could be reached, and 30 of the 40 men entered the pit. The majority of the men employed at Parkhouse were connected with benefit societies, and the agents were in the neighbourhood on Tnesday ready to satisfy the claims of the bereaved families.

ACTION FOR THR Loss OP A HITSBAND.—At the Bolton County Court, on Wednesday, Mrs. Jane Ileyes brought an action to recover damages under the Employers Liability Act from Messrs. Joon Booth and Son, cotton manufacturers, Turton Bottoms, for the loss of her husband, who died from injuries received' whilst in the employment of the defendants. Mr. Wharton appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Allen (of the firm of Messrs. Partington and Allen, Manchester) ap- peared for the defendants. Plaintiff's husband had been employed as a fire heater and engine tenter, and on the 31st of January the piston rod of the engine was blown through the cylinder and deceased was struck. No evidence was forthcoming as to the cause of the accident, but deceased was found lying in a pool of blood. It was pointed out that an inspection of the machinery had taken place within a month of the accident, and everything had been done to keep the engine in order. The jury returned a verdict for the defendants. Mr. Allen said the Messrs. Booth did not apply for cost s.

_ An English stock-jobber, well known upon 'Change as a man of unexampled parsimony, although possessed of an immense fortune, one day met a very poor man, one of his own relations. "Come hither, George," said the miser, "do you know I have just row made my will, and remembered you handsomely, my boy ?" " God bless you, brother," said the grateful man, "you will be rewarded for so charitable an action, for you could not have thought of a more dis- tressed family." "Are you indeed so very poor, George?" "Sir, my family's starving," said the man, almost crying. " Harkye, then, George, if you will allow me a good dis- count, I will pay you immediately." We need not add that the telms were accepted of, while they parted equally pleased with the bargain they had concluded.

div.p: impERIAL PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MoteDay. THE e, vCCUPATION OF EGYPT.--Sir S. NORTHCOTE gave , „nice of his intention, on as early a day as he can obtain, cab attention to the present employment of Her Majesty's fywrees in Egypt, and to move that the House is entitled to a , I,er explanation of the nature and porposed duration of , i!len employment and of the estimated cost thereof than it "alyet received. : , rtenever Coups—The SECRETARY for War announced "0 the House that he was considering the feasibility of con- rerun,' one or more companies of the Royal Engineers into a reeallwaY corp. , 'JIB CLOSURE.—kfter a large number of questions on segYntian subjects had been put and answered, the debate on 'e proposed Closure resolutions was resumed by Lard JOHN ANNERS, who moved that in any division under the first !Alle the voting should be taken by ballot, a proposal which litaPolled the PRIME MINISTER to remark upon the touch- spectacle of a member of the High Tory party stand- elllg op "with unparalleled generosity to throw over other sections of the House the shield of secrecy." The proposal Was rejected by 139 to 55.—The SPEAKER ruled that the atext three provisos standing in the names of Mr. Stanley ighton, Mr. C. Seely, and Mr. Ritchie were out of order. 4 proposal that the Closure resolution should not coma into aPeration during the present session of Parliament eves defeated.—There being no other amendments on the first rule, the main question was put by the SPEAKER' upon s "leich Sir S. NORTHCOTI moved the rejection of the rule. 4.0 referred to the great achievements which the House had trade under the old system. He did not deny there was a tliaease, but he contended that the cure was worse than the roPlaint. He made a despairing appeal to the Irish mem- iers not to believe that the Government had any intention '0 protect small minorities, and argued that the effect of the Cale would be to embarass and destroy individual effort in the House.—Sir WILLIAM HARCURT replied in a character- tally incisive speech, and the House rose at five minutes 1 , after midnight. ~ T HOUSE M ON 010. F COMMONS.—TUESDAY. NOTICE O —Sir WILFRID LAWSON gave notice motet when Sir Stafford Northcote moved his resolution on ' „the Egyptian question he would more as an amendment, ; That the House, while recognising the necessity of fuller mformation, was of opinion that no further military opera- tions in that country should be sanctioned which were cal- culated to interfere with the government of Egypt by the ' EgYptians." SERYICE IN THE SOUDAN.—In reply to Mr. Herbert, Mr. k;_rfteaeßeas said the report in the papers to the effect that British officers and men were being allowed to volunteer for service in the Soudan was without foundation. THE DUAL CONTROL IN EGYPP.—Sir CHARLES DILKE, in ..rePIY to Sir H. D. Wolff, stated that confidential negotia- uons were taking place between the Government kind the Government of France with regard to the dual control in Egypt, but he could make no statement with regard to them , at present. . THE CUBAN REFUGEES.—It was stated by Mr. E. ASHLEY : toat the Colonial Department had asked for a full state- itient from the Governor of Gibraltar, Lord Napier, as to 1 the Cuban refugees given up to Spain, and the Colonial i Secretary would think it is duty t 3 punish with due severity ' aoy Person who from negligence or otherwise had contri- buted to bring about this deplorable error. 1 THE PROCEDURE RULES.—Lord LYMINGTON resumed the ' debate on Sir Stafford Northcote's motion to reject the first I resolution.—Sir W. DILKI, in'a vigorous speech, traced the I oecessity of the Closure to the mismanagement of public business by the Government. Referring to the manifesto by Lord Randolph Churchill, the late Conservative Whip Observed that this was not a very felicitous time to force the Government to appeal to the country.—Mr. BROADHURST found in the prolongation of the present debate convincing argument in favour of the Closure.—The debate was con- tinued in a very thin House by Mr. Herbert, Sir H. Holland, Mr. Thompson, Colonel Kennard, Mr. Meller, Colonel . bawnay, Mr. Lewis Fry, Sir Herbert Maxwell (who was arlDported by the presence of four Conservative members), . Air. Lee, Mr. P. Phipps, Mr. Dixon-Hartland, Lord Ernie', Mr. Beresford Hope, Mr. C. Phipps, Lord George Hamilton, and other members, chiefly rising from the Conservative benches. The debate was adjourned on the motion of Mr. s ASHMEAD,BARTLETT. . HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. ' THE CLOSURE.—MT. ASHMEAD-BARTLET resumed the de- . hate upon Sir Stafford Northcote's motion for the rejection of Mr. Gladstone's first procedure resolution. He supported the motion, as also did Mr. Northcete, Baron Henry de Worms, Mr. Justin M`Carthy, and Mr. O'Connor Power, 'while Mr. Macliyer, Mr. Majoribanks and Mr. W. E. Bax- ter opposed it and spoke in favour of the resolution.—Mr. GLADSTONE raid the proposition • before the House was this, that, after having discussed the first resolution for seven- teen nights and taken eeventeen divisions upon it, they ahould on the invitation of the hon. baronet the member ter North Devon sweep this resolution into oblivion, and thus lose altogether the result of all their labours. The right hon. gentleman preceeded to reply on the debate rather ' than await another evening, because he and his colleagues did not think that this was an expedient or a useful expen- diture of public time. He repudiated the suggestion that Ithe country took no interest in this subject. The country could riot understand the redundancy of their speech and the small amount of work they did, and they were calling upon them now to talk less and do more. With regard to all the evils which had been prophesied by the Opposition, his belief was they would not arise, but if they did arise the ,e'eent ry would soon see that such evils did not prevail. The vover nment had strongly and steadily refused, and should Continue to strongly and steadily refuse, to accept amend- roents which would be inconsistent with the great purpose of thes e resolutions. The House shortly afterwards ad- journed.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THURSDAY. LORD DIIFFERIN'S MISSION.—The Prime Minister was asked to statd generally the object of Lord Dufferin's mission to Egypt and the nature of the arrangements proposed to be made for th e settlement of that country.—Mr. G-LADSTONE replied that the object of the mission was to conduct, with the assistance of Sir E. Malet, the necessary communica- tions with the Egyptian Government in respect to the future arrangements for the security of Egypt. If any of the arrangements wers completed before the prorogation they Vould he communicated to Parliament. The right hon. gentleman informea Sir W. Lawson that the Government had no responsibility for the telegram alleging that the dual control had been abolished, and he could not say if it

was authentic. SIR C. R. WILSON.—Mr. ARTHUR ARNOLD, who had asked a question as to the c)nnection of Sir C. Rivers Wil- eon, a civil servant, with the Eagle Pass aped Air Line Rail- was informed by the PRIME MINISTER that Sir C. R. Wilson had resigned the office of trustee to the undertaking after learning that the propriety of his holding the appoint- 'tent had been callcd in question by the House of Com- mons. , THE aosunn.—The Closure debate was resumed by Lord SANnoN, who insisted that the statement made by the Prime Minister on the previous day in reference to local self- government in Ireland was meant to hold out hopes to the Irish party of the gravest and most serious kind. The noble rerd demanded to know what was this great new scheme with which the right hon. gentleman was about to Convulse Ireland or to calm the anxieties of the Home Rulers.—ln the course of the evening there were speeches by Mr. G. Russell, Mr. Brodrick,Mr. Slagg, Mr. I'. C. Bruce, Mr. Wodehouse, Cockran-Patrick, Mr. Jackson, Mr. Stanton, Mr. O'Shaughnessy, Mr. E. Clarke, and Mr. W. Fowler, and the debate was again adjourned.
