div.head: PRIME MINISTER AT THE MANSION HOUSE.
div.p: THE PRIME MINISTER AT THE MANSION HOUSE.

The customary banquet of the Lord Mayor of London to the Cabinet Ministers, Her Majesiy's judges, and others, Was given, on Thursday night, at the Guildball.—Earl Northbrook, in responding for "The Navy," dwelt upon the Bkill displayed in taking possession of the Suez Canal.— 'The Army " was appropriately represented by the Secre- tary for War, and in acknowledging the toast Mr. Childers Made some interesting historical allusions, noticing the fact that Gibraltar was taken on the same day, one hundred Years ago as Tel-el-Kebir was fought this year, and that on the same day of the same month in. 170 Quebec fell into the hands of General 'Wolf.—" The health of Her Majesty's Ministers" was responded to by the Prime Minister, who accept the compliment not as being paid to one political A. Party or another, but because the Government •cras repre- ; centative of the power of our great empire, and received credit for a sincere endeavour to serve their country. The right, hon. gentleman reviewed the work of the Government since their last accession to power. Referring particularly to Ireland, he pointed out that the operation of remedial measures was gradually taking bold of the minds of the People of that country, and they were acquiring a con- viction that there Seas in the Parliament and the people of this country a desire to do them justice. Mr. erlad- ,,, stone noticed with thankfulness the remarkable. achieTe- , olents which have been wrought for us by our gallant fellow-countrymen in Egypt. We were, he said, at every moment exposed to new and recurring anxieties, but in regard to coming measures he looked forward with cheer- ful anticipation. Earl Granville responded for the House of Lords, Mr. Justice Denman for Her Majesty's Judges, Mr. Trevelyan for the House of Commons, and the Solicitor General for the Bar.-
r

On Thursday morning, a widow named Fenton corn- I !nitted suicide by throwing herself over a suspension bridge I In Balgay PubliC Park, Dundee. She fell a distance of 30 feet, and was killed on the spot, her body being terribly Fnutilated. The woman's mind was affected by the loss of I her husband, a mechanic, who was scalded to death.in a I Dundee millpond several years ago. The Freeman's Journal makes the following extraordi- nary allegation against Sir garnet Wolseley, on Thursday ifhorning-,in the course of an article protesting against the jeedom of the city of Dublin being conferred upon him. , We do not speak -without knowledge when we say that it ls a matter of common gossip that last year, during the debates on the Coercion Bill, Sir Garnet Wolseley expressed the hope that if Irishmen revolted he might be sent to quell the disturbance in order to teach them what war really meant. We do not speak without knowledge, when Lve assert that Sir Garnet Wolseley declared, when going to ! 'ls:pt, that he only felt one alloy to the pleasure of that anlitary promenade, and that was, that the Irish might take advantage of his absence to rise and he not there to tllPPrese them.",

M ISCELLANEOUS. Lord Derby is to be entertained by the Manchester Reform Club on the 13th December. Amelia Jordan, for whose release from penal servitude strenuous efforts have lately been made, has been liberated on a ticket-of-leave from Streatham Prison. A scholar at Clifton College, on being taken to the head- master for punishment, drew a knife and stabbed him in the shoulder. Mr. Wilson was not seriously injured. Fred. Archer, the well-nown jockey, while riding over a hurdle at Newmarket on Saturday, where his brother was engaged in training operations, fell from his horse, and was dragged some distance. Samuel Phippin, the Somersetshire farmer, who recently, without any conceivable motive, shot two men dead, has been tried at the Bristol Assizes. His insanity was estab- lished, and he was committed to a criminal lunatic asylum for life. Jean Luie, who was convicted of perjury after the Tich- borne trial, having written to Mr. Gladstone asking his assistance in recovering documents confiscated by the Treasury, has received a reply to the effect that Mr. Glad- stone is unable to comply with his request. The official announcement is made that the Queen has ap- proved of the elevation of' Sir J. Beauchamp Seymour, G.C.8., to the Peerage by the title of Baron Alcester, of Alcester, in the county of Warwick, and of Sir Garnet Wolse- ley, G.C.8., by the title of Baron Wolseley, of Cairo, and of Wolseley, in the county of Stafford. It is stated that the Prime Minister has consented to be nominated as:president of the new National Liberal Club. Among the speakers at a preliminary meeting to be held on the 16th inst., in addition to Lord Northbrook, who will pre- side, are the Marquis of Hartington, Sir William Harcourt, the Attorney-General, the Solicitor-General, and the lion. Evelyn Ashley, M.P. .LIVERPOOL LIBERALS AND MR. GLADSTONE. The leaders of The Liberal party in Liverpool have resolved to invite the Premier to a public banquet in his native city in celebralaon of the approaching fiftieth anniversary of his entry intO Parliament. It is hoped that Mr. Gladstone will be able to visit Liverpool either on his way to Midlothian towards the end of December, or on his return journey. RELEASE OF THE REV. S. F. GREEN. The Rev. S. F. Green was released on Saturday evening from Lancaster Castle, and proceeded by the 8.50 train to Morecambe, ar- riving there about nine o'clock. Notwithstanding that his release was not generally known, he was identified by several persons at the station, but no demonstration was made, and he at once proceeded to his wife's lodgings. He appeared to be in fair health and excellent spirits. Another accident has befallen a sleeping car which was travelling at full speed on the Highland railway on Satur- day. The car suddenly left the rails, it is believed, at some points, and the result was that the wheels were forced off, and in this fashion the van proceeded unnoticed by the engine driver until the train was pulled up in the ordinary course of stopping at the platform of a station. The pas- sengers were severely shaken, but fortunately no serious iiajuries were sustained. The accident was the cause of a suspension of the traffic for several hours. EXTRAORDINARY RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—An extraordinary' railway accident occurred at Hanley, ou Monday morning. About eleven o'clock a mineral train was, proceeding on Earl Granville's railway from some of his lordship's col- lieries to his ironworks, and when near a level crossing the engine, whilst proceediag at a rapid speed, struck the points and performed a complete somersault, pulling the trucks loaded with coal on the top of it. Some of the trucks were smashed into matchwood, but the driver and stoker miracu- lously escaped uninjured. The Government Inspector of explosives has prosecuted Messrs. Whittle, ironmongers, of Whitehaven, for importing 22,0001 b. of dynamite which had not been purified in ac- cordance with the licence granted by the Home Secretary. It was stated that the dynamite, which had been imported from Rottemlam, would not stand the authorised heat teat, and that it had been re-shipped to Germany at a serious cost to the importers. A fine of £5O was imposed. PRISONS AND Prasoeriarts.—A return has been issued, moved for by Sir Massey Lopes, showing for ten years before and three years after the transfer of the prisons to the State the expenses of local prisons now borne on the vote for prisons. This shows that, as against an average expenditure per prisoner of £3l 7s 9d during the ten years preceding transfer to the state, the average in 1878-9 was £224s 4d; in 1879-80, £25 2s; and in 1880-81, £26 Sc 3d. The number of prisons, which was 129 at the end of 1867 and 113 at the end of 1870, was only 67 at the close of 1880. MURDER IN BRADFORD.—Another murder is reported from Bradford, which took place late on Saturday night. The victim is the wife of a man named James Bradley, who is said to have been idle and sottish, and dependent on his wife for home and sustenance. She was a rag- sorter, earning Bs. per week, and becauae she did not give him as much mcney as he desired on Saturday evening, it is supposed that the ill-usage which followed resulted in her death. A post-mortem examination showed that death had resulted from an extensive fracture of the skull, caused by a violent kick. A SINGULAR CASE.—A singular case was mentioned to Mr. Justice Day at the Manchester A ssizes on Tuesday. At the July assizes two men were brought up charged with assaulting a woman at Oldham, but the trial had to be post- poned owing to the absence of the prosecutrix, whose recog- nisances were entreated. It was now stated that there was every reason to believe that the woman had been induced by prisoner's friends to go to America. The Judge said he should give the police time to bring the woman back, and the men would be kept in custody till the assizes in January. ANOTHER RITUALIST'S LIVING DECLARED VACANT.—The Bishop of Worcester has forwarded a notice to the patrons of Holy Trinity, Bordesley, Birmingham, announcing that under the Public Worship Regulation Act the benefice is vacant, the three years from the date of the monition against the vicar, the Rev. W. Enraght, having expired. The action of the bishop was altogether unexpected by the parishoners, who, during the past few months, have been making strenuous efforts to provide a church for Mr. Enraght, should he be compelled to leave Holy Trinty, and promise of contributions amounting in the aggregate to nearly £6,000 hard already been made. The parishioners have issued an extensively-signed pi otest against thr " un- canonical, unconstitutional, and cruel action being taken to remove the vicar". REMARIIABLE ESCAPE.—On Monday morning four youths employed in the drying stove of Messrs. Tomlinson's fulling mills, situate at Gnat Bank, just off the Bury and Rochdale Old Road, near Heywood, narrowly escaped death. About half-past nine o'clock they were engaged in the drying stove, when the roof suddenly fell in, and they were buried in the debris. All were got out badly shaken, and their bodies scratched by the tenter hooks. The scratches were poisoned by the arsenic which is used in the business, and Dr. Tor- rap took steps to counteract the effects of the poison. The injured youths are Abel Br ierley,- Samuel Hinclicliffe, Wil- liam Richardson, and David Butterworth. The accident is attributed to the timbers of the roof having dried in to such an extent as to be to weak to support the slates. RAILWAY COLLISION AT WANDSWORTH. A collision occurred on Monday at Wandsworth Common, to the North- W'estern train from East Croydon, due at Victoria-about 9 o'clock. A Brighton company's engine which was on its way from Brighton to Battersea Yard, had been stopped by signal, and into this, from some cause at present unexplained, the Croydon train ran. The driver and fireman of the latter were severely cut and bruised, and had to be removed to the local hospital, where they are reported to be progressing favourably. The guard's brake next to the engine was tele- scoped, but the guard himself escaped with his life, though much hurt. Eleven persons were so injured as to require medical attention' but several others received a severe shak- ing. The work of clearing the line was care id on through- out the night, and traffic was resumed earl' on Tuesday morning. All those injured, except the driver and stoker, are now at their homes. SHOOTING A RIVAL AT HOLYNTELL.—A shocking occur- rence took place ltte on Saturday night, on the mountain table land known as Penybalt. Shortly before midnight some persons returning from Holywell met on the ascent a man who cried out that his brother had been shot. Proceed- ing further they found the body of Edwd. Thomas, labourer, of Bagillt, lying on the *roadside. The police and a doctor were summoned, and the latter pronounced life to have been extinct for some time. Subsequent inquiries led to the arrest of a young man residing in the neighbouring cottages on the charge of murder. The motive of the crime is said to-have j been ealoosy, the prisoner haying about last June married a young woman, who is alleged Co have been engaged to deceased's brother, Thomas Thomas. The two brothers were walking about near the prisoner's house or. Saturday night, when he suddenly came up with it gun, and in a state of excitement shot Edward instead, it is presumed, of his rival Thomas. Deceased's breast Was riddled with shot. THE BETTING ON MANCHESTER RacEcounen.—The pro- ceedings instituted by the Watch Co.mnittee of the Salford Corporation with the object of repressing open betting on the racecourse have been settled without going to the length of a public trial. The cases were to have been heard at the Salford Borough Court, on Tuesday, but by an arrangement which was entered into by M 7. Russell, Q.C., M.P., on be- half of the defennants, with Mr. Leresche, who appeared for the prosecution, all the summonses were adjourned sine die, with the exception of two, in which persons were charged with using a box and a stool for purposes of betting on the racecourse, thereby bringing themselves clearly within the cope.s of the Betting Act. In each of these cases a fine of £lO and costs was imposed. With regard to the other cases, it is understood that if the law be not further violated the summonses issued will not be put in force. An assurance was given on behalf of the Racecourse Company that they would carefully co-oporate with the 'police in preventing infractions of the law. STOPPING RAILWAY TRAINS.—The accident to the Pull- man car on the Midland Railway brings to light a serious defeot in the Regulation of Railways Act, 186$. By that Act (section 22) companies are required to provide and maintain "in every train which carries passengers, and travels more than twenty miles without stopping, such effi- cient means of communication between the passengers and the servants of the company in charge of the train as the Board of Trade may approve." A penalty of £5 is imposed on the passenger who starts the communication without sufficient cause; but, with singular want of reciprocity, no penalty is imposed on the company which refuses to answer the call. Neglect to stop a train on the call being made, if it conduced to the death or injury of a passenger, might giro ground to a civil action; but, if the company choose to run this risk, and are only careful to provide an apparatus for signalling in working order, they may take notice of the signal or not as they like. The passenger, in fact, is in pre- cisely the same position as Glendower in regard to the spirits He can "call," but whether there will be any result is quite another question.—Law Journal.

Two men were killed at a colliery at Rhondda on Monday evening through the breaking of a guide rope. At Croydon, on Wednesday, John Llewellyn Cooper, accountant, was committed for trial on a charge of forging cheques to the amount of £2,000. Lord Northbrook, the First Lord of the Admiralty, has consented to take the chair at the meeting to be held at the Westminster Palace Hotel, on the afternoon of the 16th inst., for the formation of a National Liberal Club. Several other members of the Government have promised to take part in the preliminary meeting. The Board cf Trade returns issued on Wednesday show that the imports for October increased £2.844,702, und the exports decreased £363,368, as compared with the corres- ponding month of last year. For the first ten months the imports increased £13,637,086, and the exports in?,reased £9,951,864, as compared with the first ten months of 1881. In referenee to rho St. Luke's mystery, the police seeffl to have got bold of an idea that there has been a homicide and a cremation. for a despatch received on Monday night says they have in their searches of the house discovered some bones over one of the ovens. There is much excite- ment in the district. The officers, non-commissioned officers, and men who have beea selected to represent the Indian troops who took part in the Egyptian campaign, landed at Portsmouth on Wednesday. They were very cordially reteived by a large crowd which had assembled. The 87th (Royal Irish Fusiliers) came home in the same ship. SHIPWRECK AND Loss OF TWELVE LIVES.—The Austrian barque Petroslave, which left Cardiff on the 29th ult. for Pols, with a cargo of coal, has been wrecked off Milford. With the exception of one man, named Simon Marilich, who was thrown violently on the cliffs, the crew of twelve hands were drowned. At the meeting of the Central Chamber of Agriculture, on Tuesday, a letter was read from Mr. Gladstone, stating that the question of the appointment of a Minister of Agricul- ture and Commerce was one strictly for the Cabinet, who had a plan read's', and every representation which might bear upon it would accordingly have to go to the Cabinet. At the Liverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, the summons against the publisher of the Liberal Review for alleged libel upon a Mr. John O'Brien in an article headed "Election Scenes and Incidents" was withdrawn, an apology having been tendered in the last issue of the paper. A gentlemanly-looking man named Lewis G. Wynne was on Tuesdv fined £5 and costs by Mr. Raffles the Liverpool stipendiary, for using the title " M.D.," he not being a legally qualified doctor of medicine. He was also charged with attaching the name of Dr. D. M. Kennedy to two vaccination certificates without authority, and was com- mitted for trial at the sessions.
ALTRINCIIAM,

The ratA of the Altri—n—clTa-rn—Cocal BOard for the next half- year is one of a shilling in the pound. The number of deaths which occurred in Altrincham dur- ing the quarter ended September is 91. This is equal to a death-rate of 18 per 1,000. The birth-rate is 31.5 per 1,000.

_ Before Mr. Justice Field and Mr. Justice Stephen, on Monday, Mr. Bradlaugh moved to quash the indictment in the Central Criminal Court against Messrs. Ramsey, Foote, and himself for blasphemous libel. At the conclusion of the arguments their Lordships granted a rule nisi on one point in reference to counts which were stated to have been .abandoned and then added again, but refused a rule on upon five other points raises by Mr. Bradlaugh. The Right Hon. Spencer Walpole, M.P., has intimated to the Vice Chancellor of Cambridge University, which has given him a seat in the House of Commons since 1856, that he intends to retire from Parliament before the close of the present session. The right hon. gentleman says he has been induced to come to this decision by both private and public reasons. He is in his 75th year. In 1852 Mr. Walpole was Home Secretary, and he filled the same post in 1858-9, when the Conservative attempt at reform drove him from office. In 1866-7, however, he was again at the Home Office. A NATAL OFFICER DITORCED.—In the Divorcq Court, on Wednesday, the suit of Mrs. Elizabeth Ponsoby for the dis- solution of her marriage with Lieutenant Ponsonby, R.N., came on for hearing. Defendant made the acquaintance of a Criterion barmaid named Cumming, who committed suicide after he left her. The facts which were elicited at the inquest caused considerable sensation. He was no charged in the petition with adul try and desertion, and Sir James Hannen granted a decree for the dissolution of the marriage. THE CHARGE AGAINST 4 LIFEBOAT CREW.—The in- vestigation instituted by the National Lifeboat Institution into the conduct of a crew on the 28th ult., held before Cap- tains Chetwynd and Nepean, was concluded at Lowestoft, on Tuesday. The inquiry has been searching and exhaustive. The investigators reserve to themselves to make a report to the parent institutioa respecting the conduct of the cox- swain and superintendent, which is most unaccountable, and that of the boatmen reprehensible, arising, it is believed, out of money divisions and saleage. LORD ROSEBBRY AT EDINISURGH.—The Earl of Rosebery delivered his inaugural address as rector of the Edinburgh University on Saturday afternoon. He spoke on the sub- ject of patriotism. There was; he said, no word more prostituted. •It was used es a cover for every crime and every virtue in history, but he would only offer a defini- tion to serve his present purpose. Patriotism was self-respect of race. It was a motive which had animated the-noblest efforts and inspired true heroism. Dealing more especially with Scotland, he contended that it was good for the empire that it should preeerve its nationality. REPORTED ISSUE OF FORGED BANK NOTES.—The Observer says: A statement appeared in some of Saturday's papers to the effect that forged Bank of England notes have been recently placed in circulation in Paris to an amount of 80.000 or thereabouts, and that the matter was in the hands of the French police. This statement, it appears, is based on similar statements taken from French newspapers. We are requested to state that the inquiries made in Paris show that there is no truth in the report, and that neither the bankers nor the meney changers, nor the French police, know anything of the supposed issue of forged Bank of Eng- land notes. SnocKiNo TRAGEDIES: MURDER BY A SOLDIER.—AIfred Harris, corporal of the let Wiltshire Regiment, at Woolwich, while intoxicated, stabbed Corporal John Edgar on Saturday night in the barrack-room, as the latter was attempting to arrest him. Edgar was pierced through the heart, and fell dead. Harris then stabbed Private Light, who came to Edgar's assistance, and made off. The sentry tried to stop him, but was also wounded. Scouring parties were sent out in search of the prisoner, but during the night he returned alone to barracks, and was secured. He afterwards became most violent, snapped two handcuffs, and was finally strapped down. The weapon used was a swordstick. RETURN OF THE DUKE OF CONNAUGHT.—The Duke of Connaught arrived at Dover on Monday afternoon, and was met by the Duchess, who was accompanied by the Duke of Edinburgh. There were also present Earl Sydney, Major General Newdigate, Captain Sir Thomas Bruce, &c. The Duke arrived at Charing Cross Station shortly after five. On the arrival platform to receive him was a detachment, about 100 strong, of the London Irish Volunteers, under the command of Captain Lloyd. Their band struck up " God• Save the Queen." The Duke was met by the Duke of Cambridge, the Duke and Duchess of Albany, the Duke of Westminster, an others. In the Strand a crowd had assembled, and a band pldyed "See the conquering hero comes." THE PULLMAN CAR DISASTER.—The inquest on the body of Dr. Arthur, who perished through' the burning of a Pull- man car a few days ago, was concluded at Leeds on Wed- nesday. The jury were of opinion that the fire was "accidentally caused by Mr. Cranston's reading lamp." They thought that in the trying circumstances the railway officials did their duty, and that Dr. Arthur would have been able to escape had he not been labouring under n trcotic stupor. The use of reading lamps in Pullman cars was condemned by the jury, who further expressed the opinion that railway travellers are placed in jeopardy by the rule as to the condi- tions under which drivers should pay heed to signals made by the communication cord. THE REPRESENTATION OF PRESTON. —A vacancy is about to occur in the Parliamentary representation of Preston, Mr. Rsikes having decided to seek election for the University of Cambridge. Mr. Tomlinson, the favourite of the workingmen Conservatives, has already issued an ad- dress asking for support. The Conservative Parliamentary Executive Committee met on Tuesday night and adopted Mr. Gorst, M.P., as their candidate, but though in the com- mittee's announcement to the constituency on Wednesday morning it was stated that the hon. gentleman had con- sented to stand, he has excused himself from doing so on the ground that his retirement from Chatham " would place the Conservative party-there in a position as embarrassing as that in which Preston is now involved by the sudden desertion of its recently elected member." FATAL ENCOUNTER BETWEEN A CONVICT AND A WARDER.—On Wednesday afternoon a determined attempt was made by a convict, named Wm. Murray, at Dartmoor convict establishment, upon the life of Warder. Kelly. Murray was one of a-small ging employed in a quarr.y out- side the prison, and after coming out from dinner he attacked Kelly, irst by throwing stones, and then by striking at him with a spade. Kelly closed with him; and in the struggle the officer's rifle was discharged, and the convict received the full charge, sustaining such injuries that he died Almost immediately afterwards. Murray was undergoing a sentence of five years penal servitude, only one of which had expired. The warder was muck bruised. MRS. LANGTRY AND MADAME PATTI.—The Philadelphia correspondent of the Times, telegraphing on Tuesday night, says:—" Mrs. Langtry and Madame Patti made each her first appearance on Monday night, both having large and fashioneble audiences, and many prominent personages managing to see both ladies. Mrs. Langtry attracted most attention, and drew the larger number of spectaters that Wallack's Theatre ever held. The receipts were $6,800 $l,OOO over Madame Bernhardt's first night. She certainly made a most favourable impression on her audience, and was applauded to the echo. Over a wagoa-load of flowers was showered upon her, and she .was called out 12 times. New York cities differ upon the question whether she possesses perfect beauty, but most of them ire satisfied with her acting, though some maintain she has not yet managed to thoroughly merge the fine lady in the actress." TIIE "BIG BIG D."—ls "damn" a profane. word? The question has come up before the District Court of Philadel- phia, which is hearing the suit brought by a printer against a telephone company. The latter removed their instrument on the ground that it was being made the medium of profane and vulgar language. The former denied the charge, but admitted the use of "damn." The point, therefore, for the court is whether that word is profane. Their decision, says an American temporary, will be "awaited with deep interest by a host of worthy men, and possibly by devout women not a few,' who in moments of great physical or mental torture have found a grateful solace in the•use of that com- pact and cogent expletive." It ought hardly to need a law court to decide such a question; but perhaps the court may hold that a special dispensation should allowed to printers. The writing with which they often have to deal may fairly be held to justify a plea of "extenuating circumstances..— Fall Mall Gazette.
THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 11, 1882. DISTRICT NEWS.

div.head: BOLD.
div.p: BOLD.

- STEALING A MANURE FORIL—On Tuesday at the Prescot Petty Sessions, John Ryan, was charged with having stolen a manure fork, the property of John Welsby, Cinder-lane, Bold.—An officer said that he had been on duty, about half- past one o'clock on the morning of the Ist inst., and saw the prisoner and another man coming along the lane carry- ing the fork in question. As soon as the men saw him they ran away, but he followed them and caught the prisoner. On charging him with stealing the fork, prisoner made no reply. Witness made enquiries, and found that the fork belonged to Mr. Welsby.—The prisoner, who was not known to the police, pleaded guilty, and was sent to gaol for one month's hard labour.

FRODSHAM. TEMPERANCE MEETING.—The members of the Order of Rechabites had a successful meeting in the Town Hall, Froisham, on Friday evening, when the Rev. D. Schofield Presided, and addresses were delivered by the chairman and Mr. Hinds and Mr. Dutton, of Norley. The Rev. A. P. Reynolds, senior curate for Frodsham, also gave a capital speech on the temperance question. A lengthy programme of recitations, dialogues, and songs was given by the mem- _ _

hers of the order. FRODSHAM LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY.—The second meeting of the above society was held in the girls' school, Church-street, Frodsham, on Monday evening, when the Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A. vicar, presided. The subject was whether museums, &c., should be opened on Sundays, and the Rev. A. P. ;Reynolds opened the discussion in a very able manner, answering the question in the negative by a series of exhaustive arguments. The following gentlemen took part in the discussion, viz.: Messrs. Henry Linaker, Samuel Davies, R.J. Wallace, Peter Riley, Thomas Hough, Henry Smith, and Henry Tiley. On being put to the meeting a tnajsrity voted in favour of Mr. Reynolds' conten- tion that museums should not be opened on Sundays. A vote of thanks to Mr. Reynolds was proposed by E. A. Wright, Esq J.P., seconded by Mr. Thomas Lewis, and carried unanimously. FREEMASONRY AT FRODSllAM.—Consecrated little more than a year ago, the Cholmondeley Lodge, No. 1,908, has ' already made considerable progress, secured an excellent reputation, and holds a well recognised position in the pro- vince of Cheshire, so admirably governed by Bro. the Right Hon. Lora de Tabley. The first annual installation meeting held on Tuesday at the Commercial Hotel, Frodsharo, was influentially attended, and the whole of the proceedings were of an eminently satisfactory nature. The chair at the opening was occupied by Bro. J. K. Digges, P.P.A.D.C., the W.M., and he was supported by a full complement of officers and a large representation of members and visitors. After some preliminary business, the chair was taken by Bro. J. Salmon, P.P.G.S.D., who, in a manner which could hardly have been excelled, proceeded to instal Bro. G. Hammond Danby as the Worshipful Master for the ensuing year. The following officers were invested for 1882-3: Bros. J. K. Digges, P.P.A.D.C., 1.M.P.; J. J. Yapp, S.W. ; H. E. Hey- wood, J.W. • J. Salmon, P.P.G.S.D. and P.M., treasurer; Rev. Samuel Hague, M.A., chaplain; J. J. Radford, secre- tary; John Ashton, S.D.; T. H. Hitchen, J.D.; C. H. Lewin, 1.G.; R. H. Turner, S.S.; C. Behrend, J.S.; W. Humphreys, 0.; and Bro. John Roberts was elected tyler. The musical portion of the ceremonies was admirably con- ducted by Bro. Humphreys; and before the lodge c:osed an artistic P.M.'. jewel was presented to Bro. J. K. Digges. About 30 brethren subsequently sat down to a capital ban- quet, most satisfactorily served by Misses Harrison and Hood , (late James's), at their confectionery establishment in Frod- sham. The usual loyal and masonic toasts were given ' during the evening, and an excellent selection of music was furnished by Bros. Yapp, Ellis, Knowles, Humphreys, dm.

_ GOLBORNE. MEETING OF THE PAROCHIAL COIIIIITTRE.—A genera. meeting of the members of the Go'borne Parochial Commit- tee was held at Messrs. Breeds's office, on Wednesday after- noon, when there were present Messrs. Fearns (in the chair), W. H. Arnott, A. Jackson, J. Lowe, W. Gorton, and Chas. S. Bennie (surveyor). The minutes of the last meeting were read and confirmed.—The Diversion and Obstruction of a Footpath: The Surveyor reported that he and Mr. Fearns had waited upon Mr. Mayhew, solicitor, of Wigan, with reference to the obstruction of the footpath at the Legh- street extremity, by the erection of property by the orders of Mr. Legh's agent. The following correspondence fol- lowed :—" Wigan, 20th October, 1882.—Dear Sir,—We have been consulteel by the surveyor of highways for Got- borne respecting the obstruction of a public footpath from Bank Heath to Legh-street by the buildings on Mr. Legh's land. We are informed that no order was made for the diversion of this footpath, and it is therefore the duty of the Surveyor of Highways to take steps to maintain the public rights. We should be very averse, however, to institute legal proceedings against Mr. Legh or his lessees, and think that if there was a meeting on the ground the matter might be arranged to the satisfaction of both parties. An early reply will oblige, yours faithfully, MAYHEW, SON, AND PECK. J. E. Pardey, Esq., Newton-le- Willows." Mr. Pardey wrote to say that he was quite pre- pared to fall in with the suggestion made as to a meeting on the ground, and presumed that they would have been made aware of the circumstances under which the diversion of the footpath was made, as explained in his letter on the 28th September. The Surveyor added that he and several members met • Mr. Pardey on Friday, the 3rd instant, and a conver- sation ensued with reference to the dangerous foot- bridge, and also with reference to the obstruction of the foot- path. The interview resulted in Mr. Pardey promising to erect a new footbridge, and to improve the line of footpath on condition that the township repaired the same after- wards. This arrangement was considered a very satisfactory eine by the Committee.—The Surveyor stated that at the last meeting of the Committee he was instructed to write to Mr. Moore, solicitor, of Warrington, in reference to the pro- ceedings being taken against Mr. Siddall, for nonpayment of water rates. Mr. Moore had since written to Mr. Siddall, and the latter had paid the amount claimed.—The Gas Meters: The Surveyor read figures with reference to the various gas meters in the township, and reported that the • one in Church-street, and one in Bridge- street were not registering the gas satisfactorily.—Mr. Gor- ton proposed, and Mr. Lowe seconded, and it was resolved, that old meters and lamp pillars be removed and replaced by new pillars, with meter boxes and meters combined, the obi pillars to be re-fixed in Cross-street and Bridge-street.—The State of the Water : The Surveyor submitted a report from Dr. Hall on samples of water taken from various wells in the township, but the question was adjourned for a month, when it was expected that the analysis of all the suspicious wells in the parish would be completed. It was resolved that legal proceedings be taken against all persons who had not complied with notices served upon them to obtain a supply of the town's NI ater.—The Street Lamps : Mr. Lowe moved, and Mr. Arnott seconded that the street lamps be put out half-an-hour later every evening, and that on Saturday nights the regulation as to their lighting. be. discontinued. The motion was carried.— Finance : The following accounts were passed for payment: C. S. Bennie, £5 Is. lid.; J. Tyrer and Sons, £3 6s. 11d.; W. H. Rigby, Gs. 4d.; R. L. Pennington, £1 ss. 7fia James Walton, £5l Gs. 11d.; William Pimblett, £3; Richard Wilcock, £2O Bs. 4,1,--This was the only business. KNUTSFORD. -

There was a daily average of prisoners in Knutsford Gaol list year of 221 males and 60 females. The average cost for prisoners was £2l 16s. 81. There was a daily average at Chester of 150. The first of a series of ten entertainments to be given fortnightly was held on Saturday evening last, at the Town Hall, Knutsford, when there was a large and respectable audience. Last year these gatherings proved of great service to the working classss, and the pecuniary success was also most gratifying.. LYMNI.

WESLEYAN BAND or HOPE.—On Monday, the usual enter- tainment in connection with this Band of Hope took place in the Wesleyan school. The attendance was very good, and the programme of the evening was thoroughly enjoyable. Mr. Itobert Naylor was in the chair. DROWNING CASES.—On Monday, a sad occurrence took place near the coal wharf, at Lymm. It seems a little girl named Sarah Haddin had been with her mother to one of the !ustian cutting places, and was going back horn alone, when it is supposed she fell into the canal, and was thus drowned. Unfortunately, although some men were working I in the wharf, yet they did not see the girl fall in—in fact, i did not see her at all .until a boatman called attention to the ' circumstance of having seen what appeared a bnndle of clothes in the water. On being told of what had happened to her daughter, the mother fell down senseless, and had to be carried from her work ha Ate.—Another case of drowning is roported from Oughtrington, the unfortunate victi.n in this case being a young person of about 18 years, named Elizabeth Clare. She, on Saturday night, was returning home from a party to which she had been invited, when at a point a little to the south of Dunham she was blown into the canal, and drowned. ADVENTURES OF A WIFE HUNTER.—Any one paying par- ticular attention to the advertisements in the Warrington papers lately might have seen that an amorous gentleman hailing from Birmingham was in want of a wife. He bad evidently a careful eye to the cash, for the advertisement stated that he would like a "lady" with means, in order, as I he afterwards stated in a letter, to improve his business. He explained that if he obtained a partner in his transac- tions he would be obliged to share the profits, whereas if be got a wife all the gold would be landed safely at home. As Lymtn is usually such ayery quiet spot, one of the ladies, to wit,a shopkeeper in the village, took it into her head that she ' would " have a lark ; " accordingly she answered the loving Brum's advertisement, saying that she was a widow with £2,500 at her disposal. This easily hooked the fish, cartes were exchanged, letters written, and Monday was appointed as the day of meeting. He arrived in due course, and pro- ceeded to the abode of the rich widow, who answered the door in the garb of servant, saying that her mistress was out—would he kindly sit down a little while, as she was expecting him. Meanwhile, wind of the business had got quickly abroad, and the would-be lover was very soon sur- rounded by upwards of 100 fustian cutters, who gave him to understand that they were well aware of his intentions in Lymrn. Thanks to his age about 65), he got off much more easily than if he had been a younger man. As it was, one blocked his hat, others threw wet sods, until the unlucky fellow was glad to make the best of his way to the station,

div.head: NANTW ICH.
div.p: NANTW ICH.

At Leicester Assize3---.To—lin—Win-zar, solicitor's clerk, formerly of Nantwich, has been sentenced to 14 years' penal servitude fcr the forgery of deeds by which he obtained nearly £2,000. The Nantwich Board of Guardians, at their meeting on Saturday, discussed the question of hospital accommodation, of which there is a lack in the neighbourhood. The matter was referred to a committee. CHEESE FAIR.—A fair for the extensive pastural part of Cheshire, of which Nantwich is the centre, was auspiciously inaugurated on Thursday morning. Between 700 and 800 eine cheeses were pitched, and the pricesfor best quality were fully maintained, 80s. per cwt. being realised for one dairy ; inferior, 453. to 505.; medium, 503. and 60s. ; superior, 60s. to 755. At these figures all the dairies were cleared out.

OVER. The -Primitive Methodist Sabbath school of Littler, Over, had a juvenile service on Sunday last, when Mr. Jabez Hulse presided, and gave both afternooa and night very appropriate addresses, while the children recited pieces and dialogues with suitable hymns between. The collections were for the benefit of the school.

• W HISTON UNPROMISING JITTENILES.—On Tuesday, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, two small lads named Thomas Donnolley and James Ilinnegan, were charged with having stolen a 2ft. rule, a piece of leather, and some iron, valued at 45., the property of Richard Prescot and Company, brick manufac- turers, Whiston.—Each of the prisoners was ordered to receive six strokes with a birch rod.—Mary Makin was charged, in custody with having received some of the stolen property into her possession.—The boy Donnolley said he took the piece of iron to the prisoner and asked her to sell it for him. She asked him where he had got it and he said he had picked it up in a ploughed field. She afterwards sold the iron end gave him 3p. for it, and wanted lid. back but he only gave her a id. He never told her that the iron had been stolen although he said he •did to Superinten- dent Barker. The prisoner was dismissed.

WIGAN. At a meeting of the executive of the Liberal party in Wigan, on Saturday evening, Mr. Walter Wren was unani- mously adopted as the Liberal candidate at the forthcoming election to fill the vacancy in the representation of the borough. The Conservative candidate will be the Hon. Algernon Egerton. It is expected that the writ will be moved for at the end of the present session. At Wigan, on Monday, a youth, named John Harrison, was committed to Liverpool Assizes, charged with the man- slaughter of James Lowe, whom he struck with iron pincers.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

RE-OPENING OF CHRIST CFIURCH.—The first Or re-open- ing services of this church in High-street, Winsford, after it has been taken down and re-built in a style more consonant with the tendencies of the Winsford vicinity in which it stands, took place on Tuesday last. The Rural Dean of Con- gleton, the Rev. Canon Blackburn, M.A., of Vrarmingham, preacned in the afternoon, and the Rev. A. J. Blencowe, M.A., of Witton,Northwich, in the evening. There was a public tea in the interval of public worship for the friends, dm., from a distance. WORKINGMEN'S INSTITUTH—A lecture was given tinder the auspices of this institute on Thursday evening last, by Mr. J. Buckley, F.R.G.S , in the Academy, Weaver-street. Subject, " The history of chemistry," with experiments. The lecturer showed the rise and gradual, but very slow, development of this science, and the misconceptions under which its students laboured. He presented the probable way in which, as an experimental and practical science, its career opened out to the days of Priestly. The lecture was in three-parts with music between. Mr. Thompson played an organ solo with much effect. Mrs. Buckley and Mr. Jno. Beswick, a pianoforte duet which was much applauded. Mr. J. H. Crosbie, who occupied the chair, spoke of the interest which the lecturer bad thrown around the subject, and the facilities which young men had now-a-days for progress in learning. He urged the many young men present to avail themselves of the excellent library of the institute as well as of the lectures, and cultivate their minds as the best way to rise and be useful. He proposed the best thanks of the meeting to the lecturer for his indefatigable efforts to profit and amuse them, which, being seconded, and carried unani- mously, Mr. Buckley acknowledged, and proposed alike compliment to the chairman. The National Anthem ended a pleasant evening. SALT TRADE.—The strong association is beginning to take the inevitable effect. With stocks lower than they have been for years, with a stoppage of works, which has already caused a deficiency of half a million tons in actual production, and with large coal strikes before us, it is clear that a considerable rise of price must follow soon. This will be accelerated now by the reduction of freights con- signment on the great demand for tonnage in United States Ports. The prices remain as they were last month, indeed as they have been ever since April, while the salt freights stand at the following figures : America: New Orleans, 10s, Os 6d, 8s; Savannah, 5s ; Charlestown, ss; New York (steam), 10s, 7s 6,1, and sa; Boston (steam), 7s 61; Norfolk, Os; Montreal (steam), 12s 6d ; Calcutta, 13s 6,1 with consignment. Australia: Mel- bourne, 22s 6d ; Sydney, do. ; Baltic Fallen, 83; New Fair Water, 6s 6d ; Copenhagen, 7s 6d ; Fredericia, 83; and North Sea, Harlingen, Os 6d offered. The varied amounts sent abroad Juring the previous month of October reach : To United States ports, 19,707 tons (less than within the last ye Irs, except 1878) ; to Eritish North America, 2,959 (which is but a half or third of recent years) ; to the West Indies and South America we have seat 2,023, which is the second best month of October return for seven years ; Africa has received 2,723, which was exceeded in 1880 only of the seven years; to East Indies, viz., Calcutta, Chittagong, Rangoon, dec., 23 336 tons, nearly half of last year; Australia has had 960, or three-quafters or last year, and one quarter of year 1880; Prussia has had less than half of year before in 2,747 tons ; Russia 889, or about one-third of previous years; Baltic ports 2,682, against 3,319; France and the Mediterranean 657, against 314 last year; Newcastle 0, against nearly 1,000 tons, and 5.796 against 12,983 for 10 months of this year with last. This shows how the Tees salt works :are telling in the North-East of England; 80 tons "ewe supplied rest of England against 2 for last October; 385 Scotland, against 1,063 last year; 103 for Ire- land, against 254 in 1881; Holland 2,284, against 1,468; Belgium 5.483, against 5,007; and from Liverpool 66,973, against 90,203; from Runcorn, de,, 11,880, against 17,187; or a total from Mersey of 78,853, to be set against 107,450 in October, 1881. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

Heavy westerly gales, accompanied by drenching showers of rain, have been experienced at Chester. The river Dee overflowed its banks below Farndon, and at Chester it was level with the embankment. The total number of patients seen by the medical officers\ of the West Cheshire Provident Dispensaries during the year amount to 6,168. The number of prescriptions dispensed was 4,976, againat 2,604 last year. A pig dealer named Robert Broster Los been convicted at Whitchurela for riotous conduct in the parish church. Dur- ing the sermon, he expressed the opinion that the minister's remarks were "all bosh," and that "any fool knew what he was saying." Before the magistrates, he explained that he "felt the church go round him," and that he did not know what he said. He was committed for a month. The Congleton magistrates have convicted a man named Woolfenden as an accessory, under the Poaching Act, for having been found in possession of 52 rabbits. For the defence it was said that the rabbits had been purchased from tenants en a local estate, who had power under the Ground Game Act to kill and sell. If otice of appeal has been given. Last Friday, when the Cheshire hounds were drawing Mr. Howcroft's willow bed at Duddon Heath, no less than five foxes were seen afoot. Evil-disposed persons becoming acquainted with the circumstance have set traps and poison for them, a fine fox, on Thursday, being found poisoned, while a second was struggling in a trap. The greatest in- dignation was felt at the occurrence, and a reward, it is expected, will be offered for evidence leading to the convicp tion of the offenders. The Sandbach Local Board have been threatened with dissolution. Some time ago the Local Government Board called their attention to the fact that a supply of wholesome water was much needed for the town, and reminded the Board that grave responsibility would rest upon them should any evil consequence arise from their neglect. They also asked for information with regard to the disposal of the sewage of the town. The Board instructed their clerk to simply acknowledge the receipt of the letter. This week the Local Government Board have sent another letter stating that if the Local Board continue to withstand their duty it will remain with the Local Government Board to determine whether it will not be necessary for them to take §teps for obtaining a provisional order to dissolve the urban authority of Sandbach and resolve it into a sanitary au- thority.
Eight persons were injorecl on 'Mondty by an enlosion of gas at Parkhead, near Glasgow.

div.head: Xetteto to the editor.
div.p: Xetteto to the editor.

THE SHIP CANAL SCHEME. Sir,—Would you kindly allow me to say to the public, through your valuable paper, that the proposed Ship Canal scheme from Liverpool to Warrington, and so on, to Man- chester, Oldham, from Warrington by plateway is voted a sure success by many very practical and far-seeing gentle- men, and would be by them richly supported in funds, but not so by canal from Warrington to Manchester.—Yours C. E. Warrington, November, 1882.

Sir,— Permit me to point out how seriously this question affects the manufacturers of Lancashire. In the case of foreign competition every charge that increases the cost of a piece of cloth, either turns the scale and prevents business, or else lessens the margin of the manufacturer's profit. Generally speaking, all cloth on its outward journey passes through Manchester; if it could be shipped there, not only will the carriage to Liverpool be saved, but also some of the shipping expenses, amounting in all to about a halfpenny on each 811 b. to 91b. piece, or about 17s. 61 per annum saved on every loom in Lancashire. Besides this, the spinner will effect a large reduction in his ctrriage and Liverpool charge account, and be in a positimq to sell cheaper yarn, and still make a profit. Also as food will be cheapened, the operatives will be benefited, because 20s. will go as far as 21s. does now. If Lancashire is to stem grow- ing competition, she must cast aside the weights that burden her, or in time she will be found wanting. BOSDIN T. LEECH. Back Pool Fold, Manchester, 6th November, 1682.

THE ELECTION OF MAYOR. Sir,—l rejoice to see that our Town Council has con- ferred the honour of chief magistrate upon so worthy a townsman as Mr. John Crosfield. I have long been of opinion that of all men in our Town Council, Mr. Cro:field was deserving of this distinction. lam glad also that the neutral " Guardian" is not to be allowed to dictate to the Council as to who shall be Mayor of Warrington. Alder- man Davies deserves the thanks of the whole community for his manly and indignant protest against such conduct. There was one remark in Alderman Davies's speech which all must thoroughly endorse, with reference to the speeches of Dr. Mackie being reported in full and these of his oppo- nents on many occasions carefully curtailed. I would ask whether, in adlition to this, is it not a fact that pe-sons who have been personally obnoxious have not been reported at all in the columns of the "Guardian ?" Let the doctor deny this if he can. Surely this is a reflection upon the impartiality of the Press, and which most of its representa- tives would indignantly repudiate. It was high time that our Town Council resented such conduct, and I am delighted that it has done so in such an unmistakeable manner. I am sure that in Mr. Crosfield, as Mayor, we shall have a gentleman who will maintain the impartiality so characteristic of our excellent ex-Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and that for the present, at any rate, Warrimgton will continue to enjoy the satisfaction of having for its chief magistrate one of its noblest and most benevolent men.—l am, sir, tic., RECTOR. Warrington, November 9, 1812._

PROPOSED SKATING RINK FOR RUNCORN. Sir,—An idea has prevailed in my mind for the past two years, and which I have abstained from mentioning before owing to circumstances best known to myself, namely, that of providing a skating rink for Runcorn. I think if some enterprising party—say the Commissioners—were to select a piece of hrnd situate near the railway station, in the gar- den at the corner of the Co-operative Stores, or on the north- east side of Greenvray-road, and build such a structure as that near the Chester railway station. I think their efforts in that direction would be crowned witla success. Suppose the erection; as a matter of conjecture, cost £lOO, and was opened to the public three nights per week—say, Monday, Wednesday, and Saturday—if only 100 persons visited the place each night, at 6d per head, £7 lOs would be realised. It could also be utilised on the intervening nights for balls, concerts, religious assemblies, &c., when the Public Hall was engaged; and in addition to this the charge for the privilege of keeping a refreshment stall would be a clear gain. The expenditure, I think, would be trifling. A con- tract might be made with Miss Jukes, or some other compe- tent pianist, for say £1 or £1 is per week, and another for some person to clean out the building and deliver the skates for lOs ar 15s per week. The gas bills and insur- ance would be mere bagatelles. lam sure the structure would soon pay for itself, as it would not only be an attrac- tion for the Runcorn people in general but also for the adjacent districts, such as Frodsham and Halton, and per- haps Mc:nes. Look at the distance some people travel during frost to get to a nice sheet of ice. We have no public parks, no concert halls, no respectable theatres to wile away the dreary winter months. The possession of a free public library is certainly a great boon to the town, but young people who have been confined in shopsand offices all day do not want to sit night after night reading novels, &c. They require a little exercise, and where will they find a more healthy recreation on leaving business than at the rink? There is one thing to be added, Mr. Editor, se., if it is to be well patronised and its recpectability maintained, keep away loose characters. The idea has now, of course, been mooted, and I leave the matter for some more able pen than mine to take it up. A FEELER. Runcorn, November 8, 1882.

A TAME HARE AND A FATED CAT. Sir,—The following account of the late Mr. Buckland's tame hare may interest your readers. It is taken from the deceased naturalist's" Notes and jottings of animal life ": " When at Rye, in Sussex, in 1879, I saw a live hare, which, when quite a little thing, had been caught by a dog. My friend, in whose collection it was, kindly gave me this hare in order that I might see what I could do in taming it. When I turned the hare, which I called Joe, down on to the floor of my own room he exhibited great alarm, rushing about the room in all directions, eventually concealing him- self behind some books. I tried the experiment of seeing whether Joe would live in the cage with tbe monkeys. It was interesting to watch the monkeys' reception of the hare. One called Little Jack was the first to try experi- ments. Leaning over the bars of the cage, he pulled the tips of the hare's ears; finding the hare did not fly at him, he came down on to the floor of the cage with extreme caution and circumspection; then stretching out his hand and arms as far as they would go, he gave the hare's fur a touch finding that nothing happe.ned, he became bolder, and gave the hare's fur a good pull-. The bare jumped round quicklyond gave battle to Little Jack, who, like most bullies, showed himself an arrant coward. The hare showed fight by holding up his fore-legs and scratching at Little Jack's face, implanting the blows in a most workmanlike manner. It was curious to see Little Jack's subsequent mode of attack. He would not face the hare, but backed up towards him using his tail as a sort of shield. He then put his bead on the ground, and looked at , the hare from between his hind legs. The battle being finished, an old crippled monkey, called Carrots' Jane, came down from her perch very cautiously and inspected the hare. The latter squatted quite still in the corner of the cage— Jane went close up to his bead, and the two remained there for some minutes, gazing with wideopen eyes steadfastly into each other's faces. The result of this congress between Jane and the hare was the conclusion of peace. Jane began a chatter. The hare showed that he approved of the friendship IT a quick move- ment of the upper lip, while Jane showed her approbation by looking for fleas in the bare's fur. Joe lived in my room for several months. He chose for his residence the in- terspace betwee my writing desk and the wall, and there he would sit all day. At night, when everything was quiet, Joe used to hop out cautiously, and, having looked me straight in the face for a minute or two, would go to the fire, sit up on his hind legs, and warm his white waistcoat. Lam afraid I did not succeed in taming Joe, though I tried my best ; I therefore sznt him to the Zoological Gardens, to elucidate, if possible, the question of leporines, which are said to be a breed between a bare and a rabbit. Our friend Mr. Bartlett feels sure there is no such breed ; and one of his reasons is that hares are born with their eyes open, and that they can run almost immediately after birth. Rabbits, on the contrary, are born in holes, with their eyes shut for some days, and it is many days before they can run. To Mr. Bartlett are brought sometimes sup- posed hybrids, between a cat and a rabbit. Our friend says a cat with a short tail will not proce the argument. lie wants a rabbit with a long tail. In connection with hybrids I have heard the following story of the great Duke cf Wel- lington being completely:sold by a showman :—"A man had advertised an exhibition of a hybrid creature between a tench and a hare. When the Duke went to examine it, the exhi- bitor told him he was very sorry he could not show the specimen itself, as it load gone to Court to be exhibited to the king; but, if it was any sasisfaction, he would show him both the father and the mother stuffed, and in glass cases !" It may not be Possible for our naturalists to blend the carnivora with the rodentia, but it would seemto ba possible for a Dutch - American baker to successfully 'turn" a cat for a rabbit,

nudging from the following story, taken from fie "Editor's drawer" of the October number of Harpers Monthlv :—"lf any one doubts that the highest honour as, integrity reside in the bosom of a Ditch baker, the follow- ing adventure of Mr. Kloptenfussen will be a very useful study. A neighbouring family recently sent to Mr. K.'s bakehouse a rabbit smothered in onions, to be cooked for the Sunday's dinner; but while the dish stood on a low shelf in the larder, awaiting its turn in the oven, Mrs.Kloin, fussen's tom-cat (whose inherent knavishness of disposition i ,no virtuous examples could counteract) slipped n and devoured the rabbit entirely. To remedy such a loss, or to punish such a crime, would have seemed difficult to ?lust people ; but Mr. Kloptenfussen accomplished.nu both objects- at once, and in the most complete and admirable manner. Though the cat was a great favourite in the family, and of much use as a ratter, his Roman-like master put him to clath, skinned and properly prepared him, and substituted him for the rabbit in such a satisfactory manner, that the people to whom the dinner belonged ate it with great relish, not suspecting that any change had been made in the ingre- dients. .Here was an unparalleled triumph of equitvl—the robber being made to take the place of the stoleriarticle, and full reparation being made to the party robbed, without any of those vexatious delays which usually attend the administration of justice." I should think it wanted something stronger than a draught from the Zuyder Zee to wash that game down. It is a pity the story does not tell what-was done with the " haggis " containing the rabbit. -- I am, sir, &c., ANGLO-SCOTUS. Newington, London, October 28, 1882.

Writing on "some peculiarities of the hare," the same co'. respondent says :—Sir,—The Lancet publishes the follow- ing explanation of the " query " alluded to in the postscript tarey letter of October 13th :—" Dr. Pratt writes to say that the cause of the discolouration referred to has been found to be an ointment used by the patient which was not officiaal, and the composition of which was not known until after the note appeared. This ointment produced a copious ink stain, which has disappeared from the dressings since the ointment has been discontinued." And it is a curious if not quite coincident fact, that in connection with the change of colour that takes place in the coat of the Scotch hare at various seasons, Mr. Manley, in his "Notes on game," says :—" Most naturalists speak of this transformation as an actual change of coat,and sh,edding of the entire fur ; but I be- lieve the correct view is that there is no such shedding of the fur at all, and that no hair falls from the animal, the trans- formation being effected simply by a change of the fluid colouring in the hairs; just as there is a change is the I colouring of the feathers in many birds without moulting." The same author suggests that heat and cold has some- thing to do with the change of colour. There is a story in the same book I am quoting from of an old courser of the hare whose "ruling passion," showed itself "strong in death," imparting when in estemis what he considered a valuable bit of information to his sen about hares. Beckon- ing the lad to his bedside, he whispered into his ear, "Jack, I have little more to say; but always look for a hare on an oat arish directly after harvest," and with these words his earthly career was finished. Another argument against public exhibitions of cruelty in connection with so- called sport and of its debasing effect upon some natures. It is recorded of another "veteran sportsman" that he I would have shot a greyhound that "ran cunning "—that is to say, be would have destroyed an intelligent animal that acted on instinct in preference to following the routine of training it had received with the view of prolonging the period of a run. Oh, man! what have you to answer for in the shape of cold, pitiless cruelty? And yet you flip- pantly assert that all the evils of this world are the result of one woman's fondness for apples. In some parts of Essex the hares are called "Sarahs." A brace of hares in a walled garden multiplied to the number of 57 in a year. Black hares have been shot in England, and the existence of parti- coloured ones has recently been reported. The average weight of an English hare may be put at 611 i. to 71b.. but unique specimens have scaled 131 h. 14oz. and 131 b. 40z: In connection with the Mosaic prohibition of the hare as food, Mr. Manley says that all animals, as Biblical stndents are aware, were forbidden, except those which "divide the hoof and chew the cud." The ox, the sheep, and the goat were lawful food, because they fulfilled both conditions: the pig was prohibited because it did not chew the cud, though it divided the hoof; and the hare is specified with the camel and the coney (?rabbit) as also prohibited, because they did not divide the hoofs, though they chewed the cud. Now, as a matter of fact, the hare does not chew the cud, though to an ordinarY observer it would seem to do so. The hare has neither the character of teeth nor the fourfold stomach possessed by animals that chew the cud. When reposing at its ease it continually moves its jaw about as if actually chewing some- thing, and the action might easily he mistaken for true rumination. In reality, this mumbling or grinding of the teeth is performed by instinct, its result beingthe preser- vation of the edge and shape of the ch!sel-like inciso r teeth—the hare rubbing its teeth together instead of working them, as do other redents (especially rabbits in wooden hutches) on various hard substances to keep them in order • The Fey. J. G. Wood explains the Mosaic state rnent by saving that the hare was spoken of as chewing the cud because it appeared to do so, and the object WAS to guard the JAWS against mistaking the hare for one of the ruminants which were permitted as food. And he adds that things would in all probability have fallen into that mistake, from the fact ._that Arabs are ex- ceedingly fond of the flesh of the hare, and accept it as well as the camel as lawful food, because it (the camel) chews its cud, the division of the hoof not being considered by them essential. This explanation is not considered quite satisfac- tory to the mind of Mr. Manley, who quotes it in his very readable book for what it is worth. And I for one quite agree with him when he remarks that it must always be remembered in connection with questions of Biblical difficulty and interpretation, that the Bible was never meant as a handbook of science," and that in physical matters it speaks in language suited to the know- ledge, and in accordance with the phraseology, of the times inwhick the different books were written. According to Cow- per, the hare kept in a " parked " state will eat grass, leaves of all kinds, sovethistle, dandelion, lettuce, Sze. They are also fond of clam sand as a digestive. Bread in all shapes does not come amiss to them. The hare is in seasen from August up till January, but gourmets assert that a hare before Christmas is far superior to one after. ee

• - • ANOTHER THAEATENED DISPUTE. Contrary to expectation, the recent settlement of the dis- pute between the firm of Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., of the Ilaytiock, Ashton, and Gol borne collieries, and the hands employed thereat has not been of that lasting and final character that everybody hoped it would be. The men are far from being satisfied at the manner in which the advance of ten per cent. recently granted is being paid, and already they have held one or two meetings, at which consider- able dissatisfaction was expressed. It is stated that they are not receiving the ten per cent. which the firm, through Mr. Glover, promised to give them, and that they mean to press their contention in an unmis- takeable manner. The firm, however, state that they are giving the advance, and unless a reconciliation by some means be come to, it is expected that the district will again 'be troubled with another strike. On Tuesday afternoon last Mr. Glover, the manager of the firm, was at the Pewfall collieries, and a deputation, consisting of re.° colliers, representing those pits, waited upon him in the manager's office. The deputation wished to know the new prices to be paid for the different classes of work. They were the prices would simply have ten per cent. added. " Ton- nage " which in October, 1881, was Is. Id. would become 15.211.; tonnage, is. 21. would become is. 31d. ; yardage, ss. 6d. would become 65., &c. The men stated that what they would require was that the gross earnings should have ten per cent. added in the office. This, Mr. Glover con- tended, meant that the men should have a proper per cent- age paid upon the recent advance, and the reply was that the firm entirely declined to adopt any such method, as the managers in the pits were the persons to judge as to what should be paid for the different classes of work, and they would be paid for accordingly. He mentioned the case of two men working in the pits as examples of what the firm proposed to do. On the old principle they had 22 tons 11 cwt. at is. id. per ton, making £1 4s. 41-d. To this was added 6 yards at 2s„ 121.; 2 yards at 2s. 21., 45. 4d.; and 2 yards at 45., Bs.; total, £2 Bs. 81. Ten per cent. added to this would make L 2 13s. 611. Under the new arrangements 22 11 cwt., at is. 20., would be £1 Gs. 81.; 6 yards at 25. 21. would be 135.; 2 yardt at 25. 41. would be 4s. 81.; and 2 yards at 4s. 41. would be Bs. 81. , making a total of £2 13s. This was really .6D. less than 10 per cent., and that divided be- tween two men was not dii. per day. The deputation then retired, but it is said the men are tell' dissatisfied, and the prospect for the future is not entirely clear.

Writing in reference to the proposed Irish National Museum, Mr. Lyons, M.P., suggests that Irish architects should prepare plans for the new Irish National Museum, with the view to the rejection of the five plans now on view in Dublin. Mr. Lalor, M.P. for Queen's County, Ireland, has announced to his constituents his intention of resigning his seat as soon as a suitable successor can be found. Mr. Lalor finds that his health does not permit of a continuous attend- ance in London. On WedneNlay night a horrible fatality occurred-on the Lancashire Union Railway, at Heapey, near Chorley. Jas. , Wignall, a labourer, and another man were walking along the line from Briscall Works when they were overtaken by a passenger train. The driver whistled, but Wignall step- ped from the six foot in front of the engine. He was.knocked down, and his bead and both arms were cut off. At the Nottingham and Lincoln ASFiZCS, on Thursday morning, James Temporill was indicted for having wilfully murdered Annie Burton, in September. The jury returned a verdict of manslaughter, and a sentence of ten years' penal servitude was passed.—Ambrose Fletcher was sentenced to four months' imprisonment for unlawfully wounding John Linnell, in September. The first fruits of Lord Dufferin's mission to Cairo are e n in the issue of a decree by the Khedive whereby the 7&'e uropeatt Control is abolished. The French Ministry in their " declaration" before the Chambers on Thursday re- ferred to the Egyptian question. The occupation of Egypt by the British—a "novel event in European politics " had raised questions which specially concerned France. The British Government a day or two ago," spontaneously" made ceitain propositions which the French Government were discussing, and they promised to inform the Chambers of the result, " whatever tt might he." . .

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 11, 1882.

IT does not require much foresight to discern that Lord Randolph Churchill is to be the future leader of the Conservative party. He managed to make for himself a name for his audacity before the downfall of the Beacpnsfield Administration, and ever since the present Government came into office he has so per- sistently kept himself before the attention of the House and the country that he has at laid become a power amongst us. The present chiefs of the Con- servative party cannot afford to reckon without his support; and they would only be too glad if they could always depend upon his allegiance. The member for Woodstock is a veriW)le free lance, and he allows no opportunity to slip hen he fancies he

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOTEMBER‘II, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOTEMBER‘II, 1882.

. - can make a cut and score a point. Laugh at him as we may, we cannot close our eyes to the fact that the noble lord is possessed of abilities of no ordinary type, and it only requires care and discretion on his part to turn them to excellent account for his Own ad- vancement. But the noble lord is not always discreet. On two or three occasions during the present sittings of the House he has shown up both to the advantage and disadvantage of his own party. The mine which he attempted to spring upon the House at the com- mencement of the autumn sittings showed the noble lord was net wanting in resource, though, of course, there was nothing in it, yet it served a very good party purpose; on the other hand, this was, we think, more than counterbalanced by his recent attack upon the oecupants of the Front Opposition bench: whom he severely twitted with leaving the House without voting on certain of the Closure amendments. In the letter of the noble lord, published in the Timis of Monday, and which, we presume, was composed during the intervals of devotion the previous day, many writers recognise that he makes a distinct bid for the leadership of the party. We do not for a moment dispute that his lordship's ambition soars in that direction, and we believe that he will some day attain that, to some Conservatives, enviable position; but we think he has considerably weakened his chances of rapid promotion by the letter be has published. The noble lord's communication, which deals solely with the Closure, is speculative, and it is ingenious, and much that it 'soul ains will, we believe, he fahill-A by events. To us it is rather amusing haw his lordship makes out that the debates on Mr. Gibsou's amend- ment and Other& were only skirmishes prelimi- nary to the conflict on the Cloeure. which the noble lord says is only raised for the first time on the amendment negativing the first of the procedure rules sabmitted to the House of Com- mons by Sir Stafford Northoote, on Tuesday. Until die noble lord wrote we were under the impreasian that the Closure had been raised in the early part of the present session, when Mr. Marriott moved an amendment against it, and that the House had taade up its mind, and that, too, by a decisive majority, that the Speaker should have the power to close a debate. It is absurd, and a reflection upon the in- telligence of the House, to say that the Closure has only been raised by Sir Stafford Nortlacote's amend- ment. The fact is, it is only a waste of time to sub- mit such an amendment as Sir Stafford's ; and if it means anything at all, it only means this, that all the days, weeks, and months which have been spent over the irst resolution, as now amended, should be entirely thrown away. For this it cannotioe expected the House is prepared, and if it is not to stultify its action it must abide by the resolution. By a curious process of reasoning the noble lord estimates that the majority for the Government will range from only fifteen to thirty; but it appears to us it should be a matter of indifference what the majority is if there is a majority at all. The majority ought to rule, and we are sure that Lord Randolph Churchill would coincide in this opinion if he were on the Government side of the House. But the noble lord is a member of the Opposition. He sees the matter in another light, and therefore he argues, "It is a serious question whether the Conservative party would be justified in allowing so narrow a majority to make the Closure a standing order of the House of Commons, and thus permanently to crush freedom of speech." Why, the Conservative party cannot help itself. It must accept the decision of the majority; and if the noble lord wil only consult the records of legislation for the past century he will find that measures far transcending in their importance a mere rule of procedure have been passed and entered upon the statute book by very much smaller majorities than that which will be ob- tained to-night. To say the least, it is rather con- temptible of the noble lord even to suggest that, be- cause the Opposition is beaten, there should be re- course to obstruction in order to prevent the question of procedure from going forward, and if possible to intimidate the Government into dissolving Parlia- ment and appealing to the constituencies. This is not a question of confidence or no confidence in the Government, it is one which affects the members of Parliament a great deal more than it affects the con- stituencies ; and why there should be a dissolution when there is a majority at the back of the Govern- ment we are at a loss to understand. We are also .very much inclined to question the accuracy of the noble lord's prediction that an "appeal to the con- stituencies would be decisive against Closure and in favour of freedom of speech." We deny that freedom of speech is in any way endangered; we assert that if it were the Conservative party would net be true to its traditions if it defended free speech; and if the feeling af the constituen• cies may be judged by the very general support given in public and other meetings to the Closure, then we say the constituencies are decidedly in favour of the Government proposals. The mem- ber for Woodstock exhibits a greater lack of intelli- gence than we have u‘ually given him credit for when he says that the Tory party could not "choose a better moment or a more advantageous battlefield than is now offered to them." At any rate, Sir William Hart-Dyke, who ought to know something of these matters, thinks otherwise ; and, indeed, after the signal success which the Government has achieved in Egypt no less than in Ireland, there can, we believe, scarcely be two opinions that an appeal to the constituencies would result in a great Liberal gain. Lord Randolph pleads eloquently for his party, yet it is impossible in reading his letter not to be impressed with the fact that he is pleading for what is in reality a lost cause. Toryism has had its day ; it has been weighed in the balance of public opinion and found wanting. The two con- cluding sentences in the noble lord's letter contains the kernel of the whole thing. He says :—" If this opportunity is neglected either from pusillanimity or political miscalculation, Closure becomes the law of Parliament, and under its baneful influence legisla- tion aimed at the vitals of the Tory party will be pressed home. In two or three years, when this Par- liament draws to a natural close, the Liberals may have successfully manipulated the electorate, and the chance of the Tories will be gone." Lord Randolph knows what is the nature of the reforms which the present Government is pledged to carry through; he also knows the present Government will perform what it has promised; and he is not slow to recognise that I with an extended franchise and a more equitable re- presentation the chances of his, party vanish. He and they may stave off what may be considered by them the evil day; but come it must, and the sooner the better, say we. It may be, however, that when once tke member for Woodstock succeeds in upsetting the dual leadership, and when he finds himself installed by common consent chief, that he will lead the Conservatives again to victory; but we question whether that can be done by a policy of obstruction such as he advocates. We are disposed to think that if " obstruction " is to be the noble lord's cry he will, as Lord Salisbury found himself recently, have to advance to battle without an army behind him.

From information I have ',le to gather, the general iikee'6 feeling in the town is that the COan r,..°ners' in refusing to accept Mr. Hazlehurst's offer of a put-fl'er' PA.' ling-room, have acted 'somewhat unfairly with that gen'tnati, and have stultified one of their own actions; while, on t 119,3 othe: hand, it is believed Mr. Hazlehurst acted too precipltetely. In August last the Board decided to remove to Waterlo' House, when they could let their present offices at a fair rental, and they went to the expense of advertising that fact. Mr. Hazlehurst makes an offer which, after some vacillation, the Board postponed its consideration for six months without so much as giving a teason for the delay. True, Mr. Norman said the Committee, which had the matter in hand, had discussed the advisability of opening the library every night as a news-room up until March. But he was not prepared to pledge the Board to that course' and even if he had, Mr. Hazlehurst pointed out it wauld be unsatisfactory, as the lending of books and the reading of newspapers could not possibly take place in one small room. It can well be understood that the Board would not wish to take so import- ant a step as that proposed by Mr. Hazlehurst without coneideriug how it was to bb carried out, and hoar the funds at the disposal of the Library Committee would be effected. But surely Mr. Hazlehurst's promise that he would pledge himself that no financial difficulty should arise—legally pledge-himself, as he replied to a somewhat invidious ques- tion by the chairman—could be accepted. The terms of the promise were, perhaps, somewhat vague, but the inten- tions of the speaker, I think, could not be doubted. It is a pity that Mr. Hazlehurst vacated his position on the Board, which he has filled with credit to himself and advantage to the ratepayers, becatase his generosity did not meet with the recognition it merited ; but I am convinced that I ant speaking the feelings of the public at large when I say I hope his decision is not irrevocable, and that at the next meeting of the Board he will again be occupying his seat in our local legislature, and watching over the interests of his native town.
