LEcrunE AT WIDNES.—In behalf of the funds of the new Oakland-street Chapel, which is fast appfoaching comple- tion, a lecture on " Martin Luther " was given in Laces - street schoolroom, on Monday evening, by the Rev. W. Par- sonage. The Rev. R. Harper occupied the chair. GOOD TEMPLARY AT WIDNES.—The. usual weekly meet- ing of the members of the Star of Widnes lodge, 1.0.G.T., was held on Wednesday evening, when a miscellaneous en- tertainment of an enjoyable character was given by the members of the Hope of Appleton lodge. Bro. T. Baron' presided, and Bro. T. Reay delivered appropriate addresses. ELLESMERE-STREET MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUN- CORN.—At the usual meeting of the above class, held on Monday evening last, an interesting essay on " Air" was read by Mr. John Holfo:d. A discuskin ensued, in which the Rev. John Billington, Mr. E. Jones, Mr. J. Stubbs, and the essayist took part. o'rliere was a large attendance of members. The chair was occupied by Mr. E. Gandy, the president. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY LECTURES.—As we stated in these columns a few weeks ago, the Library Committee have decided to give a course of free lectures during the winter months. The first of the series will be delivered in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Thursday evening next, by Mr. J. R Frith. The subject is" Illuminating gases," in which Mr. Frith is well able to deal, and it will be made extremely interesting by numerous experiments. The Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., RD., is announced to presid3. It is to he hoped that this laudable effort by the committee will meet with the success it merits.

WIDNES BRANCH OF THE CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPER- ANCE SOCIETY.—Under the auspices of this society a lecture was delivered in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes, on Thursday evening, by the Rev. J. R. Eyre, M.A., rual dean, of Toxteth, and incumbent of St. Michael's, near Liverpool. The chair was occupied by the Vicar of Widnes, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams. The clergy of the district were present. The lecturer spoke on the aims of the society. At the con- clusion of the lecture, inseconding a vote of thanks to the chairman, the Rey. George Bond said, until a few days ago he had belonged to the non abstaining section of the com- munity; but at the recent meeting of his own society he had taken the pledge for the sake of example to some who seemed half inclined, and yet needed stron;ly urging to Join.

A WORKMEN'S CLUE FOR FARNWORTEL—Temperance organisations in and around Widnes are displaying great zeal in their work, and adopting many methods by which to reclaim the drunkard. But a project which has not before been attempted in connection with a temperance society, was decided upon at a meeting of the Farnworth Church of England Temperance Society, on Tuesday even- ing. This was to open a reading-room. The vicar of the parish, the Rev. J. Bond, presided, and in his advocacy of the establishment of the reading-room, he was warmly supported by the Rev. J. Holden, Mr. J. W. Davies, and others, and the meeting seemed unanimously in favour of the project. A committee of workingmen was appointed to manage the club, which it was decided should occupy the boys' school-room. It was also decided that the officials of the temperance society should occupy the same positions in regard to the committee, viz., the Rev. G. Bond, president; the Rev. J. Holden, Mr. J. W. Davies and Miss Hilbert, vice-presidents, and Mr. F. Whiteside, secretary. • The club, we understand, will be opened to-day (Saturday). LECTURE ON CHINA AT H ALTON.—At the meeting of the members of Halton Parish Church Mutual Improvement Society, on Tuesday, a lecture on China and the Chinese, was delivered by the Rev. F. L. Farmer, vicar of Millbrook, Stalybridge. The Rey. J. Lockwood, vicar, presided, and there was a good audience. The lecturer, at the outset, said China possessed the oldest government in the world, the Chinese themselves asserting that it had an existence many thousand of years before Noah's flood. They had an ancient . organised system of standing militia, awl their written language, their historians and poets went hack to the im- mediate successors of Moses. There had been many changes of dynasty, but the policy of the Chinese had re- mained the same, and generation after generation inherited the same intense jealousy of foreigners. The practical qualities of the Chinese and their mechanical ingenuity, were remarkable, and to them we were indebted for the in- vention of printing, paper making,- gunpowder, spectacle lenses, and the mariner's compass. The lecturer comm,nted upon the teachings of Confucins, the father of Chinese philosophers, and the Chinese system of religion; and dwelt at some length upon England's opium war with China, and its results. He related some interesting particulors of the labours of the Church Missionary Society in Chins, and quoted statistics showing the extent and value of the work. The proceedings concluded with the usual votes of thanks.

THE WIDNES LABOURER AND nrs CLOGS.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Henry Stowles and Catherine Matthews were charged in custody with stealing a pair of clogs of the vane of 33, the property of William Shea, a labourer living at 34, Cromwell-street, Widnes. It appeared that Shea purchased the clogs on Saturday night, and whilst conveying them home between 11 and .12 o'clock, he stopped near the White Star Hotel, Queen-street, talking with a woman named McDonald. The prisoner Matthews came up, took the clogs from under his arm, and walked rapidly away. Subsequently, he again saw Matthews who denied any knowledge of the clogs. Witness admitted that he had had some drink.—Ann McDonald corrotorated this statement, and Miss Winifred Short, who keeps a cloo-4er's shop in Anne-street Wee, identified the clogs.—Wm. Lock, of 20, Gerard-street, Widnts, said, whilst working on the railway near the Arch Hotel, he saw a person whom ha be- lieved to be the prisoner Stowles walking past with the pair of clogs produced in his possession. He SW the man throw the clogs into a pool of water.—Peter Riley, seid on Sunday he saw the prisoner Stowles wearing a pair of clogs similar to those produced. He asked him where he had got , them, and he said " Kate bought them for me on Saturday night."--P.S: Robinson deposed to apprehending the pri- soners on Tuesday. When he charged Matthews, she replied, "it's a lie, Ann McDonald stole them." He also charged Stowles with receiving the clogs knowing them to have been stolen. He replied "I knee, nothing about them. Bate said she had bought them."—The prisoners were com- mitted to the sessions for trial. GALE AT WIDNES: CHIMNEY BLOWN DOWN.—A gale of unusual intensity, accompanied with heavy rain, broke ever Widnes on .Wednesday afternoon, and continued for some time. Whilst it was at its height, the top part of the tall chimney of the Composite Ore Works was blown down, and the falling brickwork alighted upon the roDf of one of the sheds, doing considerable damage. Many people were at work in the shed at the time, but fortunately they all escaped uninjured. The same afternoon the wall of Mr. Robert Shaw's works was also levelled to the ground.

ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A 'WIDNES WIDOW. OR Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, James Bate, a young man, was summoned to answer a charge of assaulting a widow named Jane Shaw. It appeared that on Sunday night Mrs. Shaw was speaking to the wife of the defendant with reference to some false reports which had been circu- lated about when the defendant came rushing from his house. He attempted to strike complainant's daughter, but the mother placed her between them, and the defendant struck her a blow in the face with a tambourine.—Witnesses were called on each side, and the Bench dismissed the case AN OLD OFFENDER AT RUNCORN —At the Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, a woman named Fanny Roscoe was brought up under a warrant charged with being disorderly on the licensed premises of Sarah Abrams, the Blue Ball Inn, and refusing to quit on the 7th June. She was also charged with having, on the same day, committed a breach of the peace by fighting. Evidence having been given, she was fined 10s. and costs on the first charge, or 14 days' hard labour, and on the second she was bound over to keep the peace, or in default, a month's hard labour. She went to gaol.

MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR AT WEsroN.—The inhabitants of the ordinarily quiet village of Weston are at preent labour- ing under some little excitement consequent upon the dis- appearance of three men from the locality. The men in question are natives of Northwich, but for some time past have worked at Weston Works, and are named John and Daniel Dalton (uncle awl nephew), and John Gandy. On Wednesday afternoon, it is stated, they were drinking to- gether at the Dock Hotel, which they left in a state of in- toxication. Since then they have not been seen in the place, and a very general opinion is held that they have been drowned in the canal. No reason can be given for this opinion, we understand, except the state of the men, but it is the most probable explanation of the my stery.

POTATO ROBBERY AT HALE.—William Thorpe, a young fellow, living in High-street, Hale, was brought up on re- mand, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, ona charge of stealing a quarter of a cwt. of potatoes, the property of David Penk, who is a painter, residing at Hale. The pro- secutor said in his garden, which was enclosed, was a thorn fence, there had been a heap of potatoes for the past month, and ten days ago were covered with soil. On Saturday evening, about four o'clock, the potatoes were safe. From something that was said to him about half-past ten, on Sun- day morning, be examined the potato heap and found that a hole had been made in it and more than a peck of pota- toes abstracted. The hole had been filled up again.—P.C. Roberts deposed that about three o'clock, on Sunday morn- , , leg, he was on luty in Hale village, when he saw the pri- soner come out of his home and go in the direction of Peuk's garden. About an hour afterwards he saw him re- turning and noticed that he had a bag under his arm. Wit- ness stopped him and found that he was carrying the bag of potatoes produced. Witness charged him with stealing them. He said he had found them ; but the constable took . him into custody. He subsequently ascerta,ned that they , had been stolen from Penk's garden.—lt was stat6d that the prisoner had been previously convicted of a similar offence and twelve months ago he was convicted of stealing half a sovereign.—The Bench committed the prisoner to the , Quarter Sessions for trial.

UNLAWFUL WOUNDING AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions., on Wednesday, Mary Clarke, a young woman, and John McHugh were emerged on remand with unlawfully wounding John Clark, with intent to de him grievous bodily harm.—The prosecutor said he was a labourer, and lived at 3, Nelson-street, Widnes. The female prisoner was his sister. About nine o'clock on Monday evening he went to the house No. 3, King-street, where his sister resided, accom. puled by Peter Riley. When he go to the house, the prisoner McHugh came out, and said they were making fun of him, addit g that they were not to do the same as they did on Saturday night. McHugh then pulled off his coat, and said he would fight "the two of them," meaning the prose- cutor and Riley, at the same time striking the former a blow in the face with his fist. A fight ensued, during which the prisoner Clarke struck her brother on the head with half a brick, inflicting a wound, and knocking him to the ground. He was rising from the ground, when he received a second blow with some heavy instrument' and he was again felled to the ground. McHugh was all this time striking witness with his fist. He would not swear that he was struck on the head with the poker produced. He did not see the poker in the hands of his sister or McHugh. He was not aware that he had stated he was struck with the poker. He was not stunned, and could remember everything that took place. He bad two wounds, one on the- top of the head and one at the corner of the left eye, and he had lost a great quantity of blood. He had recently had a quarrel with his sister.—Peter Riley. who said he lived at 74, Terrace-road, Widnes, deposed to accompanying the prisoner at the time stated, and corro- borated his statement. He saw the female pri.oner pick up a piece of a brick and strike Clarke a blow on the head, which knocked him to the ground. Clarke rose from the groinid, when the female prisoner gave the poker to the prisoner McHugh, who struck the prosecutor on the bead with it. Clarke again fell to the ground. The prisoners then went into the house, and witness sent for the police. Neither witness nor Clarke gave the prisoners any provocation.—T female prisoner, who conducted herself very defiantly, here said excitedly that the witness "transporting McHugh wrong." He was too close to her brother to strike him with the poker.— in cross-examination by Mr. McHugh, witness stated the prosecutor pulled his belt off but did not get a chance to use it.—James Clark, labourer, living at 3, King-street, with his sister, gave evidence which corroborated that of the former witnesses. In reply to Mr. McHugh, he said the prosecutor pulled off his belt and struck at the former.—Dr. Urguahart McLennan stated that on Monday night Clark went to his surgery. He examined him and found he was suffering from a lacerated wound on the back of the head. It was about an inch long and penetrated to the bone, which was exposed. There was a small punctured wound on the top of the head, abeut a quarter of an inch long, and penetra- ting to the bone. There was also a small punctured wound at the margin of the left eyebrow, and three or four super- ficial scratches on the face. He diessed the wounds. The prosecutor had lost a great deal of blood. A poker or a stone and brick, with a shirp corner, might have inflicted the wounds.—P.O. Lang deposed to apprehending the prieenere. When charged McHugh replied, "I used no poker." Prisoner Clark said, " Nlellogh never touched my brother, except with Ilk flit, I did. it all."—Tuo prisoners were committed to take their trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

Chadwick, Charles Frederick Timme, what the ptisonet's a sea captain, was summoned by Matthew John Crunnie that he refused to pay him the sum of £4, being a sum justly due to him for services performed on board the vessel Jane Hughes.—Mr. Leak appeared for the complainant, and Mr. W. H. Linaker for the defendant. From the statement of Mr. Leak it appeared that the action was taken under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1854, and the facts of the case were these : The complainant is an ableaeaman, and on Tuesday night, the 31st Oetc,ber, he met the defendant, who was the master of the vessel Jane Hughes, and agreed to ship with him as mate at the wages of £4 a month. In consequence the complainant went on board the same night, taking with him his clothes, and on the following day he assisted in lead- ilia and removing the vessel down to the basin to beready to go down the river by the next tide. No complaint was made of the complainant's work, but on Thursday evening the captain told him that he did not think they should agree together, and that he had better go; for he (the captain) would not have him. The complainant's clothes were brought up from the cabin, put on the deck, and he was told to take them away. He did so, and the summons was taken out.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Linalter complainant ad- mitted that be had not signed any agreement.—The section of the Act under which the summons was taken made it necessary that before a man could recover he should sign an agreement, and the Bench consequently dismissed the eurnmons.—The Bench thought the complainant entitled to his wages for the days on which he had worked, and the captain agreed to pay him Sc.

THE REV. W. PRETON, OF RUNCORN, ON TiTrE SIGNS or THE TIIIFS —Preaching at Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, on Sunday night, from the text "And there shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars," the Rev. W. Preston described the cornet now appearing in the heavens, and said:some might ask, were they to regard it as a phenomenon, or to accept it as a sign of the times? The visible brilliant appearance might be unusual, but the teles- cope detected the existence of more than one comet yearly. Without diligent search none might be seen, hence no special stress need be laid on such appearances. Superstitions might fill men's minds with all kinds of fearful fancies, and lead them to imagine; A dire catastrophe was nigh. Scrip- ture did, indeed, speak of signs in the heavens wiiich should i usher in the second coming of Christ. But paradoxical 38 it might seem, the signs in the heavens were to be looked for more on earth. Those images were not to be taken literally. They were too often used by the sacred writers to denote great earthly calamities. As the falling of the stars, or the veiling of the sun, would he a dire calamity, so troubles amongst nations, the overthrow of kingdoms, anarchy in states, were figured by convulsions in the elements of nature. Lloking. then, from the heavens to the earth, had they any signs they were in the last times? Yes! here -had they witnesses, and one of the strongest was I the fiend-like spirit of lawlessness which was spreading on all sides. rue apostle predicted the appearance of a ' 'lawless one" ere the end. In Franc', a secret society existed termed L' Anarchic, which had associates through- out the world. The avowed object was to overthrow every I kind of government, the weapons being the bullet, knife, I dynamite, or any other agent of destruction which could throw society into terror and confusion. Was it not strange that a Roan Catholic country, and those of that faith, should give birth to such fiendish designs ? But it was what might be expected. Infidelity was the natural outcome of Popery, and the prophecy of scripture represented the spirit of lawlessness as the offshoot of Popery and priestcraft. A marked sign of the times was thus before us. Many things , betokened the end. What was their duty? If they had 1 given their hearts to God, if they were trusting in Jesus, and repented of sin, then these signs of Christ's return might gladden their hearts.

A VAGRANT'S RUSE DETECTED AT RUNCORN.—Her- bert Marston, evidently an old tramp, was brought before Mr. It. M. Brooke and Mr. James Reynolds, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, charged with having, on Satur- day night, unlawfully applied for relief to Inspector Hol- lin,gworth. The Inspector stated that on Saturday night the prisoner went to the police station and asked him for a ticket for a night's lodgings. Witness saw that he was some- what in drink, and asked him where he had come from. He replied St. Helens," and added that a friend had paid for him two glasses of whiskey. Witness remarked that it would have been better if he had paid for him a night's lodging, and directed that the prisoner should be searched. Upon him was found a quantity of bread and cheese and sd, whereupon he was locked up.. The prisoner made a state- ment, in which be said he was a stranger in Runcorn, and was a "hard sufferer from asthma." The Bench committed him to gaol for 14 days with hard labour. YOTITIIFIIL GAMESTER AS RUNCORN WLIES.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, a youth named Edwd. Quine was charged with gaming on Runcorn fair ground on Saturday night. l•risoner pleaded guilty. Mr. Inspec- tor Hollingwort'u said shortly before eight o'clock on Saturday night he was on duty on the fair ground, when he saw a crowd of people, in the midst of whom was the priso- ner. He watched the prisoner sell five rings at 2d each, the ,1 latter each time telling the purchaser to put his hand into a box and draw forth a ticket. One person who bought a ring got a ticket on which was marked a shilling. He requested the prisoner to give him the shilling, but the latter refused, and threatened to assault the man. The man then said he would fetch the police, when the inspector stepped up and took the prisoner into custody. The priso- ner commenced to cry, and said if the magistrates would let him go he would never do anything wrong again. He haa to go to work at an iron foundry on Tuesday morning. Mr. Superintendent Williamson said the prisoner gave him an address in Manchester, where he stated his parents lived. He had communicated with the police authorities at Man- chester, and they bad replied that the persons were not known at the address. He, however, had no wish to press the case. The Bench fined the prisoner 61 and costs 6s 4d, or in default seven days' haid labour. Prieoner went to gaol.

UNITED CHESHIRE AND LANCASHIRE P. B. B. SOCIETY, RIINCORN.—The annual meeting of the society was held on Thursday night, in Holy Trinity girls' school. The report stated that owing to a large depression in trade and to the paying of a smaller dividend than usual during the past two years, there had been an almost unprecedented 1 number of withdrawal notices, and the committee were advised that until the notices were either satisfied - or withdrawn they could neither pity dividend riot advance money on mortgage. The profits of the society would have paid a dividend of four per cent., but for the fact that £674 ss. 7d. had been spent on exceptional repairs to the properties in the possession of the scalety. The balance of profit, £1,286 Sc. El, not being paid as dividend would add to the present strength of the society, and thus the profit would not be lost to the con- tinuing shareholders but only postponed until the with- drawals were satisfied. It was hardly necessary to point out that withdrawing members would not participate in any During the past year the committee had separated the reserve fund account and its investments from the ordinary accounts and investments of the society. The reserve fund and balance of profit now amounted to £4,703 145., to corer any loss the society might sustain.

ORANGE DEMONSTRATION AT WIDNES.—The mem- bers of the No. 249 Invincible Loyal Orange Lodge, held their annual demonstration on Monday evening. The pro- ceedings commenced with a tea, which was served in the! Tolunteer Hall, and of which about five hundred persons partook. Subsequently, a public meeting was held, under the presidency of Bro. W. Rankin, Master of the Widnes Lodge. The Revs. J. Wright-Williams (vicar of Widnes), G. Bond (vicar of Farnworth), W. Preston kvicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn), W. H. Duggan, and the members of the local lodge occupied seats on the platform.—The Chairman having delivered a short address, the Rev. W. Preston, who was enthusiastically greeted on rising, addressed the assembly. He remarked that he was willing to assist Roman Catholics where assistance was needed. (Applause.) In his own parish he had Roman Catholics, and where he pos- sibly could he helped them. He did not look at creed. He looked upon a Roman Catholic as a brother, a fellow-man who had got a soul. As Orangemen those present were Protestants, and their principles as gathered from one of their books were—First, to support and defend their. rightful sovereign ; secondly, to maintain the Protestant religion in Church and State; and, thirdly, to maintain the laws of the realm. :(Applause.) This being Orangeism, he thought it was deserving of sympathy, and he could not see how any right-minded person could object to it.—The Rev. George Bond expressed the hope that all those present were.; good Conservatives; adding that he supposed it was almost derogatoryto call oneself a Conservative in these davr, a remark which was received with laughter. But it was'only for a time ; there was a good time coming. The rev, gentle- man went on to explain bow the Conservatives were defeated at the last general election, by the flood of party oratory which deluged the country.—The Rev. W. H. Duggan observed that the crowded and enthusiastic audience which had gathered in that ball, showed that the Church of England was not losing its hold upon the work- ing classes, and that its power was not dead. Orangemen bad done great and undoubted service to the Church in the past, for which the Church was grateful._ The Vicar of Widnes referred to the origin of the Order of Orangemen, and said he did not care what those present were so long aa they were helpers to him, and he urged upon them as good Orangemen, and therefore, presumably, good churchmen, the duty that devolved unon them of coming to church and taking part in parochial work.—The evening's proceedings were enlivened by songs and recitations, which were given by the follosvia, :—Bros. Mdkio, Junnings, JAck,on, Garton, Powell, and Kifunt. A vote of thanks to thd chairmait iKought the meeting to a close. •

Rusconx Bunrer. BOSRD.—The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. W. Whittaker, the chairman. There were also present Messrs. H. Coleman, James Handley, William Mellor, Thos. Norman, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary).—Mr. Jas. Handley read the financial statement, which stated the amount received for fees during October was £53 12s, aril fees received from 11 certificates £2 15. The sum of £ll 13s 6Li had been received for a half year's rent of the field, and 14s 6d for grass, making a total income of .£6B 15s. There had been £ll 193 61 paid for wages, and the balance, £56 15s 6d, had been paid into bank'. The committee recom; mended the renewal of the mortgages of Mrs. Kenwright and Mr. James Ball, at 4 per cent. They also recommended the payment of the balance of £9 on Mr. Farrell's account, and £1 5s 6el for general repairs. The report was adopted. —The Secretary reported that daring the seven months end- ing October 25th, there had been 210 interments. The num- ber during the same period last year was 138, being an increase of 81. The fees received during the same period amounted to £2OB 15a 2d; corresponding period last year, £l3O 17s 4d; increase, £77 17s 10d.—This was all the busi- ness of public interest.

A VIOLENT DEIINELED AT 11,17NCOUN.—Harry Cole- burn, a strong-looking middle-aged man, was charged at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, with being drunk and disorderly, and refusing to quit the Commercial Hotel, with assaulting Thomas Ashton, the landlord, and also with assaulting Thomas Maloney. It appeared that on Saturday night the prisoner went to the Commercial Hotel in a state of drunkenness and demanded admission. His demand was, of course, refused, and without more ado be burst open time door, and, being in a combative state of mind, struck the landlord and the waiter. P.C. Davenport came on the scene, but the violence of the prtsoner was not rasily restrained, and six men found ample employment in eject- ing him from the house. When outside Maloney came in his way, and he twice knocked him to the ground by blows administered with his fist. Prisoner said he was so drunk he knew nothing of the occurrence, and, to " please the magis- trates," he pleaded guilty. For three years he had sold watercresses in Runcorn, and never in his life berore had he been before a bench of magistrates. The prisoner was fined 5s and costs in each case, total £1 us 4d.—ln connection with this case a woman named Margaret Jones was brought before the Bench charged with resisting P.C. Davenport whilst in the execution of his duty. The woman, it ap- peared, tried to rescue Coleburn from the custody of the constable, but, failing in her attempt, she too found herself in " durance vile." She was fined 103 and costs,
