WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. • ELECTION OF MAYOR. In common with the municipal authoritiestlmughout thecountry, the members of the Warrington Town Council were on Thursday called upon to elect a Mayor to preside over their deliberations for the ensuing year. For several years now this appointment, which is in many towns one of a most formal character, has• been regarded in Warrington with the greatest interest, and that that interest has in no way diminished, was shown on Thursday by the large -number of ratepayers who attended to witness the proceed- ings. For some time before noon, at which hour the pro- ceedings commenced, that portion of the Council Chamber set apart for the accommodation of ratepayers was com- pletely packed, and many of the leading townspeople who could not obtain admission there were provided with seats in the Council Chamber itself. Amongst those present were—Major Cartwright, Messrs. H. B. White, E. J. Vicholson John Harrison, W. D. Jeans, J. Fairclough, J. White, P. Davies, E. Bolton. G. H. Bolton, S. Hunt, Rev. 'S. Wilkinson, G. Blackburst, Z. Armitage, Thos. Hall, F. A. Roberts, W. Tinsley, W. Burn T. Jolley, H. Roberts, Rev. E. St. A. Duke, V. Davies, B. Percival, Arthur H. Crosfield, W. Roberts, itc. The first member of the Council in his place was Councillor Taylor, and soon after him entered Alderman Harrison, who was greeted with a demonstration of favour by the spectators. The chamber then rapidly filled, and the Mayor (Alderman Fick- mere),wto wore the robes of office, having taken the chair, the proceedings commenced. The few vacant seats at the table were presently taken possession of, and it was then found that only four members were absent—Councillors Platt, Sutton, Collin, and Ashton. It was known that two gentlemen would be nominated for the position of mayor, and the general expectation was that those gentlemen would be Aldermen Davies and Harrison, whose claims to the high office had been discussed at a preliminary meeting of the Council. In the morning of the day of election, however, it was stated that Councillor John Crosfieid would be pro- posed, but as it turned out a surprise was in store for those who attended, as a gentleman who had never been mentioned before was nominated. Alderman Thewlis had proposed Alderman Harrison, to whose long services he briefly adverted, and the proposition bad been seconded by Councillor Wright, when Alderman Davies rose. After a long speech, in which he spoke of his connection with the Coun- cil, and the opposition that had been encountered during that period, and pointed out the undesirability of his being made mayor on account of the position he occupied respect- ing the Ship C tnal Scheme, the alderman greatly surprised all present by proposing as mayor Councillor Litton, on the ground that he was the representative of one of the men who had in former days interested themselves in the free navigation of the river Mersey to Warrington. This pro- position was seconded by Alderman Burgess, but Councillor Litton, evidently as much surprised as others, declined to stand. Councillor Monks then nominated Councillor Crosfield, and Councillor Greening having seconded, a lively discussion ensued, which will be found fully reported below. The debate seemed to afford the onlookers considerable pleasure, and they gave vent to their feelings in frequent expressions of approval, which at one time became so loud that the Mayor was obliged to request them not to be so demonstrative. After nearly two hours' discussion, the vote was taken with the result that Councillor Crosfield was elected by a majority of seven votes, the division showing 18 members in favour of Councillor Crosfield and 11 on the side of Alderman Harriton. The newly-male Mayor at once assumed the insignia of office, and on taking his seat thanked the Council for the honour they had conferred upon him. Alderman Harrison also thanked the members who had sup' ported his nomination, and the proceedings terminated.

The members present were—the Mayor (Alderman Pick- mere), who presided; Aldermen Holmes, Davies, Chandley, Thewlis,Burgess,Harrison,Kean,and Webster; and Councillors Taylor, Francomb, Greening, Litton, John Pierpoint, Brown, Monks, Broadbent, Crostield, Milner, Wallington, Burgess, Woolfall, Barker, Wm. Pierpoint, Caldwell, Wright, Dixon, Mackie, Hutchinson, Wm. Bolton, and Dakin ; Messrs. W. H. Brook (tcwn clerk),. J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), and T. Longdin (borough surveyor). The MAYOR called upon the Town Clerk to read the return of the election of new members to the Council, and this having been done, the Mayor said the next business before the Council was the election of mayor for the ensu- ing year. He should be dad to hear any gentleman pro- posed and seconded. He might state that he should take the votes in the manner it had always been usual. After the proposer and seconder had concluded their observatiotss, any other gentleman might make remarks upon the subject, and he should then ask for those gentlemen " for" to stand, and then those "against" to stand up. A pause ensued, when Alderman THEWLIS rose to his feet, and said as no one seemed to propose a gentleman to fill the seat which the Mayor had so honourably and straightforwardly occupied, he begged to propose a gentleman to succeed him in office, who he believed would be a faithful and straightforward man, a man who had a large amount of tact and ability, a gentleman who had served the Council for a series of years —he thought for something like 17 or 18 years—a gentle- man who had occupied prominent positions in Warrington, and without leaving any gentleman present in further sus- pense he named the man at once—Mr. Alderman Harrison. (Applause.) Mr. Alderman Harrison had been in the Council, as he had obeerved before, for a series of years. He knew right well that in going through life whilst occupying a seat in the Council chamber, they could not always agree, but Dr. Johnson's principle was "Agree to differ for the sake of provoking argument." Possibly Mr. Alderman Harrison might pursue that course, but he believed that in every transaction since be (Alderman Thewlis) had been identified his (Alderman Harrison's) motives had been truly honolir- able, strictly conscientious, and an anxious desire to dis- charge the duties of that office—(hear, hear, and applause) —with due regard to the interests of the rate- payers at large. He could not understand why any demonstration should take er,?ace there, but he did ittiote what the public feeling of Warrington was; and that was that Mr. Alderman Harrison had long been put on one side. He hoped that that day they should have an unani- mous vote, and that staightferward and consistently. (Hear, hear.) He believed that if the Council thought fit to elect Alderman Harrison, they would find that he would discharge the duties as faithfully and honourably as the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) had done, and before he sat down he begged to reiterate his opinion which he expressed at a former meeting, that the Council had been admirably sustained in having a gentleman to fill the office in the im- partial manner in which Alderman Pickrnere had done. May his life be long spared, and may he be as useful a member of the Counsil as he had been Mayor. He, therefore, begged to propose Mr. Alderman Harrison as a fit and proper person to succeed in the office of Mayor. (Ap- plause.) The Mayor having inquired whether any gentleman would second the resolution, Mr. Councillor WRIGHT said he had great pleasure in seconding Mr. Alderman Harrison's nomination. Mr. Alderman TEIEWLIS here asked if he might be per- mitted just to add a few sentences. The MAYOR: Well, you must make it short. Mr. Alderman THEWLIS then said he would only add one sentence more. Mr. Councillor Platt was exceedingly ill at Lome, but he wished him (Alderman Thewlis) to convey to the Council how much he regretted not having the privilege to nominate Mr. Harrison that morning. Mr. Alderman DA.YIES then said he dared say they had often seen some of their lady acquaintances, aye, and gentle- men too, pass their finger down the romantic side of the catalogue of a library to find out something that should be startling, amusing, and interesting too. (Hear, hear.) He was going to give ' them the title of what he was going to talk about at that moment. It was, "Blessed is the man who can wait." (Hear, hear.) Now, he considered that he was that day the best abused man in Warrington—(hear, bear)—and he had afforded to wait. If they would allow him he wished to have a little latitude, because for two months he had received more slanderous and calumnious remarks in the papers than any man in Warrington—.(hear, hear)—and hitherto he had held his peace. Therefore he thought he could appeal to the Mayor, and he could appeal to the.members of the Council, in ask- ing for himself the utmost latitude in what he was now going to say, always bearing this in mind that whatever latitude they did giere him, he would propose to them in the end a gentleman who he thought it was pre-eminently desirable should be mayor of this borough, and especially at this moment when they hoped that Warrington would push forward the interests of the Manchester Ship Canal. (Hear, hear.) Now he thought he might trespass upon his Worship whilst in the civic throes of death—(laughter)—or rather in the throes of civic death, and ask him to suspend his dissolution, or rather allow him (Alderman Davies) to keep him for say some half hour longer, for his Worship had so well fulfilled the duties that theme dyes and the inhabitants of Warring- ton would be thankful to him that he had actually kept alive so able a mayor as his Worship had been. (hear, hear.) That morning the Council was called upon to exercise its powers as the legal representatives of the people of War- rington. Everyone round that table that day was called upon to exercise his right with independence, and without Interference from any outside influence,—(hear, hear)—and he was. bound to support a mayor who would be beyond I all outside influences in representing the people of the town. (Hear, hear.) :Therefore, be said, the Council was about to ' undergo a crucial test as to whether it was a representative ' body—(hear, hear)---.and whether it could afford to live on 1 its own means and its own powers. (Hear, hear.) He hoped the Council would be patient with him as he had asked them to be before, because when he finished he would be quite prepared to propose a gentleman for the office of mayor, as he (Aldo man Davies) wag not the best man to be the mayor at that moment. Some. thirteen or fourteen years ago' he entered that Council immediately after a defeat that the Conservatives sustained. He went into the Council im- pregnated with a sort of bitter feeling he adraitted,—they were all more or lees liable to it, as all on the other side knew—(laughter)—but when he did enter the Council he found that the men of both political parties forgot all their differences,—(hear, hear)—and were of one mind and heart in supporting the interests of Warrington, and he became thoroughly satisfied that politics in the Council Chamber were a bane and a curse. (Hear, hear.) Well, they went on to 1871. He thought he was right in saying that he believed at that time he bad only been three years in the Council, but he was unanimously elected as mayor of the town. (Hear, hear.) Knowing the responsibilities of the office he had undertaken, he begin to consider whether it

was passible to do seraethihg to show that he was worthy of the high honour he bad received at the hands of the Council, and it turned out at the latter end of his year of office that such an olreortunity presented itself, which was unique in the history of the Council. The Council had then to sit in a close unhealthy chamber in Market-street; but, through what he should call the handsome conduct of Colonel Wilson Patten—now Lord Win:narleigh—they had an opportunity of buying that valuable property in which they were that day assembled. With the assistance of Alderman Helmes.and Mr. J. C. Sutton, who was then a coun- cillor, they were successful in arranging terms acceptable to Lord Winrnarleigh and the Chrancil. One would have thought that what they were doing was outside the range of opposition; and that the advantages of the purchase were so apparent to men's minds that there could he no opposi- tion. He would carry their mlads back to the time of the ' purchase of that Hall. Ii . the local Press, identified with which was Mr. Alderman Harrison—he would mention the name as little as he could. (Hear, hear.) Alderman THEWLIS : Certainly. Alderman DAVIES: In your eloquent remaiks, Alderman Thewlis, I did not interrupt you. Alderman TH.EWLIS : I do not think it fair to make it personal. Alderman DAVIES said he would not make personal refer- ences. He was not going to appeal to any man's sympathy; and he was not going to impute motives to any man, but he was going to state facts, and if the names of persons were connected with the facts they would come out. (Hear, hear.) He was speaking of their endeavours to arrange terms with Lord Winmarleigh for the purchase of that property, the advantages of which were now so apparent, and which ought to have been apparent at the time. What was the result? He especially, and many other members of the , Council, had to submit to inuendo paragraphs, anonymous slanderous letters from week to week, aye, from month to month; and if it had not been for the determination of those members of the Council, who, he was sure, were proud to refer to that time if it had not been for the support of Alderman Holmes, himself, and Councillor Sutton received from the- hands of the Council, that property would have been lost to the town. (Hear, hear.) How was it brought about? Paragraphs had become so rife to encourage the people outside in opposition that a poor innocent man stated that he the then Mayor of Warrington, had received a bribe from Lord Winmarleig,h, to sell the property to the town. He commenced an action against the man with the result that he apologised and expressed his sorrow for what he had said; and he was so satisfied himself that the man was a victim that he let him off. But that man was the victim of persons who had prompted him to take the course he had done, and he was more or less supported by the Press of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Let him refer at that moment to the fact that so strong was the pressure and so strong were the anonymous letters written about him that many, many nights' sleep had he lost; and if it had not been for the encouragement he received from a noble man, who was not a member of the Council or in any way connected with it, and the assurance of that man that he should carry the matter to a successful issue, he would have failed. But that man not only gave him moral support, but he sub- stantiated it witb a gift which he afterwards raised from £5,000 to £lO,OOO. (Hear, hear.) He referred to Mr. George Crosfield. (Applause.) Now he did not object to honest, honourable newspaper paragraphs. They were desirable to keep men to their posts, political, or otherwise. In 1874 he worked as hard as any man in the Conservative ranks—he did not say it as a boast—and spent as much money and time as anyone, except the candidate; but he received nothing from his opponents—yes, they hit him hard, but never below the belt. (Hear, hear.) That was the sort of thing he liked. From time to time the Council had not hesitated to put their shoulders to the wheel, and at all times, not only had they done their duty, but pushed on the interests of Warrington. At another time, when Alderman Webster was mayor, and they were engaged in pushing forward the interests of Warrington, they were worried almost to death by slanderous letters that appeared from day to day and week to week; and he was bound to mention the fact that the proprietor of the Press and Mr. Alderman Harrison were again allied in this matter. He could not shut the fact from his mind. Let them follow it further. He said those anonymous letters, and said it with- out contradiction, were not the work of more than three or four men working in and around; it was not the voice of the people of Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He said, and said it advisedly, if any man would take the trouble to read those letters, to read them carefully, and look between the lines he would find there was a sentiment pervading them that could not go outside the counsel of those men. But let him refer to Mr. Alderman Webster, a man who did his duty well. But se much did he feel the responsibility of the pesition in w hich he was placed that he, poor Alderman Webster, broke down under it, and his own wife—he hoped he was not encroaching too much upon domestic life—came to him and begged and prayed of him to go into the house, and give Alderman Webster that moral support he required, as he felt he might never get over it, but might die. He went into the house, and he believed if he had not given him that moral support he did, in the face of those anonymous slanderous letters. Alderman Webster would not have been in the chair he occupied that day. But Alderman Webster was a man of kindly disposition, and he did not hesitate to read to them a letter he wrote to him (Alderman Davies). He said, writing on Nov. sth : "Dear Mr. Davies,—l think it is only right that I should explain to you that some months ago I promised Harrison I would vote for him if he were again nominated, never dreaming that you would be again brought forward. I was actuated by a feeling that he had been punished severely and enough, and that now by-gones might be by-genes. But I must assure you that, though I vote for -him, there is no feeling of antagonism against you, and I trust that you will not for one moment think there is.— Believe me, yours very truly, S. M. WEBSTER." He read that letter with a great amount of satisfaction. It told of a kindly disposition, and he respected Alderman Webster, whatever he did that thy. But listen to him. There was a greater offence against the borough of Warrington than that against Alderman Burgess—(laughter)—he meant Alderman Webster. There was an offence aaainst the tow, which, as far as they were concerned, was of more moment in their civic than their individual life. If it had not been for the opposition that he had spoken of, the town that day would have been richer, he thought he was right in saying, by nearly £2,000. He knew it was more than £l,OOO that was spent through the factious opposition that was never justified for a 'moment. He had been silent for a long I time, but of course those waters that had been stopped up must break out. They were coming out now; bat he should conclude with a proposition th it was worthy 'of their support. He was so disgusted with one anonymous letter that he took the trouble to call upon Mr. Brewtnall. He read the letter, and said it was unwarrantable, and he could in no way justify it, and so far as in him lay he would endeavour to expose the man who wrote it. He said he would consult his partner, and from him he received a letter which he considered a most insulting and annoying letter, and entirely uncalled for, refusing to give him the name of the writer or anything of the sort; and he was left to his own means to discover who the man was. There was an old story that—"lf thy neighbour conspire against thee "—this was one of a lot of proverbs he had been in- venting—" give him rope." (Laughter.) He gave him rope; and what did they think he found at the end of the rope ? The "pink circular." (Laughter.) That unique ! document was at the end of the rope, and the result was that ' notwithstanding all the denials that had been made respect- ing that circular, there was a certain conviction in each man's breast as to where it came from. He would say no more. He mentioned no names; they must think what they liked about it. He wanted to call attention to the fact, and it was in a great measure the question that would have to be decided that day, as to whether they were to be the independtnt legal representatives of Warrington' or whether they were to be written down by the Press. (Hear, hear.) That was the question. (Hear, hear.) He did not object to his friend Dr. Mackie coming into the Council. On the contrary, he was very glad to see his portly figure. But they know of Dr. Mackie he must say, speaking from Shakespeare, that Re speaks plain cannon, fire, and smoke, and bounce, He gives the bastinarlo with his tongue; Our ears are cudgell'd. Zounds we never were so bethumped with wortl,% (Laughter.) That was all very well. He was quite at liberty, and was fully entitled to do it. But they should bear this in mind, that their carefully- considered speeches were not fully reported—(hear, hear,)—while the Doctor's eloquence was beautifully garnished. He did not want to speak of anything without coming to the point. He would illustrate what he was say- ing with a fact, and as they went on they would find it very interesting. The discussion about the Town Hill—(lau.ghter and a voice: "Pig Hill ")—Pig Hill. If they would read the proceedings in the local Press they would find that no gentleman was fully reported—that his utterances in a great measure were ignored. But what was uttered by Councillor Dr. Mackie was set forth at full length, altbough tin speech he made reflected upon speeches that had gone before,which were not at all reported. Well, that made it look rather foolish. (A voice: "It's a shame.") That report was waund up by a letter—he forgot the signature, there were so many, saying honourable men, and he contended they were honourable men who voted on the question in a contrary direction to Dr. Mackie, were— But he would read the names :—Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Webster— Councillor BURGESS: I rise to order. Are we in order in discussing the question of Pig Hill and Dr. Mackie? Alderman DAVIES: We are. Alderman HARRISON: It is most absurd. Councillor BURGESS: I ask the Mayor's opinion—l ap- peal to the Mayor. The MAYOR : It is perfectly in order. Alderman DAVIES : If the Mayor will allaw me for a moment—in reply— The MAYOR: I may say this: Alderman Davies is re- ferring now to matters that took place at the Council. Councillor BURGESS: I only wished to know whether he was in order or not. Alderman DAVIES then proceeded to read the names as follow:—Aldermen Holmes, Burgess,:iWebster, Harrison, and Kean; Councillors Sutton, Platt, Litton, Greening, Barker, Pierpoint, Jeans, Woolfall, Taylor, Brown, Fran- comb, Collin, Ashton, Wright, Whittle, and the worthy Mayor. They were described in the letter, in the same paper he believed, or the one immediately subsequent, as the "dirty party of Warrington." Councillor MACKIE: Is that in a letter? Alderman DAVIES: Yes. Councillor MacKtE: Can you say positively? (Address- the Mayor.) Allow me to say that as you are allowing the earacter of the " Waryington Guardian" to be discussed

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 11, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 11, 1882.

here it may lead to proceedings for which I will hold you responsible. Alderman DIMS: You have so well conducted the affairs of the Council, Mr. Mayor, that we will back you up. (Applause.) Now came the question as to whether he was going to be mayor. Let him tell them that so far as his domestic position was concerned it was impossible for him to be mayor. He was sorry to say so, and he was sure they would be sorry too—(hear, hear) ; but in discussing the question as to whether he would be mayor or no, the first consideration with him was whether it would be to the advantage of the town. It was not a question of personal ambition, and it had no right to be so. He asked himself I was it desirable, and at one time he confessed he did think I it was to the interest of the town that he should be proposed and elected as mayor ; but when it was suggested in the local Press that he was promot- ing the Manchester Ship Canal scherne for the purpose of the canal going through his ;own property—("Shame ") —he said, aid he repeated, that it appeared as if he was promoting the scheme not for the interests of the town, but for his own private interests; but being on the Engineering Committee he suggested that it should take another course, and it hardly touched his property. But it was suggested whether he was not likely to sell the present interests of the town in the promotion of the scheme. Taking all these circumstances into considera- tion it was not desirable he should be mayor. On the contrary, he thought some man should be mayor whose present interest in the navigation of the river was a matter of identity with the town itself. (Hear, hear.) Now he could not help but call attention to another letter, and he would say this, he did not think the time of the Council would be thrown away if they could, by their action that day, show the Press of Warringtoa that they were determined they would not be over-ridden by anybody in expressing their independent views. (Hear, hear.) In one letter it had been suggested that the Mayor himself received a recommenda- tion fort the purpose of passing it at that Council, and he was described as a good, easy man, who would not look for himself in proposing a resolution in the interests of the town. That was a reflection upon the Mayor, who he knew at all times thought twice before he acted, and when he did act meant to be determined in what he did. He had not a word to say against Alderman Harrison or Dr. Mackie in their private capacities; but in their civic capa- cities, and when they came into conjunction, he had a per- fect right to doubt many things they did. In their private life they might be as honourable as other men; but when they came into conjunction, and Dr. Mackie in his paper was attempting to thrust upon them any man, that Council pat its foot down and said, "We won't have it." (Hear, bear.) That was the position of the Council • and low to wind up what he bad got to say. There had been frequent references made to Sir John Rennie's report. That report was given to him in that hall ten years ago, and that report contained some valu- able information, setting forth ably and well what was the condition of the free navigation of the river Mersey to Warrington. At this date it was a document of infinite use, and was in the hands of the promoters of the Manchester Ship Canal in the interests of Warrington. Who paid for that report? Who were the men that promo- ted that report ? If there was a man of them living in the town that man he would make mayor of Warrington that day if he could., But they were dead and gone. They were great men in their day. They were the Littons, the Croe- fields, the Clares, and others who were described as mer- chants in the good old days, and who, he must say, sup- ported by my Lord Winmarleigh, who was then Colonel Wilson Patten, were striving as much as in them lay, with all the disadvantages Warrington then possessed, to push forwards its interests. He thought, who was the man who represented these old families ? He tensed round and saw his friend Captain Litton. Captain Litton was the man for mayor of Warrington that day, and he hoped and felt that either be or sotne other representative—he did not care who he was—politics had nothing to do with him that day —would be elected. Captain Litton was the man he pro- posed, and he believed he had a right to expect, that if Captain Litton would stand, as he hoped and prayed and implored he would, they would elect him to be mayor of Warrington, when they expected the Ship Canal to go through Warrington, and make the town five, ten, aye, twenty times greater, and, commercially speaking, a great and magnificent city of which the citizens might be proud. (Applause.) Mr. Councillor Litton here rose, and was abut to offer some observations, when The Mayor and Mr. Alderman Burgess interposed. The Mayor gave way to Mr. Alderman BURGESS, who said there was a proposi- tion before the meeting chich had not yet been seconded. He, therefore, rose for the purpose of seconding the propo- sition put by Mr. Alderman Davies, that was that Coun- cillor Litton be appoiated Mayor for the ensuing year. He had never attempted to do anything in the whole of his life in that Council Chamber, which was more gratifying to his own feelings. Councillor Litton was a worthy repre- sentative of the families of the Litton's and the Clare's of past days. Councillor Litton had in that chamber shown himself so thoroughly independent that he was persuaded the Council would confer honour upon itself by electing him Mayor this year. He had heard and listened with a great deal of attention to what had fallen from Mr. Alder- man Davies, and to what he had said of the attempt, and more than the attempt, he (Alderman Burgess) was not afraid to say, to coerce the Council through the instrumen- tality of the press. The press was a grand institution, as they all knew, when used legitimately it was perhaps about the grandest institutions that they had ; but the press when it acted, as it did sometimes act, was, he was afraid, not unfrequently an instrument of tyranny that was intolerable. It was for them in that Council chamber to determine whether that condition of things had arisen in Warrington, and if so, to put their foot on it, and to put it down. It was for them to be their own judge as to the way their proceedings should be conducted, and to admit of n 5 influence in their proceedings that was not in accordance with the fair rules of debate. They ought to take care that they were not influenced by anything which took place out- side the Council chamber. (Hear, hear.) He should not attempt to detain them. Enough had been said on that sub-' ject ; they all felt it, and most of them rather acutely. There was only one point he was disposed to contest with Mr. Aid. Davies, and that was in taking credit to himself that he was the best abused man in Warrington. (Laughter.) He did not think Alderman Davies was entitled to that proud distinction. He thought he had a better share of abuse than Alderman Davies, and that he stood pre-eminent yet. (Laughter.) He did not care if he had more of it. He did not seem to loose any of his natural vigour in consequence' This, however, he did say, if they were to be criticised, let it be done in a fair and proper spirit and manner. He seconded Mr. Councillor Litton's nomination with great gratification to himself, and he sincerely hoped Councillor Litton would allow himself to stand in nomination. Councillor letrro,s said he bad a few words to say on this subject. He was very much obliged to the gentleman who had proposed him as a fit and proper person to be the Mayor, and also to Alderman Burgese for supporting it; but he had ne time, nor had he the inclination, to devote to the duties of the office. He followed an occupation which took up the whole of his time, and it was quite out of the question for him to entertain the proposal. If it were passel he might be placed in the disagreeable position of having to refuse, and if it came to the extreme he would pay the fine rather than accept. The MAYOR: I must ask Alderman Davies and Alderman Burgess if they withdraw the nomination after what they had heard from Councillor Litton. Alderman DATIES : I am pained to hear from Councillor Litton that he cannot see his way to accept the nomination. If he has fully made up his mind I cannot force him, but I thought after the appeal which I have made that perhaps Captain Litton would stand. I must withdraw if I cannot get him to stand. The MAYOR: Will Alderman Burgess do the same? Alderman BURGESS: Yes, I must, certainly, if Alderman Davies does so. Councillor Moenes said he rose to prop:is:3 a gentleman whom he believed would be acceptable to the Council. He should not enter into any lengthy remarks as to what had transpired in the Council, beyond this: He had now been a member of the Council some 15 or 16 years, and during that period of time he had observed its members, and the man- agement and conduct of its business. The name which he begged to suggest to them was a name, he was happy to say, which fulfilled one of the conditions required in the Coun- cil Chamber, and which he hoped would be accepted that day—a name of a gentleman whose family had 'pen con- nected wall Warrington for many years—a family which he believed was intimately connected with the drawing up and the cost of the report to which Alderman Davies had referred—a family remarkable Mr its liberality and public spirit. He referred to the name of Crosfield. (Hear, hear, and prolonged applause.) He begged to suggest to them time name of a gentleman as a fit member for the position of Mayor of the Borough—their friend Mr. Jobs Crosfield, whose public spirit, and whose enterprise in connection with Warrington, he thought, no member of the Council, or any person outside, would question bra moment. To his father he was sure Warrington owed a great deal—to' the liberality of his brother, whom they all knew, they were almost entirely indebted for their valuable park; and to their friend himself, in whatever light they viewed the matter, whether they took it ia active benevolence or of the most exemplary character, or in connection with the educational interests of the town, they would find Mr. John Crosfield eves ready to promote the best and trtest interests of the town. (Hear, hear, and applause.) And, therefore, in asking them to elect' him that day, he was asking them to do a duty which they would be exceedingly pleased to perform. Mr. Crosfield, if chosen, would perform the functions of the Mayoral office not only with great credit and honour to the town, but also to himself. He had referred to education. He knew that to Mr. Crosfield's munificence entirely they owed a very large increase of accommodation at the elementary school known as People's College. If they were to have a school of art, he thought to his munificence it must ha ascribed—certainly the initial step must be credited to him by his gift of £l,OOO. He understood that the committee were about to erect a school of art, which would be worthy of the fame of the school and of the borough, and he thought it would be fitting that Mr. Crosfield, as Mayor of the borough. should have the pleasure and honour of opening it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had referred to the ereetion of a school of art. But he should be sorry to base Mr. Crosaeld's claim exclusively and entirely on this thing. He believed the paramount interest of the members of the Council to select the most fitting member available, and he felt that in Mr. Crosfield they had a man who would not only he impartial but would give the Council the benefit of a busi- ness training extending over more than 40 years, and be was satisfied that the interests of the town would not suffer

in his hands. (Hear, hear.) He therefore begged to nominate, and he did it with great satisfaction, Mr. John Crosfield as Mayor of the borough. Councillor GREENING remarked thst he had great pleasure in seconding the nomination of Mr. Crosfielu. He had no idea of doing so when he came into the room, but he was very much pleased indeed that Mr. Crosfield's name had been mentioned. He was sure the Council would be doing a very good thing in electing Mr. Crosfield. As Mr. Monks had said, Mr. Crosfield was an old inhabitant of the town; and his father and family generally had done many things for the benefit of Warrington. He was engaged in trade in a very extensive way, paying a large amount of wages, and his connection with the better interests of the town entitled Mr. Crosfield to the honour of chief .magistrate. He had now been a member of the Council six years successively— (" More ")—and for semis years previously he also occupied a seat in the Council. It was his opinion that the Council would do well in electing Mr. Crosfield for the position of mayor. He had great pleasure in seconding the motion. Councillor BURGESS said he came to that meeting pre- pared to support the nomination of the gentleman who was , selected a few nights ago by the whole Council. He came Ito support Alderman Davies, and he was rather surprised to find that Alderman Davies's name was no nominated. At the meeting referred to Alderman Daviest was the only name offered; now was mentioned the names of Litton and Crosfield. As Alderman Davies was not nominated, he should think it his duty to vote for Alder- maw Harrison. (Hear, hear, and applause). He did not hesitate to say that the feeling of the townspeople was very strong in favour of Alderman Harrison—(hear, hear)—but in spite of the feeling that he had with regard to that fact; feeling as he also did, that Alderman Davies was the best man the Council could put in the chair, he had exerted his influence in favour of Alderman Davies. He was certainly rather surprised at the line which Alderman Davies had taken in proposing Mr. Litton's nomination. Mr. Davies had referred to a great many things which had been done in the Council Chamber, and he fiad made it a great objection against Alderman Harrison that he had opposed the pur- chase of the gas works in Warrington. He must point the attention of the Connell to the fact that Alderman Harrison was not the only gentleman nominated for the mayoralty who opposed the purchase of the gas' works. The only other name nominated was Mr. Crosfield, and Mr. Crosfield was quite energetic in opposing the gas works. He did not think he should be justified in supporting the name of a gentleman who was only proposed for the first time that day. If he had been proposed at the preliminary meeting, he should have been disposed to take the matter into consi- deration. As he had said on more than one occasion, there was no one he should like to see in that chair more than Councillor Crosfield, becattse he thought he was in many respects a very fitting man, but at the same time Alderman Harrison had been in the Council 13 years, anel for that alone he had some claim upon the office. He thought the members of the Council would see their way to place Mr. Alderman Harrison in the chair. Conneiller MACKIN said he rose with peculiar feelings, indeed. It so happened that at this time last year the Mayor in the exercise of his authority per- mitted an attack to be made upon the newspaper with which he was connected. That newspaper, of course, was not pre- sent to defend itself, except through him, and he cautioned the Town Council at that time that whatever provocation it chose to give him in the future he should never appear there as the defender of the Warrington "Guardian." Why Mr. Davies that morning should haye taken the course he had done, he could not understand. In speaking of the "Guardian" in such an unkind, ungenerous, nay con- temptuous manner, he had shown that he had changed his opinion very much within the last three months. Further than that, he would not be tempted to goon the present occa- sion, because until he saw the words in print, and was able to know whether Alderman Davies alluded to him personally, or to the newspaper he represented, or to any other newspaper. It might be that he alluded to others. He could simply say, speaking from memory, that there had been no letter in the "Guardian" during the time that this election had been discussed that in .the slightest degree was worthy to be characterised by those phrases which Mr. Davies had chosen to apply to them. To prove that statement he would reprint every one of them, and if any rude, unkind, ungenerous, or unfair word hau appeared, either when he had been absent or present, he would make a humble apology for it; but if, on the other hand, he had simply ventilated questions for the good of his town—the town to which he owed everything, and the town for which he had done some- thing at any rate in his day. (Hear, hear, and applause.) When he came to Warrington, he found them without either any newspaper printing machine, reporter, or editor. It had been his profit that he had found all these, hut at the same time it was something to appeal to his fellow- townsman for. And now let him dwell upon two or three things which had no connection with the "Guardian." Mr. Davies choosed to start in the history of his public life with the Town Hall. When he wrote his biography he went back fifteen years before that, an he could tell them of a public market, a cemetery, paving and sowering that he supported, and everything that had been done in Warrington, except the purchase of the , gasworks, and that was crone in his absence. He (Aldermanl Davies) told them of a Town Hall and claimed the glory of it, and insinuated that Mr. Harrison and the "Guardian" had something to do with opposing it. (Rear, hear.) He (Mr. Mackie) denied every word of such an insinuation. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Nay, what was more, he was editor then alone, and he reiterated what he then stated, that Mr. Joseph Davies had nothing to do with the discovery of ' that hall being put up for sale to the pablic of the town or applied for it directly or indirectly, for the whole thing was done by that ever-to-be-lamented and never- to-be-forgotten man, Mr. Henry White. He would turn them to the day, date, and page of the "Guardian," years before the time, when Mr. Davies held a mach simpler office in that chamber, when Mr. Henry White came to him (Mr. Mackie) in the exercise of his discretion, and wished him to ventilate the purchase of the hall. He oppose the pur- chase of that building? Heaven forbid ! Was not his in- terest bound up in everything that would make the future of Warrington ? If there was one thing more than another he had striven for during the past twelve months, it had been to throw open those beautiful walks and places in the park, not keeping theta sacred to a mere score of aldermen and councillors. (Laughter and applause.) His interests were not bound up with a three years' lease in the Council. , His interests were beund up in leaving a name in csnneotion with his daily occupation that he could boast of; and he was thankful to be able to point to every page of the "Guardian" for the past 30 years and to say that they would find written up in it the interests of Warrington, whatever the interests of individuals might be. Alderman Davies had referred to somettling or other that_ Mr. Brewt- nall said or did. Why that gentleman's name was dragged there he did not know. Then his (Mr. Mackie's) letter to Alderman Davies, which was to be read, but was not read. Why that should be brought there he did not know,—(hear, hear)—but he had no dou'st that Mr. Brewtnall—a gentle- men who had not the same experience of Warrington and Warrington men as he had wiaen he said he would show the letter, did so inadvertently. It had been his boast up to the present hour, and many of them knew it to their cost, and many of them to their ad- vantage, that under no temptation, under any bribe, under any possible coercion, had he ever given up a name yet. (Rear, hear) Alderman Davies and Alderman Burgess and many others in the town knew it well, and if it was to he brought against him as a town councillor that he did not hand over some letter to the impertinent curiosity of Alderman Davies, he gloried in it. (Laughter and ap- plause.) The MAvora : I most say that if there is BO much noise at the end of the table, I shall—l don't know what I shall do. (Laughter.) Gentlemen, I must ask you please not to be so loud in your applause; it is quite unnecessary. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Mac Ken (continuing) said: Thank heaven, there was always someone to fall back ; upon besides a mere-- well, he would not finish the sentence. (Laughter.) There was a charge made that his,speeches were better reported than others. (Hear, hear.) tie appealed •to the reporters present, those of other newspapers, besides his own, if that charge was true. He appealed to his own reporters in the face of three or four present, if ever they heard him, under any circumstances, say " report me" and "cut down my opponent." He challenged everyone of them present to say that he had done that: mean and contemptible would be the act—(leear, hear)—and what was more w3uld cut the throat of his own newspaper. ( Hear, hear.) He iras not afraid to report their speeches, and, reply to them, but if it was his fault to talk longer and plainer than seine of them, who contented themselves with mere interjections, why should he be blamed for it ? Alderman Davies had been reported all the ceuntry over by him. He had been reported in the day, and even in the night by hint, and no man had found greater kindness and assistance at his hand. He was sorry to find Alderman Burgess joiaed in the sneer. Ho had a poor memory when he forgot that when the great clique of Warrington turned upon him, and poured contempt upon him, because he was only a tradesman, the " Guardian " stood by bun through thick 'and thin, and compelled the magistrates of that day to admit him as chairman at the quarter sessions. (Hoar, hear.) There were other members of the Council, ex-mayors and others, whose cause he had fought in fact, except on the present occasion, he had always been fighting in what had turned out the successful side, and that day it would be the,same. An attempt had been made 0 throw a bane of contention between the Mayor and him- self. Heaven forbid that! They had known each other a long time, and he had had oecasion to do good service, as he (the Mayor) had to do him. Why should the phrase that the Mayor was a "good easy man" be turned to his (the speaker's) disparagement? He supposed he wrote it. It was a fact that he Was a good and easy !natl. (Laughter.) There was no doubt about it; but it was also a fact—and remember it vras forgotten—that Mr. Alderman Davies put -into his (the Mayor's) hands last week, or was instrumental in puffin.. into his hands, a motion which made over the rights and liberties of Waerington in the river Mersey for all time to the Tidal Navigation Company. ("No, no," from several parts of the room.) He (Alderman Davies) never told the Council that. The MAYOR : I will just say that Mr. Aid. Davies did not give me the resolution, and I have never spoken to him or seen him about it. (Applause.) Councillor MacktE: Will you tell me who wrote the resolution ? The MAYOR: The Town Clerk handed it to me, and I agreed. with it. I never saw Alderman Davies on the matter, and he never spoke to me about it. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Councillor MacirsE: You don't need to hear, bear, him so very soon. When he got up at that table and called'

the attention of the Council that they were selling them- selves, who was the first to get up and interrupt him ? Alderman Davies, who attempted to make out that the thing was all right as it was, but immediately Councillor Crosfield got up and spoke, he was down on his knees before them. (Loud laughter.) On his knees he went ! (Laughter.) Alderman DAVIES: Pardon ma a moment— Councillor MACKIE : I didn't interrupt you, sir. (Laugh- ter.) Alderman DAVIES: I want to make an explanation. Councillor Mackie has made a mistake—l won't say he has told an untruth. He says I challenT,ed him and said that it was all right as it was. I never did anything of the sort. _ _ _

I simply said- Councillor MAMIE : I appeal to you, Mr. Mayor, for fair play. The MAYOR (to Alderman D ivies) : Speak later on. Alderman as.yins : Very well! Councillor MACKIE : Speak next week if you like. There

were four or five gentlemen arose, Alderman -Davies amongst them, and declared there was no necessity for his (the speaker's addition. He had noticed the matter a month previously. If there was anything in it be was the original discoverer, not Councillor Crosfield ; but the latter was sharp enough to see it, and he made the remark that great minds thought alike. ( Laughter.) This discussion was not his fault. Alderman Davies had opened a story about. a

scarlet letter, or whatever it was called. They would remember at that time last year in the Council meeting, when he spoke for the first time, he was asked to pledge himself and the several hundred printers of the

" Guardian " that they had not printed that letter on his premises. He dared to do so, and he demanded in writing that the Town Council would go and inspect the proofs that they were able to give, that such a document had never been printed at his place. Alderman Davies and several other aldermen came; and they were presented with such proofs as they said convinced them that the letter had not been printed at his office. But we would tell them what convinced them more. He said "I will put

down £2O if you will put £5 or £lO each, and we will offer such a reward as will discover the writer of the letter if he is between heaven and earth." There was not one of them who would put down sixpence. Not one! (Loud laughter.) They accepted his word then, and he never dreamt that Alderman Davies or anyone else harboured a thought in their minds, but that he had cleared himself; and that he should be twitted twelve months after with such a nasty

thing as that was. He did not need to do it with letters; he could write articles. There was a clique in the Council, he was sorry to say—he was sorry Alderman Davies had put himself second in it—and the gentleman who sat at the head of the table (Councillor Crosfield), and had been proposed by some gentleman—what did he do that day twelve months? A nasty, dirty thing that was intended as an attack upon him, but which nobody would have believed it referred to him. He sent a letter to another newspaper that he might damn a man above himself. That was what Councillor Crosfield did, and he put

his name to it. He (Councillor Mackie) spoke about it at the Council meetinc, as a dirty trick. It was not ten days before that he had written a letter recom- mending that Councillor Crosfield should be made Mayor. Ha was a man who up to that point he had respected, but since then he had suspected. (Laughter.) If they were going to have these things discussed in that room, be sure that they would find their match in him. (Laughter.) He was not afraid of the whole of them. He did not wish to drag his newspaper in, but he would fight for himself. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Crosield knew that he had given him many a good lift in going through life. (Laughter.) He had spoken and written for him. There was not one of them who had held the ' Mayoral chair but had received a welcome from the "Guardian," and thanked when they bad left it. It was, no doubt, a hard thing for Alderman Davies to know that he had smashed the Conservative party in the town. (Hear' hear.) It was a hard thing to know that he would be disowned by them for many "a !ono day, until 1, he came with a white sheet around him, and made proof

of his repentance. (Laughter.) Why should he come down upon him? It was not a month since be took a most infa,nous letter sent to him, and sent it to a news- paper, with his name attached, with a desire that it should be printed, because it reflected upon him. He never did such things. He erased what was nasty and dirty in a letter, and there was not a man in the town who had been written about that he could not shake hands with that day. (Applause.) Alderman DAVIES : I sent you a copy of the letter, and you weuld not put it in. Councillor MACKIE : That is not the question ; certainly not. You sent me an infamous letter. You got it inserted in another newspaper entirely on your awn account; and you aught to have known it was infamous. (Hear, hear.) He now came to the question of Alderman Harrison's nomination. Mr. Councillor burgess had put last Friday's meeting in such a plain and business-like way that he would dwell upon it no longer. A mine has been at- tempted to be sprung upon them this day., and if the mere

election of Councillor orosfield in Alder*Man Davies's place had bees all that was wished for, it might have been done without the introduction of any of these angry feelings. Alderman Davies knew well enough that if the highest office in Warrington was vacant now, that of member of Parliament, any office in fact accept that of _Mayor, he (the . _ . _

speaker) would willingly propsse or second laim for it 'He had ability, bnt he knew that as Mayor of Warrington, and as a director of this company, he never could have acted pro- perly. It was beyond the power of an angel to do it, and that is the only reason he had opposed him, and would con- tinue ts do so. He would oppose any set of gentlemen trying to rule the Council in the way they had been trying for a long time. (Hear, hear.) He was prepared to call their attention to the fact that the greater number, far more than half, of the first-class men who hare been mayors of the borough, with one solitary exception, and he did it for political reasons, were contented to serve but once and re- tire. But what had been the fact of late years ?—that they had only had ten men kept out of the Council through re- elections in 35 years, that was since the Council was formed, but they had had no less than six of these men kept out of the mayor's chair during the last ten years. If Alderman Dories had been elected that day he had not the slightest doubt that he would have gone in for _three

years. It :would not be vrorth his while to do anything else—(laughter)--because the Queen I would not coma to open the decks under three years. ' (Leughter.) He would be glad next year, or the year after, to see him Mayor, but net this year, when the bargains have to be made—about buying and selling land and rights. If this sort of thing had gone on, in 14 years they would have simply had five or six new men brought into the office of Mayor. What is the whole theory of the Municipal Corporations Act? It Iva:, as they knew, to bring forward the best men who were prepared to act as Mayor, aid as I chief magistrate afterward, and as Chairman of I the Watch Committee, and, if necessary, to head the police if a riot were to break out. (Applause.) Thirty- three out of 36 first-class men retired from the Council in the first ten years. Why? They found the principle of —he would not say cliques, coteries, and caucuses existed, for they were ugly words—but the principle of governing by little parties had been introduced, and it had gone on, year by year, until it had arrived at the state that during the last ten years they had only had four new men in the mayor's chair. Was that the way to grow mayors? Was that the way to encourage young men to give over wasting their lives in brandy, wine, and billiards? They had had some excellent young men in the Council lately, bat at the end of their short eetvice they had retired. Why? They were all excellent men, and amongst them were Councillors Ridgway, Guest, and Jeans. But these men saw nothing in the Council but a little set of six or eight men who made the ball spin round between . them, and who aleterminEd that they would have 15 years' possession of the mayor's chair between not more than six of themselves. He protested against that. It was not that he was madly in lave with Alderman Harrison that he had taken part with him. (Laughter.) He had never written in favour of him per as. He knew him to be a useful towns- man, and a man who had laboured for the Mechanics' Institution, and for other institutions, for the good of the town. He was not there for a moment to praise him be- yond measure, but he was there to say that this clique- isrn must be put an end to, or they would have na one com- ing into the Council who would be worth being made Mayor. Captain Litton, Alderman Kean, Mr. Crosfl.4ld, and Councillors Monks and Milner had been mentioned in the " Guardian" as fit to be Mayor. There were also Mr. Wallington, Mr. Pierpoint, and other men who had been in the Council a long time. Mr. Davie was not in the Council 12 years ago. Alderman DAVIT:IS: Rather more than that. Councillor 1111aCaLH said: Well, he got honoured early, and he no doubt deserved it. He wished him now every success as a director of the Tidal Company, end promised to assist in making him Mayor at the proper time, but that was not now. Of Mr. Crosield he would not say an unkind word—he never did of his opponents (laughter)—but the present year was the wrong one to put Councillor Crosfield ' in the chair, for this simple reason. The great question of navigation was now in the theses of its birth. Mr. Crosfield most unfortunately said—he would not have said it if he could have foreseen what would have taken place that ; day--

• Councillor CaOSFIELD : I should. Councillor Mectin said that was just like him—straight- forward and honest Mr. Crosfield was now befsre the public as a gentleman who had declared that the canal could not be made to pay. LCouncillor CROSFIELD : Hear, hear.] That was nothing to Councillor Crosfield's disparagement, but if they were to raise a fund to get it made, whether it paid or net, in the interests of Warrington, Mr. Crosfield was not the gentleman to succeed the Mayor in the chair. He thought there was an incongruity in it, and he should put off the day of his election, for it would come to him if he lived. That day they were writing history for Warrington. Those who came after them would read what they had been saying, and some would blush at many things that had been said- that day, and said with- out cause. But there would be "'none of their successors who would not be glad to find amongst the records and chronicles of the Town Council of Warrington that they had assisted in that grand and glorious tidal scheme. He took the opportunity when in London of seeing several engineers about the scheme, and he found they were far more interested in it than they in Warrington were, for he supposed the money would have to come from there. But if they, with this great matter to decide, voted for Mr. Crosfield, an opponent of the scheme, and a man who declared he would not subscribe a penny, and who, no doubt, would influence his highly-esteemed brother, it would be a blow to the proposal. If he would take

his advice it would be freely offered, and it would be that he should retire for at least 12 months until the scheme is fairly floated, and for his good deeds he would no doubt receive all the honours that could be awarded
him there or in any other place. He had pleasure in supporting the nomination of Alderman Harrison as mayor. ._

6ouncillor CROSFIELD said he must offer a few observa- tions after the speech of Dr. Mackie. In the first place from the draft of the speech they had just listened to they might imagine that he was longing to get into that chair (pointing to the Mayor's seat). He begged them to understand that he had no desire whatever to be Mayor of Warrington. The state of mind that be WAS in now was such that he would _
give anything to be out of the office, and had it had only been great pressure put upon him, not by his own political friends, .but more by geutlemen on the other side—bath

„ parties had pressed him to take the office—that had induced him.to allow himself to be nominated on that occasion. If elected, he should feel it his duty to take the office, but he should take it with very mixed feelings indeed. It would be very painful to him on many accounts. Dr. Mackie had

referred to him, and about what he did against Dr. Mackie 12 months ago. He begged to say in that Council Chamber, and before his fellow-townsmen, that he had never said anything by word of mouth or with his pen that was not absolutely true. (Hear, hear.) What Dr. Mackie complained of was an expression of opinion which he (Mr. Crosfield) put into the paper by a clergyman—a minister of religion. It was not his opinion; he had never expressed any opinion about Dr. Mackie, and he defied Dr. Mackie to bring the paper before the public and to show that he (Mr. Crosfield) had. He was not a person who was fond of dealing in personalities. His desire was to go through life, and, as far as he possibly could, live peaceably with all men. (Hear, hear.) He could say there, honestly, that there was not a man in the world, or a creature, that he hated. He was thankful to be able to say that. He differed with people; he had a right to have his own opinion, and he had a right to express it; and if he had not expressed his opinion about the canal scheme he would not have been an honest man. (Hear, hear.) He could tell them, and he could tell Councillor Dr. Mackie, too, that if they were spared to live for the next five or six years it would then be found out who was correct about that. (Hear, hear.) There were a great many abler men than he who did net speak, and they knew more than be did, and held the same opinion. They had not heard the other side yet. He thought the probability about that canal scheme was that there were such difficulties in the way of getting a bill through Parliament—and Alderman Davies knew—that the scheme would not succeed. There were Walton Bridges to get through. He wanted to see a ship of 5,000 tons burden go through Walton Bridges. Mr. Alderman DASIES :Sodo I? (Leughter.) Mr. Councillor CROSEIBLD, continuing, said his opinion was the sensible scheme was to make a ship canal from Warrington to Liverpool, and if that were done he would put his hand in his pocket, and give it has much pecuniary aid as ever he could afford. (Applause.) But they could not get through Walton Bridges with a big ship, and any man who liked to go upon the river would find that out. They could not get a ship with a 75ft. mast under a bridge that was not more than 15ft. high. It would take a cleverer fellow than Mr. Alderman Davies to do that. (Laughter.) Mr. Alderman DAVIES : I admit it, Mr. Crosfield. You cannot put a pint of ale into a quart bottle. (Loud laughter.) I mean a quart into a pint pot. (Renewed laughter.) Mr. Councillor CROSPIELD, continuing, said he only wanted to say that he was not going to blow his own trum- pet. If he exercised his own feelings he should retire from the position he was in now, and go out of the Council alto- gether. It was only for a feeling of public duty—a duty he owed to his town and townsmen—that he stood there that day. (Hear, hear.) He did not think, laying everythirg else aside, that the fact of his expressing an opinion about the canal scheme was an objection,because he had expressed an honest opinion, which might be of some value some day in some manner that was not at present seen ; and if the scheme did turn out as he expected, and if the canal was made from Warrington to Liverpool, he should subscribe as much as ever he could. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. Alderman KEAN observed that .the tone running through the speeches they had just listened to was keep omit Harrison, but he hoped they would, by giving that gentle- man a majority of votes, keep him in. Mr. Alderman Har- rison had been very useful, and his services as a Guardian and chairman of the Board of Guardians reflected great credit upon him. He deserved their, best thanks and best support that day. He accorded Alderman Harrison his own support without in any shape or form saying Mr. Coun- cillor Crosfield was not a fit and proper person for the office, but Mr. Councillor Crosfield would be more helped if he waitod'a little. (Laughter.) Mr. 'Councillor BROADBENT asked to be allowed just two or three minutes to make a very few observations' because as Warrington people dined in the middle of the day, he knew many of them were anxious that the business there should be finished. He only returned from London the previous night, and was extremely glad to hear that Mr. Councillor Crosfield had consented to allow himself to be nominated as mayor. He knew very well from what he had said that Councillor Crosfield had no personal ambition to occupy the civic chair, but he was exactly one of the kind of men that ,they wished to bring forward as mayor of that as well as other boroughs, and the difficulty had generally been to get such men to stand. He (Councillor Broadbent) thought that considering their position that day, members should be more cireful about making promises before they knew of the conditions to be placed before them. He had had a circular, an anonymous circular, asking him to go to a meeting of the friends of Mr. Alderman Harrison. He had himself told

Mr. Harrison that he should be sorry not to be con- sidered his friend, but he had no idea of going to the meeting so called. He also heard that the meeting was largely attended, more largely attended than was expected by mem- bers of the Council. He believed four members of the

Council were present. (Laughter.) He repeated it was unwise for members to give promises until they knew what was to be brought before them. With regard to Councillor Crosfield, his own position and that of lics family had been very properly re- ferred to by Mr. Councillor Monks. M. Crosfield was present, though he need not listen; but he (Mr. Broadbent) held there was no family in Warrington who had done so much, or was more respected than his family: and as, as a cynical French critic said, " gratitude was a lively appre- ciation of favours to come," he thought they might live to. see other favours come from the same quarter. Mr. Cros- field was a gentleman who would make a valuable meyor of this borough at the present time; and, as this was not a I party question at all, he believed that every member of the Council—both Conservative and Liberal hoped that Councillor Crosfield would allow himself to be brought for- ward as mayor of the borough. With respect to the Ship Canal, Mr. Crosfield's honest expression of opinion that ha did not think it would pay, might be right or it might be wrong, but he thought they all respected Mr. Crosfield for that honest opinion. • He had at the last Council meet- ing stated that the river was to him worth £l.OOO a year, and had pointed out its value to Warrington, which was overlooked by some, and tkat being the case it was i-ery fitting that Councillor Crosfield should be appointed mayor during the time of these negotiations, because they must be sure that the interests of Warrington, and the interests of the free navigation of Warrington, would be watched by:him in the Act of Parliament about to be applied for. He was thankful that Mr. Councillor Crosfield had allowed himself to be brought Torward as mayor of the borough, because he had done a good deal for Warrington, and he would be a credit to those.who elected him. (Applause.) Mr. Alderman HARRISON said that before the Mayor put the election to the vote, he should just like to say a few words, because it was the only opportunity he should have. He wished to impress upon the Council most particularly that he had never thrust himself forward as a competitor for the office of mayor. He had never asked a single per- son to vote for him, not a single person had been asked by his request, nor had he any art or part in calling a meeting to promote that object. He wished to tell them how he came to be nominated at all. A certain number of gentle- men, representing both political sections in the Council, had waited upon him and asked him to permit himself to be nominated or the mayoralty. They said that Mr. [ Aid. Davies had, at a private dinner party, expressed his I willingness to be nominated, and that kind of thing should • not be perpetuated. They said that he had obtained his spurs before he had won them, and that if he (Alderman Harrison) would promise or allow himself to be nominated, and would fight the thing out to the end, they should be very glad to support him. His then [ said that he would fight not for the office of Mayor; but for this principle which it was considered was involved, and endeavour to do away with that system which had been in existence so long. Under those circumstances a promise was extorted from him. The object of those who waited upon him was to discard usurpation by a few, and to introduce a better state of feeling in the Council—a policy of fair play and honourable treatment without aldermanic usurpation. If anything was calculated to degrade a body of men, it was a partial mode of distributing favours, which every man had a right to expect if his qualifications fit him. He was not a candidate for the office, or a competitor for it in any way. He placed himself entirely in the hands of the Council, whose prerogative it was to decide. Whatever the Council did would meet with his complete approbation. He should shed no tear if he was not elected, and he should shed no tear if Mr. Councillor Crosfield was elected. He yielded to no member in his respect for Mr. Councillor Crosfield's private character. He believed Mr. Councillor Crosfield was a public benefactor to War- rington, an honourable man in every sense of the word, one whose word would be his bond under all circumstances ; and if he had known that Mr. Councillor Crosfield had the I slightest desire to be mayor of Warrington, his own name I would never have been put in opposition to his. He was sorry that so good a man should be used for such an ignoble purpose as that of perpetuating a system which ought to have no place in the Council. He should say no more be- cause he could not trust himself. He had only intended to be a silent observer, but could not refrain from saying what he had done. The MAYOR said he should vote for "whom he considered would be the best man for the interests of Warrington, and he would support the man who he thought would add dignity to the chair, and Would also be beneficial to the in habitants of the town. (Hearahear.) He had known Mr. Harrison many years; and he had known Mr. Crosfield more years tan he cared to mention; but he be should like to ask Mr. Crosfield one question, as the answer thereto would in a great measure influence his vote. Mr. Crestield hitherto had been a strong party man,. D the time he (the Mayor) had had the honour of Ming that chair he had always endeavoured

lad to keep politics out of the chamber; and he should be g. g if Mr. Crostleld would answer this question: " SuPP4TI4 you were elected, would you bring party politics „ this chamber, or would you act impartially (at I have done) between both parties?" (aid Councillor CROSFIELD, in answer to the question, he could assurs the Mayor and Council that if 110:13i5 elected to be mayor of the borough, he should make it rule to act as impartially as the present mayor had done' he (Mr. Crosfield) had a leaning either way, he shoultl.o7.. inclined to lean against his own party. He shoul4 feel hi, to self contemptible if he made use of his position of nlaY°' further his own political party in any way. The Council then divided, with the following tesul". For Alderman Harrison: Aldermen Thewlis, Webster, all Kean; Councillors Mackie, John Pierpsint, Hutchingn Burgess, Wright, Bolton, Francomb, and Litton-11. Councillor Crosfield : The Mayor, Aldermen liolmesT-r:i., ' gess, Davies, and Chandley; Councillors Broadbent, lila) Dakin, Monks, Greening, Brown, Woolfall, Dison, Barker, Wm. Pierpeint, Wallington, and WhittleDP-7hr =Alderman Harrison, and Ccuucillors Crosfield and "
did not vote.

The MAYOR afterwards said: I beg to announce that 12 have voted for Councillor Crosfield, and 11 for Alder Harrison. I have to declare that Councillor Crostiel° elected Mayor for the ensuing year. (Applause.) 0031 Alderman Pickrnere then retired to the committee r ,e with the newly-elected Mayor and other members of t7l Council, and Councillor Crosfleld having been ioves„A with the robes and chain of office, returned to the Cea" Chamber and took the chair amid applause. Having made the usual declarations, enr The Masora said he must thank the gentlemen we- ~or, posed and seconded that he should fill the office of 313.1ba and he must also thank the members of the Council:lbl) voted for him. He could only repeat wba"hold said before, that he did not seek to Id the office, and that he took it in great doubt. But he do his best. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He would (13ii best to perform the duties of chief magistrate of the bot°„,'s; and he promised them that he would act as impartiellithe he possibly could. (Hear hear.) He had said at one °' previous meetings of the Council that there was no (15311. amongst the many good qualities possessed by the Mayor, which he more admired than that of his impartiall%!,, He had admired it in him more than lid ,thing else during the last three years, aste it would be his (the Mayor's) endeavour to inl'fief his excellent example. He had now lived, as knew, in Warrington for 50 years, and his interests were bo'l,, upon the place, and it would be his endeavour to do evee:if', thing he could to premote the welfare of the town. 011,0 hear.) He should not let the strong political opinions he held—many people thought him a much etrolo partisan than he was—he should not let them influenq bto in any degree on any questions which might arise 113 TOOI Council Chamber. He should endeavour to treat member with courtesy and consideration. (Hear, bear.) hoped that they would not have too long speeches. ( e hear.) He had a dread of long speeches, and therefore's' would not trouble them any longer. (Hear, hear, and i° applause.) biel Alderman HARRISON asked if the Mayor would alloW the privilege of saying a word or two. He begged to tlaro-y every gentleman who had been pleased to pay him the 700 pliment of voting for him, and he wished to sae,' t° tool gentlemen who did not vote for him, that he left that!ieaft without the slightest trace of animosity on his part. (13e.iee hear.) He also wished to say what a pleasure it wol him to sit under so estimable a man as Mr. Croeisv Mayor of Warrington. (Applause.) Me and '- Alderman Pickmere was appointed deputy-mayor, Rev. W. Quekett chaplain. Shortly afterwards the Council adjourned, but met 113er on te appoint the various committees for the year.

ST. HELENS. upi j This movement, which was inagurated in St. fortnight ago, under the direction of Mr. MurphY, ua'A carried on with signal success. Nearly six thonsan".,oo ribbons have been donned, a large proportion by P. `;;01, who have not hitherto been either advocates or pract's`sideo temperance. On each evening there has been 01203eilf meetings which have been addressed by local gent including the Rev. Canon Carr, Rev. R. J. Ward, IteTioel' Chaplin, Rev. J. W. Walker, Huyton, and Mr. H. L.ev fc'r On Wednesday afternoon a meeting was held specloo women, at which there were present between feceijoifeo eight hundred. On the same evening a lecture was 7,011' before an immense audie4ve by Dr. Anderson, of Vice'', 0 on the "Medical aspects of the temperance questioll'efii which he showed both by precept and experiments Wog, effects of alcohol on the human body. On each evertipro, large and well organised choir is present, and sings As fusion of popular hymns. Mr. Murphy, it is believe"' hold his last meeting on Sunday or Monday evening.
