WIDNES BRANCH. The annual meeting of the Widnes branch of the Primi- tive Methodist Home and Foreign Missions was held in Hutchiason-street Chapel, on Tuseday evening. Mr. Shuttleworth occupied the chair, and on the platform were tke Revs. J. Morton (superintendent minister, Warrington), J. Crompton, F.G.S., and Mr. Bray. The weather-was very unpropitious, but there was nevertheless a good audience. A hymn having been sang, the Rev. J. Crompton offered up prayer. 1 The CHAIRMAN said he was thankful that he had another opportunity of meeting with his friend Mr. Morton on the missionary platform. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to meet him in this place, as he had done in other places in days and minths and years gone by. He was glad to be identified in any way with so great and noble a cause as that they met to advocate that evening. (Hear, bear.) It was a cause for which all Christians, he thought, should be fully devoted. He could not understand how a Christian could be still in the work of Christ. He should be glad to see the missionary spirit existing more strongly than it seemed to do at the pre- sent time. He had seen in days gone by when their chapels would be crowded on missionary meeting night (hear, hear)—more than on any other occasion; but Christians of the present day seemed to have lost their interest in this great and noble work, whose aim was to bring abeut the glorious tims when the kingdoms of the world should become the kingdoms of ear find, and of his Christ, and when he should have the heathen for his inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for his dwelling place. How seldom in the present day did they hear Christians saying "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do ?" He exhorted them 'o be more deeply earnest in reference to those with whom bey were surrounded, and say 0! for a trumpet's voice On all the world to call. To hid their hearts rejo'ce In Him who died for all.

(Applause.) The Rev. J. MORTON read the third annual report, from which it appeared that the missions were prospering in Australia, Canada, and Africa, as well as at home. The nuenber of home stations was 63, places 392; colonial stations 176, places 829; foreign stations 4, places 6; total, 245 stations and 1,227 places. The number of home mis- sionaries was 100, colonial ministers and miesionaries 2n5. Foreign : European and African 6; total,-.311. The gross smount of missionary money contributed on the home Wiens was £16,501 2s lid; on colonial stations £1,419 105 Td; South Africa (for Church work), £520 73 91; total, £18,441 is 3d. But besides this there was raised for schools, building chapels, and sustaining misssionaries, the sum of £16,784 us 5d ; total, £35,225 12s 8d; being an-increase of £215 lls 9d for the year. The total increase of members for the year on home and foreign station and colonial dis- tricts was 1,253. Mr. BRAT said whatever might be thought of missions now, they would all be prepared to admit that there had been very dark and very evil days; when religion was almost at a discount, when piety was not fashionable, and when drinking and profane swearing were the accomplish- ments of gentlemen. If a man embraced religion he was termed a hypocrite; if a woman did so, a fool. Missionary societies were repudiated by the Church, and eyed with great suspicion by the officers of the Crown. Robert Man- drake was refused the consecration of his fortune to the cause of Christ in India, and other men in their efforts to convert the Hindoos were driven from British territory, and had to seek assistance from a foreigu power. And those who organised missionary societies a few years back did so with the anxiety and prayer of her who cradled her infant in an ark of bulrushes and committed him to the waters of the Nile and the provi- dence of her God. So they saw that rank and power had been arrayed against everything that had for its end the glory of God and the salvation of men. But the times had changed some little. God had touched the heart of the Egyptian and he had adopted the outcast as his son from the dens and holes of the earth. Religion had found its way into the mansions and palaces of the great and noble; infidelity assumed a Christian-like aspect; iniqeity was ashamed and made to hide his face. If a man embraced re- ligion he was no longer opposed to the spirit and stream of the age. Nothing of the kind—the times had changed, for which they were thankful. Yet caution was very neces- sary on their part, since it was looked upon as very fashionable indeed to be religious. Mr. Bray made an appeal for aid to the missions, remarking tbat there were many families of the earth, who, it asked what their hopes were as regarded eternity would scarce be able to answer. Yet all these people were certainly under a law of righteous- ness, which said the soul that sinneth shall surely die. It was their duty to endeavour to save these by the Gospel, I and if they did what they could they would see the work of the Lord revive and, transporting thought, the thousands whom they would never see in the flesh, and thousands that should be called into being when they would have returned to -their fathers, would bless the instrumentality that had 1, been put forth for the extension of the Gospel of our God and Lord Jesus Christ. (Applause.) The Rev. J. CROMPTON then addressed the meeting. He said when they considered that Primitive Methodism had only been in existence about 70 years, and had 200,00 church members, and that last year had an increase of about 6.000 church members, he thought they were progress- ing. (Hear, hear.) Let them remember, too, all the lay preachers, class leaders, and Sunday school teachers they had, and they would agree with him that they had got -a mighty army of workers, who ought to form a grand bise of operations from which they should move forward into the territory of the enemy, and perform -a mighty work in the name of the Lord. Big drums and fife bands would not convert people to Christ. They must have the Gospel. He did not obj, et to ringing bells to bring people to chureh ; he would not objeet to a band to call the atten- tion ef the people to what they were going to say. If they liked, tike an instrument such as the bellman had, and go individually and ring the bell to call attention, and then tell their story; but never be led to the opinion that the simple noise of shouting and drumming would be enough to reach the hearts of the people—(hear, hear,)—to renew the con- sciences of people aild purify the minds, control the passions and expel the devil from tbe human heart. (Hear, hear.) Our Lord Jesus Christ gave men the command, "Go ye out into the world and preach the Gospel." Preach the Gospel! They must not forget or deviate from that; and whether it be in Widnes or anywhere else, at hOme or abroad, if they must reach the hearts of people and weild an influence for good that should be co atinuous and permanent, it must b 3 by the word of the Lord. (Hear, hear.) It must be by the truth as it was in Jesus. The rev, gentlemen concluded by a reference to the universal adaptibility of the Bible to minds of men, and resumed his seat amid applause. A collection was then male, and the proceedings concluded in the castomary way.

Mr. Alderman PANTIES seconded the resolution, and ob- served in doing Se that if the names of any germ tlemen who Would like to att upon the committee had been omitted the committee sectild be most ready and willing that those gentlemen should join them in their labours. He had been very much struck by the fact that in ancient history all the towns and cities which were alive to this day in name were cities that had grown up on the sea coasts, and were ports ; and he found likewise that those towns that were made cities and were not on the sea coast, were cities that had been built by despotic princes, and brought about by what was termed slave labour. He repeated that the great cities they read of in ancient times were on the sea coast, and had the advantages of being a port; but as civilisation advanced in England trade progressed and manufactories grew, and it was a fact that the large manu- facturing districts in and around Manchester—the population of the district being five and a half millions, including our own town—had been brought about by the most strenuous efforts, and by the aid of manufactures almost alone. If that could be done without a port, slut, he asked, would have been tile result with a port ?.Why, that these five and a half millions would have been developeci.to a very much larger number—beyond the conception of any of them in that room. As regards himself, he asked " How is it I have taken this warm interest in this scheme ?" and he replied "Why should not every man in Warrington take a warm in- terest in it ?" Warrington, like sister towns and cities, would benefit, and it seemed to him Warrington should not stand idly by, but put her own shoulder to the wheel. (Hear, hear.) The fact that they Came there in their crowds showed that they were determined not to be behind in the race, and that Warrington was going to be equal to the other towns around. (Applause). • Perhaps there was a special reason why he supported this scheme, and it was this : In that very house before it became the property of the town, Lord Winonarleigh, in parting with some of his heirlooms, gave to him a document which was prepared in the year 1833. It showed that the merchants and manufacturers who were then to the fore in pushing on the interests of the town celled in the services of an engineer. Sir J. Beanie, with the view ef seeing what could be done to improve the navigation of the river, so that it might be more extensively used by the people residing in the town of Warrington. Sir John Rennie thought the work could be aone by the people of War- rington, even then, and surely now Warrington, with three times the population and five times th 3 wealth of Sir John Rennie's day, would not be behind in joining heartily in the work now and doing its share. They had nothing to fear in this scheme; and he might tell them that he held in his hand a letter from the Provisional Committee, written in acknowledgment of the resolution passed by the Council, in which they said they would be glad to meet the representatives from the Corporation for the purpose of considering the claims of Warrington. (Applause.) A month ago it was well established what' the rights of War- rington were,—that vessels drawing eight feet of water were allowed to pass up the river free; and these would be free as heretofore. (Applause.) He was pleased and proud te push forward this scheme, which he believed would do so much good for the town. (Applause.) The resolution was put, and carried unanimously. Captain RHYNOLDS moved, "That Messrs. Lewis Voisey and Walter Milner be requested to act as honorary secre- taries." He observed that the names of those gentlemen would- be a guarantee that they would be very good secre- taries. He might say that he thought an opportunity now occurred for Warrington to take up those advan- tages which in past years she had lost. They had now an opportunity, he hoped and believed, of getting cheaper rates for all goods manufactured in Warrington, which was very necessary if they were to compete with the manufac- turers of other countries. (Applause.) He had no doubt the committee they had appointed would strictly watch the rights of Warrington as well as promote the furtherance of the Canal, and they had a very important duty to perform. Captain Lirrosr seconded the resolution, which was car- ried. Mr. Alderman DAvirS said the committee would be glad to receive the assistance of the workingmen, and in fact it was an instruction to the local secretaries to enlist the sympathy of the workingmen in this matter. LATEST NEWS.
The Crown Princess of Germany is expected in England

to-day. The new Dean of Windsor, Rev. Canon Connor, was formally installed yesterday. Mr. Herbert Spencer was entertained at dinner yester- day evening by two hundred of the leading citizens of New York.
_ The Freeman's Jourrial says :—" We are authorised to state that there is no foundation for the statemeut that the
Under-Secretaryship for Ireland has been offered to The O'Connor Don."

The Press Association Newry correspondent telegraphed intelligence had reached there that the Rev. Father Mc Gurk, parish priest of Belleek, County Armagh, was shot yesterday morning. Sir Henry Ripley, Bart., who represented Bradford from 1874 to 1880, died on Thursday night at Bedstone, his Shropshire residence. Deceased was aged 68, and was the head of a large dyeing firm at Bradford. Lloyd's agent at Lowestoft telegraphs that the Maria Josephine, brigantine, of London, Captain Smith, from Shields to Whitstaple laden with coals, struck the Leman Sand, on Thursday, and foundered. Three hands were drowned. The remainder were saved, and landed at Lowestoft. After the Salvation Army demonstratioa at Hereford, on Thursday night, the mob followed General Booth's cab to Black Marstone, hooting and yelling, and finally smashed the windows of the house in which he was staying. The rival army denies all knowledge of the outrage. Yesterday morning, Philip Abbis, aged 60, a roadrnan, in the employ of the Rowley Local Board, died under shock- ing circumstances. For some time deceased has been in a desponding state, and during the temporary absence of his family he drank a quantity of hot water through the kettle spout, which caused him to sustain shocking internal injuries. He afterwards died in great agony. Yesterday morning, Mr. Pickard, of lia.rnsley, as secre- tary of the recent conferences held at Manchester, issued a circular to the various districts in the United Kingdom call- ing a national conference to be held at Leeds, on Tuesday, December sth, for the purpose of thoroughly discussing a restriction of the output of coal, so as to enhance the prices of coal and wages of the miners. All districts are requested to send delegates prepared to vote on the subject. At Blackburn, yesterday, Henry Richard Crouch, draper, was charged with stealing £63 worth of goods from a former employer. On certain days when the prosecutor was away from home, the prisoner was engaged to look after the shop, and he took advantage, it was said, of the opportunities to send parcels of goods to his own premises. He was also charged with robberies at two other establishments at which he had made purchases. He was committed for trial at the Preston Sessions. By Her Majesty's command, two men of each battery, troop, and company, engaged with the army in Egypt, have been selected for decoration at the hands of Her Majesty at the forthcoming review, and their names are requested to be sent to the War Office. It is expected that the whole of the officers attending the review will be personally decorated by the Queen, and the same favour will be extended to the Indian troops. The men selected will be, as far as possible, men who took part in the battle of Tel-el-Kebir. The Central News understands that Admiral Dowell, first in command, and Admiral Francis Sullivan, second in command of the Channel squadron' have received orders.to be present at the review to be held in London by the Queen on the 20th inst., together with a contingent of the Channel squadron to represent the Navy, and those vessels which took part in the Egyptian cam- paign.

div.head: CLAY CROSS EXPLOSION.
div.p: THE CLAY CROSS EXPLOSION.

The Press Association Alfreton correspondent telegraphed yesterday :—Up to nine o'clock this morning 33 bodies had been recovered, and it was estimated there were still ten in the pit. These would be in the cross-cut workings, and nearly two miles from the bottom of the shaft, which the exploring party were unable to descend. THE FLOODS.—FATAL ACCIDENT NEAR CHESTER.

The residents of the houses alongside the river Dee have been driven to take refuge in the upstairs apartments. A family at Shoclach were beset by the waters which dashed so violently against the house that they signalled to some boatmen to come and bring them off. An old man named Parker gallantly put out with his boat, but he had only pro- ceeded a short distance when it was completely engulphed, and he was drowned. DUBLIN AND SIR GARNET WOLSELEY.

At a Meeting of Liberal burgesses in Dublin on Thursday night, the proposal to confer the freedom of the city on Sir Garnet Wolseley was strongly condemned. One speaker said if things came to a crisis in Ireland they would probably have some of Sir Garnet's exploits along the canal and a Tel-el-Kebir outside the city. Sir Garnet I was described by another speaker as "an Egyptian butcher."

div.head: STRIKE AT GLASGOW.
div.p: THE STRIKE AT GLASGOW.

FRESH ARRIVAL OF MANCHESTER WORKMEN. Another batch of workmen from Manchester, to fill tho places of the joiners on strike on the Clyde yards, arrived in Glasgow yesterday. At the railway station they were divided into three detachments, and were taken in convey- ances, accompanied by policemen in plain clothes, to different yards on the river. They were not molested on this occasion by the men on strike. THE REPRESENTATION OF PRESTON. No candidate other than Mr. Tomlinson is yet before the electors. It was expected Mr. Raikes would apply for the Chiltern Hundreds yesterday and immediately lie has done that the Conservative committee will, it is stated, issue the address of their candidate, who is rumoured to have con- sented to stand, and who is said to be a member of the family of one of the Conservative leaders. Mr. Tomlinson I is at Preston, but he is waiting the resignation of Mr. Raikes to begin his campaign. An effort was first made to get Lord Randolph Churchill, to fight, but this has failed.

WIDNES PRIIIIONERS AT LITEEPOOL QUARTER SESSIONS. —At the County Sessions held at Liverpool, the prisoners from Widnes were dealt with as under :—Robert Connor an old mai, was indicted for wounding, on the 24th Oct., Patriek Howlett at Widnes. Dr. Coalmine, M.P., prosecuted. It was stated that the prisoner and the prosecutor were in the same lodging-house. On the night of the 24th October, the prisoner, who was in drink, commenced to abuse the prosecutor. The prisoner took a knife, deliberately com- menced to sharpen it, and making use of a threat, said he would stab the prosecutor. He thereupon made a blow at the prosecutor. The latter jumped up, "dodged "the blow, but was stabbed in the hip. The prisoner's defence was that he was abused, and was drunk at the time of the occurrence. He was convicted, and sentenced to 4 months' imprisonment. —Patrick Quinn (14), Edward Duggan (12), and Thomas Leigh (10), were each sentenced to three days' imprisonment and ordered to be flogged for bovine., at Widnes, on the 13th of August, broken and entered the warehouse of John W. Wareing, and stolen therefrom us 9d, a canvas bag, 36 post- age stamps, and 100 cigars.—Five boys, Jeseph Carey (14), William Lavin (10), Thomas Devereaux (9), Thomas Feeley (10), and Peter Mitchell (11), were charged with stealing 7s from a shop at Widnes, and there were other small charges against Carey and Feeley. Carey was sentenced to three days' imprisonment and twelve strokes of the birch, and all the others to a similar term of imprisonment and eight strokes of the birch.

James Fair- dough &Sons. of Warrington, to SELL BY PUBLIC) AUCTION, on MONDAY NEXT, NOVEMBER 13th, 1882, the STEAM SCREW FLAT " Pilot," of Warrington. The following are a few par- ticulars respecting the " Pilot," viz. : length over all, 72ft.; beam, 14ft. Gin.; burthen, 56 tons, at a water draught of sft. 21n. forward and sift. aft. She is fitted up-w!th Brotherhoods' three-cylinder engines (20-horse power) and boiler complete, quite new, and in good condition. She is also well found as regards anchors, chains, ropes, &c., &c., and fitted up quite ready for work. The sale will take place in the Old Quay Dock, Runcorn (on board the flat), where she is now lying, at 2 for 3 o'clock prompt. The Auctioneer wishes it to be distinctly understood that Messrs. Fairclough's only reason for disposing of the fist is that her carrying capacity is to small for their increasing trade, and that, consequently, they have been obliged to build a larger steamer to suit their requirements.
